## STANDARD OF REVIEW

BCO 39-3 outlines certain principles that should guide any review of the judicial
proceedings of a lower court by a higher court. It states that these principles are "to
insure that this Constitution is not amended, violated or disregarded in judicial process."
We think principles 2 and 3 therein are particularly pertinent in setting a Standard of
Review in this case. Therefore, we set them out in full below, to-wit:

### BCO 39-3(2)

"A higher court should ordinarily exhibit great deference to a lower court regarding
those factual matters which the lower court is more competent to determine, because of
its proximity to the events in question, and because of its personal knowledge and
observations of the parties and witnesses involved. Therefore, a higher court should not
reverse a factual finding of a lower court, unless there is clear error on the part of the
lower court."

### BCO 39-3(3)

"A higher court should ordinarily exhibit great deference to a lower court regarding
those matters of discretion and judgment which can only be addressed by a court with
familiar acquaintance of the events and parties. Such matters of discretion and
judgment would include, but not be limited to: the moral character of candidates for
sacred office, the appropriate censure to impose after a disciplinary trial, or judgment
about the comparative credibility of conflicting witnesses. Therefore, a higher court
should not reverse such a judgment by a lower court, unless there is clear error on the
part of the lower court."

The Session was charged in the decision in Case 97-9 with the instruction that, "until satisfactory evidence of repentance is given to the Session of Christ Covenant Church, to impose such conditions concerning Dr. Shive's involvement in the life of Christ Covenant Church as the Session may find." (ROC 35).

This instruction places the responsibility and burden upon the Session of Christ
Covenant Church to determine when and how Dr. Robert M. Shive exhibits
"satisfactory evidence of repentance". To judge a man for repentance, the judges
should be very familiar with the man. This case is an example of one in which the
higher court should exhibit great deference to the lower court. The Discipline
Commission of the Session of Christ Covenant Church voted unanimously that Dr.
Shive did not exhibit such repentance. The Session of Christ Covenant Church voted
unanimously that Dr. Shive did not exhibit such repentance. The Judicial Commission
of Central Carolina Presbytery voted unanimously to affirm the Session's judgment that
Dr. Shive had not exhibit such repentance. Central Carolina Presbytery voted 47 to 6 to
affirm the Session's judgment that Dr. Shive had not exhibited such repentance. These

<a id="ga29-p123"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=123 printed_page=94 -->

<u>Issue 4</u>. "Were there procedural and substantive errors committed by Central Carolina Presbytery in this case which require a remand in this case?"

Judgment 4. "No. We do not find that errors were committed by Central Carolina Presbytery requiring reversal and remand."

This clear and unambiguous language in defining the issue and stating the judgment shows without question that Dr. Shive's interpretation of the decision in SJC Case 97-9 was in error.

Issue 5. "Did Central Carolina Presbytery err by affirming the decision of Christ Covenant Church Session's infliction upon Dr. Robert M. Shive the highest censure based on the Record of the Case?"

Judgment 5. "Yes. Central Carolina Presbytery erred in affirming and the Session of Christ Covenant Church erred in going straight to the highest censure of excommunication in light of the lack of compelling evidence in the Record of the Case to reflect that Dr. Shive is contumacious or impenitent. See BCO 30-4 and 33-3. Pursuant to BCO 42-9, we reverse <u>that portion of the judgment</u> by the Session of Christ Covenant Church inflicting the censure of excommunication on Dr. Shive, and we remand the matter back to the Session of Christ Covenant Church for it to impose the censure of indefinite suspension from the Sacraments upon Dr. Robert M. Shive in accordance with BCO 36-5, and with the instruction that, until satisfactory evidence of repentance is given to the Session of Christ Covenant Church, to impose such conditions concerning Dr. Shive's involvement in the life of Christ Covenant Church as the Session may find." (Emphasis added).

In this judgment in Case 97-9 there is absolutely no language that gives any indication that the four guilty charges against Dr. Shive were reversed or remanded. Only "that portion of the judgment by the Session of Christ Covenant Church inflicting the censure of excommunication on Dr. Shive" was remanded to impose the censure of "indefinite suspension from the Sacraments upon Dr. Robert M. Shive". We think the language is clear and unambiguous that the verdicts of guilty were not changed nor reversed and the findings of guilt of Dr. Shive remained in force. Only "<u>that portion of</u> the judgment" dealing with censure was remanded. The penalty was reduced from "the censure of excommunication on Dr. Shive" to the censure of "indefinite suspension from the Sacraments upon Dr. Shive". There is no language in the judgment that affects any other part of the decision by Christ Covenant Church. We conclude that the sin and guilt were not overturned by the decision in SJC Case 97-9.

That the sin and guilt were not overturned is further evidenced by the recommendation of indefinite suspension from the Lord's Supper as well as by further instructions "that, until satisfactory evidence of repentance is given to the Session of Christ Covenant Church" that the Session has the right to impose any further "conditions concerning Dr. Shive's involvement in the life of Christ Covenant Church as the Session may find."

<a id="ga29-p124"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=124 printed_page=93 -->

1. SJC Manual 11.11 (2) II defines "a Statement of the Issues" as a concise framing by the Court of the specific issues being judged in the case.

2. SJC Manual 11.11 (2) III defines "the Judgment" as a definite conclusion rendered on specific issues being judged.

3. SJC Manual 11.11 (2) IV defines "the Reasoning and Opinion of the Court" as the explanation by the Court of the resolution of disputed facts and reasons for the judgment rendered.

4. It thus seems to us that the heart and decisive portion of any Judicial Decision is: its "Statement of the Issues" and "the Judgment."

The Summary of the Facts is defined as "a presentation in chronological order of
the relevant history and facts that bear on the case," and the Reasoning and Opinion of
the Court simply deals with certain facts and factors as they are applied to the principles
set forth in the Book of Church Order and SJC Manual. We therefore suggest that after
looking at the whole case, a person should center on the heart of the case which is "a
Statement of the Issues" and "the Judgment." We think the failure of the Appellant, Dr.
Robert M. Shive, to properly interpret the decision in SJC Case 97-9 is a failure to
center on the clear and unambiguous language stating these specific issues being judged
in the case and the definite conclusions rendered on the specific issues. Dr. Shive
interpreted the SJC decision in Case 97-9 that the "decision clearly challenged and
struck down the allegations" of the Session and reversed the verdicts of guilt on all four
charges. (ROC 56-57). On the other hand, the Discipline Commission of the Session of
Christ Covenant Church stated its interpretation of the decision, as follows:

.. In so doing we are working with the understanding that General Assembly, based on the Record of the Case, has altered the censure of excommunication to indefinite suspension. Neither Presbytery nor General Assembly have overturned any of the Session's judgments with respect to your guilt..." (Emphasis added).

We think Dr. Shive misinterpreted the SJC decision in Case 97-9 and the Discipline Commission of the Session properly interpreted it. This is supported by the interpretation given by Dr. Paul Gilchrist in his letter of April 16, 1998 (ROC 61) in which he stated the following, to-wit:

"... First the heart of the decision is in II. STATEMENT OF THE ISSUES and III. JUDGMENT IN THE CASE... the SJC did not reverse the charges of sin and the finding of guilt against Dr. Shive..."

Two of the panel members on SJC Case 97-9 confirmed that interpretation. We concur.

In the light of these facts and factors, we suggest we look at Issues 4 and 5 and Judgments 4 and 5 in SJC 97-9.

<a id="ga29-p125"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=125 printed_page=92 -->

On July 11, 2000, a Panel of the SJC held a hearing in Charlotte, N.C., at which it heard the oral arguments of both Appellant and Appellee, framed the issues in this case, voted unanimously for the judgments, and announced these to the parties.

### II. STATEMENT OF THE ISSUES

1. Did Central Carolina Presbytery err by affirming Christ Covenant Church Session's interpretation of the Judgment of SJC Case 97-9 (<u>Robert M. Shive vs</u>. Central Carolina Presbytery) that the guilt of Dr. Shive was not reversed but affirmed as to the 4 charges of (1) sexual immorality, abuse, and licentiousness
- **(2)** premeditated sexual exploitation, (3) lying and bearing false witness, and (4) scandalous living?

2. Did Central Carolina Presbytery err by affirming the Session of Christ Covenant Church's decision to increase Dr. Shive's censure from indefinite suspension to excommunication?

### III. JUDGMENT

1. No. There is no mention in the Judgment in Case 97-9 (26th GA Min. p. 137) that the guilt of Dr. Shive was reversed on any charge. Thus the guilty verdict of Christ Covenant Church Session stands unchanged on all 4 charges. The penalty of excommunication was recommended to be changed to indefinite suspension from the sacraments. With this recommendation, the Session complied. Hence the guilty verdict of the Session in SJC Case 97-9 remained unchanged.

2. No. The Judgment in SJC Case 97-9 gave the Session these instructions:

that, until satisfactory evidence of repentance is given to Session of Christ Covenant Church, to impose such conditions concerning Dr. Shive's involvement in the life of Christ Covenant Church, as the Session may find." (M26 thGA, p.137)

Thus, Central Carolina Presbytery did not err in affirming the action of the Session of
Christ Covenant Church in imposing the censure of excommunication on Dr. Shive
after the Session determined that Dr. Shive had not given "satisfactory evidence of
repentance." Central Carolina Presbytery properly followed BCO 39-3(2) in giving
"great deference to a lower court regarding these factual matters which the lower court
is more competent to determine." We do likewise.

### IV. REASONING AND OPINION

### INTERPRETATION OF A JUDICIAL DECISION

Since there was a "fundamental disagreement" between Dr. Shive and the Session as to the interpretation and intent of the SJC in its decision in SJC Case 97-9, we think it would be helpful to delineate some of the principles involved in a proper interpretation of a Judicial Decision. Of course, one must look at the entire decision, Facts, Issues, Judgments, and Reasoning and Opinion. We know that each judicial case contains the four items mentioned above. We suggest that it would be helpful to see how the SJC Manual defines certain of those items. For instance,

<a id="ga29-p126"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=126 printed_page=91 -->

the timeliness of filing was made by Central Carolina Presbytery; and we make no issue of it in this decision. The issue of timeliness of filing was raised by motion at the July 17, 1999 meeting of Central Carolina Presbytery; but the motion failed and a motion was passed assigning the appeal to a 6 member Judicial Commission (ROC 79).

This Judicial Commission heard the appeal of Dr. Shive on September 21, 1999, rendered its decision and submitted it to Central Carolina Presbytery on October 23, 1999 (ROC 113). The decision of the Presbytery Judicial Commission was unanimous (ROC 89).

This recommended decision of Presbytery's Judicial Commission was affirmed and approved by Central Carolina Presbytery at its October 23, 1999 meeting by a vote of 47 for and 6 against (ROC 113). The decision adopted by Central Carolina Presbytery appears in full in ROC 10-14. These are the Issues and Judgment stated in Central Carolina Presbytery's decision:

### <u>Statement of Issues</u>

1. Did the Session of Christ Covenant commit reversible error in its December 17, 1996 conviction of Dr Shive?

2. Did Christ Covenant clearly err by not carrying out the expectations of the General Assembly in the appeal of Robert M. Shive v. Central Carolina Presbytery (Case 97-9)?

3. Did the Session of Christ Covenant err when it proceeded from the censure of indefinite suspension from the Sacraments to the censure of excommunication on April 13, 1999?

### Judgment in the Case

1. No. The Session'$ 1996 judgment of guilt was affirmed by the Presbytery, the SJC, and the General Assembly. Although the SJC Panel identified errors in Dr. Shive's trial, none of the four original charges were reversed. The highest court did set aside the censure of excommunication in favor of a less severe censure appropriate for a guilty offender willing to work toward repentance. (BCO 36-5)

2. No. Although we have reservations about the method used to assess repentance in this particular case, there is no clear error on the part of the Session in its efforts to implement the highest court's decision.

3. No. The Session of Christ Covenant did not err when it proceeded to the highest censure in 1999. Suspension from the Sacraments is designed to be a "temporary exclusion." (BCO 30-3) After more than two years, Dr. Shive remained unwilling to admit guilt on 3 of 4 charges. The Session had the authority to increase the censure under BCO 33-3.

On November 19, 1999, the Office of the Stated Clerk of the General Assembly received the Appeal of Dr. Robert M. Shive from the decision of Central Carolina Presbytery.

<a id="ga29-p127"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=127 printed_page=90 -->

Whereas, Dr. Shive appealed the Session's judgment and censure to the Presbytery (where it was sustained in full) and then to the General Assembly, and

Whereas, General Assembly in its January 19, 1998 ruling sustained the judgments in the case but, deeming the censure of excommunication too severe at the time, did reduce the censure to indefinite suspension, instructing the Session to attempt to bring Dr. Shive to repentance through a deliberate course of shepherding, and

Whereas, in submission to and compliance with the ruling of General Assembly, the Session did engage such a course with Dr. Shive communicating the plan, expectations and possible results to Dr. Shive in writing (reference attached letter to Dr. Shive dated March 6, 1998), and

Whereas, through a series of correspondence and meetings with Dr. Shive during the Spring, Summer and Fall of 1998, a Commission representing the Session failed to bring Dr. Shive to a point of admission of guilt and repentance to the particulars of the judgments against him (with the exception of the judgment of scandalous conduct), and

Whereas, the Session, now at what it considers an impasse, does consider Dr. Shive's condition to be incorrigible and contumacious,

Therefore, be it resolved that the Session of Christ Covenant Presbyterian Church does impose the censure of excommunication upon Dr. Robert M. Shive. This censure is to be imposed by the Session's Executive Discipleship Commission in a meeting with Dr. Shive at a date and time to be determined by them but before April 1, 1999."

The Session of Christ Covenant Church Session unanimously adopted this recommendation and notified Dr. Robert M. Shive by letter of March 18, 1999 (ROC 75), which letter stated:

> "Therefore, it is with soberness and solemnity that the Christ Covenant Session has considered and approved the following resolution:
>
> (Then follows the exact recommendation of the DC and Executive Discipleship Commission above quoted.)
>
> At a Stated Executive Commission meeting on April 13, 1999, as directed by the Session of Christ Covenant Presbyterian Church, the sentence of excommunication was imposed on Dr. Robert M. Shive (ROC 76).

By letter of May 1, 1999, received by the Stated Clerk of Central Carolina Presbytery, Dr. Robert M. Shive gave notice of his appeal of the Session's decision to said presbytery (ROC 19). There is a handwritten but unsigned note on ROC 19, Dr. Shive's letter, indicating "Received June 7, 1999". This would have been more than 30 days from May 1, 1999; but in Dr. Shive's letter to the Stated Clerk of Session of Christ Covenant Church, dated July 13, 1999, Dr. Shive states that his appeal of May 1, 1999, was received by the Presbytery Stated Clerk on May 9, 1999. This would have been within the 30 days from April 13, 1999, allowed for notice of appeal. No issue of the

<a id="ga29-p128"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=128 printed_page=89 -->

Dr. Gilchrist cautioned in his letter:

"Please understand that this is my opinion only, but by copy of this to the Chairman and Secretary and two Panel Members (of the SJC) they may wish to correct or add to this opinion." (ROC 61).

There is no evidence in the ROC that there was any further communication from or to Dr. Gilchrist, TE Aquila or RE Leopard by the DC or by Dr. Shive.

At a meeting of the DC of Christ Covenant Session on December 14, 1998, a "Status and Course of Action with Dr. Robert Shive" was unanimously adopted (ROC 71-72). This memo began:

> "It has been right at one year since the appeals process initiated by Dr. Robert Shive with respect to the judgments and censure of Christ Covenant's Session against Dr. Shive completed their course through Presbytery and General Assembly (Case 97-9). The final outcome of these appeals was to sustain the four judgments of guilt but to change the censure of excommunication imposed by Christ Covenant to indefinite suspension."
>
> This memo then recapped the DC activity in this case in compliance with General Assembly's expectations, listing dates and actions. This memo concluded with an action taken on October 27, 1998, as follows:

"The Commission's conclusion is that barring a definite work of the Spirit, we should recommend to the Session that Dr. Shive be excommunicated." (ROC 72).

On February 5, 1999, the DC, unanimously adopted its "Recommended Disposition of the Discipline Case for Dr. Robert Shive" for submission to the Executive Discipline Commission of Christ Covenant Church (ROC 73-74).

This document ended with a formal recommendation as follows:

"Whereas, the Session of Christ Covenant Presbyterian Church, after a comprehensive trial on December 17, 1996, found Dr. Robert M. Shive guilty of sexual immorality, licentiousness, premeditated sexual exploitation, lying and bearing false witness and scandalous living, and

Whereas, Dr. Shive pled innocent and defended himself to that end on all charges, and

Whereas, the Session, due to the heinous nature of the sins and Dr. Shive's refusal to acknowledge guilt to any, did assign the censure of excommunication, and

### 18. PROCEDURES FOR ASSUMING OF ORIGINAL JURISDICTION OVER A MINISTER (BCO 34-1)

18.1 Upon proper receipt of a case filed against a minister under BCO 34-1, the SJC shall in accordance with the provisions set out below:

- **a)** Appoint a panel in accordance with RAO 15.3 to investigate the matter and determine whether or not that the case is in order, i.e., that the provisions of BCO 34-1 have been followed.

- **b)** If the case is determined to be in order, the panel shall conduct an investigation of allegations against the minister under the provisions of BCO 31-2.

- **c)** The panel's findings and recommendation shall be mailed to the full SJC, said minister and the stated clerks of the INVOLVED presbyteries that instituted this action under BCO 34-1. The matter shall be scheduled for review at the SJC's next stated meeting or a meeting called under the provisions of SJC Manual 3.2.

- **d)** Said minister and the stated clerks of the involved presbyteries within 14 days of receipt of the panel's findings and recommendation may submit a brief citing reasons as to whether the panel's recommendations should be approved or rejected. Such brief must comply with the requirement of Section 9 of this Manual.

- **e)** Briefs under these paragraphs shall comply with the requirements for briefs in SJC Manual 9.4, but shall not exceed 5 pages.

18.2 At its next stated meeting or meeting called to hear the matter under the provision of Manual 3.2, the SJC in closed session shall discuss the panel's findings and recommendation. The SJC shall vote to accept or reject the panel's findings and recommendation.

18.3 The SJC decision shall be mailed to said minister and stated clerks of the presbyteries. Within 14 days of receipt of the decision a party may request a reconsideration of the decision by filing a supplemental brief as set forth in Section 9.2. This supplemental brief shall state the reasons for requesting reconsideration of the decision. Copies of the supplemental brief and the SJC decision shall be mailed to members of the SJC. Reconsideration of the judgment shall be granted only by majority vote of the full Commission either by mail or by conference call, as determined by the officers.

If reconsideration is granted, the Officers shall call a special meeting, under Manual 3.2 (a) and (b), to discuss the case, consider its merits, and render a final judgment. If reconsideration is not granted, the previous judgment shall become final in accordance with BCO 15.5 (a).

<a id="ga29-p130"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=130 printed_page=128 -->

18.4 If the SJC's final judgment is that the above investigation does not raise "a strong presumption of the guilt of the party involved," the SJC shall dismiss the case and advise the parties to the case.

18.5 If, however, the SJC's final judgment is that the above investigation raises "a strong presumption of the guilt of the party involved," it shall institute process under BCO 31. In such event, the SJC shall conduct a trial in accordance with the provisions of BCO 32, BCO 35 and SJC Manual 13.5 through 13.10.

### 16. PROCEDURE FOR HEARING A MEMORIAL (BCO)

16.1  
The only memorial which the Commission may entertain is one which may  
demonstrate an important delinquency or grossly unconstitutional proceeding of  
a lower court which cannot be addressed through appeal or complaint (BCO 40-  
5).

(a.) When such a Memorial is received by the Stated Clerk, a determination shall be made under Section 10.1(a) of this Manual as to whether or not the Memorial is found administratively in order.

(b.) If the Memorial is found to be administratively in order, the Officers of the Commission shall determine whether or not the Commission should address the concerns memorialized.

(c.) When the officers decide that the Commission should not address the concerns memorialized, the matter shall be placed on the docket of the next stated or called meeting of the Commission for final determination.

16.2 A Memorial accepted for consideration by the Commission under Section 16.1(a) above may be addressed by a Panel established in accordance with RAO 15.3

16.3
The court alleged to have offended shall be cited to appear by representative or
in writing, providing such documents as bear on the alleged important
delinquency or grossly unconstitutional proceedings, showing what it has done
or failed to do in the case in question (BCO 40-5). The Stated Clerk shall collate
these documents which shall be considered the Relevant Documents.

16.4 Any hearing on a Memorial shall not be conducted as in a formal judicial case but in accordance with BCO 40-5.

16.5  
All hearings shall convene with prayer. The Panel or Commission shall then  
proceed to hear the response of the representative of the court alleged to have  
committed an important delinquency if such a Respondent is present. The  
Respondent shall have a maximum of 40 minutes to respond to the citation.

16.6 At any time during which the Respondent is presenting an argument a member of the Panel or Commission may ask questions of the parties if present; the time taken for such questions shall form a part of the response time. The time for response may be extended one time for an additional 20 minutes by majority vote of those qualified members present.

16.7 The party memorializing the General Assembly shall not present a brief nor will he be given time for argument, except to answer questions posed by the Panel or Commission.

16.8 After the response has been heard, the Panel or Commission shall go into closed session to discuss the Memorial and consider its merits.

16.9 In the case of a Panel, it shall then make a full report to the Commission including such recommendations as

- **(a)** to reverse or redress the proceedings of the court below in other than judicial cases; or

- **(b)** to censure the delinquent court; or

<a id="ga29-p132"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=132 printed_page=130 -->

- **(c)** to remit the whole matter to the delinquent court with an injunction to take it up and dispose of it in a constitutional manner; or

- **(d)** to stay all further proceedings and declare that all matters relating to the Memorial, now or previously pending before the General Assembly, are ended, concluded and terminated. 16.10 When the full Commission has completed its discussion and is ready to vote, the vote shall be taken on each recommendation. The report as a whole shall then be voted on by roll call without change or amendment. All qualified members present shall participate in the vote. 16.11 In the case of a hearing before the full Commission it shall proceed to deliberate the merits of the matter and make a determination as provided in Section 16.9 (a), (b), (c), or (d). A vote shall be taken on the decision(s). The report as a whole shall then be voted on by roll call. All qualified members present shall participate in the vote. 16.12 After a decision has been reached by the Full Commission, any member may file, within 20 days after the day the decision is reached, a concurring or dissenting opinion, which if it is couched in temperate language shall be appended to the decision. 16.13 When a report with its recommendations on the Memorial has been adopted, a copy thereof shall be mailed immediately to the parties and shall be included in the final report of the SJC to the General Assembly.

COMMUNICATION 7 From Greenville Presbyterian Theological Seminary "Regarding Concurring Opinion in John Wood Matter"

Chairman GPTS Board Communication to the 29th General Assembly of the Presbyterian Church of America, meeting in Dallas, Texas, June 19, 2001

Fathers and Brethren:

The Board of Trustees of Greenville Presbyterian Theological Seminary desires to express its concern regarding the concurring opinion attached to the report on the John Wood matter, and signed by RE W. Jack Williamson, TE Charles McGowan, TE Ben Konopa, TE Dominic Aquila, RE John White, and TE William Lyle. Our concern has to do with inaccuracies in the concurring opinion, which we hope will not become a permanent part of the Minutes of the General Assembly.

First, TE's Morton H. Smith and Joseph Pipa, who are members of our faculty, without being informed that they would be charged with any improper activity whatsoever, were defamed in the concurring opinion in a manner totally unbecoming of Christian brethren. The opinion states that if they had more carefully investigated the

130

<a id="ga29-p133"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=133 printed_page=131 -->

circumstances, they would not have brought this matter to the church. However, the chairman of the investigating panel, RE Mark Belz, confirmed to TE Pipa and to TE Smith and TE James Phillis of Western Carolina Presbytery that Messrs. Smith and Pipa had been thorough and careful in the pursuit of the charges. They had a lengthy conference call with Mr. Wood in which the entire matter regarding Mr. Wood's opinions was thoroughly discussed. Mr. Wood admitted that he told them a woman might preach. Had Mr. Wood not changed his statement to the investigative panel, they were ready to recommend that charges be brought against him. What makes this such a serious matter to our Board is that if these brethren indeed erred as the concurring opinion says, they should be charged with disturbing the peace of the Church before their respective presbyteries.

Second, the opinion said that two Greenville Seminary students were present when the woman spoke at the evening worship service of the Cedar Springs Presbyterian Church. This is not accurate. No Greenville Seminary students were involved in the John Wood case. TE Pipa has informed our Board that an older man, who had taken courses at Greenville Seminary a year before the event, heard the message at Cedar Springs. He approached both his Session and the Session of Cedar Springs and wrote Dr. Pipa to ask if he was correctly concerned. TE Pipa responded that his concerns were valid and that he should contact men in the Presbytery of Tennessee Valley. TE Pipa has had no further contact with the gentleman. He was not at the time a student at Greenville Seminary nor has he attended since then.

Third, Greenville Seminary was accused of carrying the report across the denomination. This is untrue. The seminary never was involved in the John Wood matter. Apart from the original letter, we knew nothing about it until the issue was made public.

All of these points are well documented and we hope that this letter will be taken into account if the General Assembly chooses to consider the concurring opinion. We as a theological seminary were not a party to this matter, and unfortunately it appears that the Book of Church Order of the Presbyterian Church in America gives us no technical recourse to respond to such wholly inaccurate and unfounded charges as discussed above.

We as a theological seminary are not in a position to appeal any actions of the PCA's Standing Judicial Commission. However, some of our board members who are members of your Assembly have noted that there is no provision in the SJC Manual for concurring opinions to be attached to a report on a matter. We are told that they are only provided for in connection with the adjudication of judicial cases. The John Wood matter apparently never reached this level, and thus your Assembly might wish to consider whether it is proper for the SJC to publish such concurring opinions as a part of a report on a non-judicial matter.

131

<a id="ga29-p134"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=134 printed_page=132 -->

We further note that the SJC Manual does require that concurring opinions be couched in "temperate language." While arguably the language described may not be "intemperate," it would seem that expressions which are demonstrably in violation of the Ninth Commandment should also be excluded. Therefore, as Christian brothers, we plead that our letter be considered by the Assembly if it chooses to consider the concurring opinion as part of the documents in the matter.

Respectfully yours, /s/RE John Van Voorhis Chairman of the Board of Trustees For Greenville Presbyterian Theological Seminary June 13, 2001

29-28 Report of Committee on Constitutional Business TE Craig Childs, Chairman, led the Assembly in prayer and presented the Report. After reviewing the report, the Assembly received it as information.

### REPORT OF THE

### COMMITTEE ON CONSTITUTIONAL BUSINESS

### TO THE 29TH GENERAL ASSEMBLY

### PRESBYTERIAN CHURCH IN AMERICA

- **I.** Introduction Your Committee on Constitutional Business (CCB) met one time subsequent to the 28th General Assembly, on April 23 – 24, 2001 in Atlanta, Georgia. The CCB was able at that meeting to complete all of the work then assigned to it. Attendance was as follows:

TE Craig D. Childs (03), Chair – present RE Frederick (Jay) Neikirk (04) – present TE Karl F. McCallister (04) – present RE Richard (Ric) Springer (03) – present TE Bryan S. Chapell (02) – present RE Calvin Poole, III (01) - present TE Morton H. Smith (01) – present RE John Ward Weiss (alternate) – present TE Mark Rowden (alternate) – present RE Joe B. Johnson (02) – resigned

In the absence of RE Johnson, RE Weiss was seated, by proper motion, as a voting member. TE Rowden was seated as a non-voting member. A quorum was present and the Committee convened to conduct business.

II. Minutes of the Standing Judicial Commission

1. The CCB approved the minutes of the October 19 - 20, 2000 meeting of the Standing Judicial Commission as being in conformity to the Manual of the SJC (20-5) and RAO 15 with the following notations.

132

<a id="ga29-p135"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=135 printed_page=133 -->

- **a.** The SJC's stated rationale for disqualification of some members in the adjudication process was only that those members were members of the presbyteries that were parties to the case. The CCB has previously issued its opinion that this alone is not a sufficient grounds for disqualification, even though it is likely that a member of such a presbytery would be disqualified for other related reasons (see Minutes of the CCB April 17, 2000, response to Question #5).

- **b.** There is confusion as to the Attachment referred to on page 6.

- **C.** The proposed SJC Manuel 18 dealing with "Original Jurisdiction Over a Minister", which is referenced as being amended on pages 6 & 7, is missing. If this is not a new section, then the minutes are not clear at this point.

2. The CCB approved the minutes of the March 1, 2001 meeting of the Standing Judicial Commission as being in conformity to the Manual of the SJC (20-5) and RAO 15 with the following notations.

- **a.** Although the procedures described by the minutes are in order, it is impossible for the CCB to know precisely if the procedures involved in reaching decisions are proper without the dates indicated for timely or untimely filings relative to our standards.

- **b.** There are typographical errors (“20001-20002" on page 16, and "Adjournment" on page 17).

3. The CCB approved the minutes of the conference call meeting of the Officers of the Standing Judicial Committee of March 30, 2001 as being in conformity to the Manual of the SJC (20-5) and RAO 15.

III. Non-Judicial References Reference 1 – Westminster Presbytery: Question 1 – There is a desire on the part of some within Westminster Presbytery to leave the PCA, carrying with them the cherished name of Westminster Presbytery. They do not want to simply withdraw as individual churches, but rather as a group, taking with them the name Westminster Presbytery. Can this be done in the manner proposed? If not, what remedy for these brethren do you suggest that would satisfy their desires and be in accord with the BCO?"

Response: It is the advice of the CCB in reference to the inquiry of Westminster Presbytery (4/21/2001) related to withdrawal from the PCA as a presbytery that:

- **a.** There is no provision within our Constitution for a presbytery as a whole to withdraw.

- **b.** The right of an individual church to affiliate with whomever it will, however, cannot be impinged upon by a higher court (BCO 25-11; cf.11- 3, 4). The principle of the BCO that is most closely related is that of 133

<a id="ga29-p136"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=136 printed_page=134 -->

Chapter 25-11, which allows, "A particular church may withdraw from  
any court of this body at any time for reasons, which seem to it  
sufficient".

- **C.** Should a group of churches choose to leave the PCA in order to form a new affiliation, or to continue an affiliation that they perceive as antecedent to the PCA, then they can peaceably withdraw as a group subject to the consent of each congregation in the group.

- **d.** In the event of a group of churches withdrawing from the PCA with the consent of each church involved, those congregations remaining within the bounds of that presbytery that decline to withdraw with the departing group would stay within their present denomination. Those congregations not departing would constitute the continuing presbytery of the PCA.

- **e.** There are no standards regarding continuing the name of a departing group and such matters should be left to the discretion and charity of the brothers involved. Additionally, any division of assets or attachment of corporate identity, where applicable, will need to be determined by the brothers involved. Adopted by CCB

Reference 2 -- from Eastern Carolina Presbytery re Voting Requirements: Question: Does a Session or the Moderator of a Congregational meeting have the authority to require a greater vote than that required by the Book of Church Order for the call of a pastor or for the dissolution or a pastoral relationship of for the election of a church officer? That is, may the provision of BCO 20-4 and 24-4, "a majority of all the voters present shall be required to elect," be made more restrictive? Response: It is not within the purview of the Session or Moderator to require a greater than majority vote for the election of a pastor or church officer. The BCO nowhere gives such powers to Sessions or Moderators. Allowing them to claim such power would open the door to the possible thwarting of the right of the members of the Congregation to determine those who will rule over them, a right which undergirds BCO 20 and 24. Adopted by CCB

Reference 3 -- from Southern Florida Presbytery re Divestiture: Question: Is the Presbytery required to divest Teaching Elders without call, "for a prolonged period, not to exceed three years," (BCO 13-2) and is the process of divesting a minister of the gospel in BCO 34-10 in conflict with BCO 13-2. Response: BCO 34-10 and BCO 13-2 are not in conflict, i.e., the Presbytery is not obligated to divest every minister who has been without call for three years, but the Presbytery is required to inquire into the matter and then use its discretion. Adopted by CCB

Reference 4 -- from Pittsburgh Presbytery re Minimum Voting Age: Question: May a Session set a minimum age requirement for communicant membership in their church?

134

<a id="ga29-p137"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=137 printed_page=135 -->

Response: It is the prerogative of each Session to determine when one has a credible profession of faith and a proper understanding of the sacraments (BCO 6-2). "The time when young persons come to understand the Gospel cannot be precisely fixed." (BCO 57-2) Therefore, sessions must consider requests for admission to communicant membership on an individual basis, regardless of age.

We note that the questions raised by this Reference are separate from the issue of establishing a minimum voting age for communing members, which was the issue before the 27th General Assembly.

In addition, we would point out that if a Session refuses to receive a child (or an adult) who is being transferred that person would remain a member of his or her original church. Adopted by CCB

Reference 5 -- From Great Lakes Presbytery re: BCO 58-4 Question 1: What issues or concerns should a presbytery consider when it decides whether to allow an exception to BCO 58-4 in the use of "communicants in good standing in any evangelical church"? Response: BCO 58-4 does not require the use of the exact terms of 58-4, but allows no exceptions of practice in the administration of the Lord's Supper. "The minister may either invite all those who profess the true religion, and are communicants in good standing in any evangelical church or may invite those who have been approved by the Session, after having given indication of their desire to participate." (BCO 58-4)

If a Presbytery considers receiving a TE who has expressed an exception in his views with respect to the language of BCO 58-4, then Presbytery should be guided by BCO 34-5.

Note that the Introduction to the Directory for the Worship of God indicates that BCO 56, 57 and 58 have been given full constitutional authority by the 11th GA. Adopted by CCB

Question 2: Do previous actions of the GA imply that presbyteries should not allow an exception to BCO 58-4 in the use of "communicants in good standing in any evangelical church"? Response: Yes, particularly with regard to practice. Refer to the Minutes of the 1993 GA, p. 141, 21-56, III, 18 and the Minutes of the 1986 GA, p. 330, Appendix I, 10, and the Minutes of the 1987 GA, p. 129, 15-63. Adopted by CCB

Question 3: If Presbyteries may allow an exception to BCO 58-4 in the use of "communicants in good standing in any evangelical church", may the Teaching Elder practice this exception?

135

<a id="ga29-p138"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=138 printed_page=136 -->

Response: A presbytery may allow an exception as to views, but not as to practice. Presbytery must be guided by BCO 34-5 in terms of teaching of the view. Adopted by CCB

Question 4: Since sessions have the authority over the Sacrament, what should a session do if it will not require teaching elders to use the full language of BCO 58-4 when the Lord's Supper is administered under this provision? Response: See our response to questions 1 and 3, above. Adopted by CCB

Question 5: What should presbytery do if a Session takes exception to BCO 58-4 in the use of "communicants in good-standing in any evangelical church", either in belief only or in belief and practice? Response: See our response to questions 1 and 3, above. Adopted by CCB

Question 6: If a particular teaching elder was granted an exception to BCO 58-4 in the use of "communicants in good standing in any evangelical church" at the time of his ordination or reception into his current presbytery (as applicable), does he have permission to practice it? Response: See our response to questions 1 and 3, above. Adopted by CCB

Question 7: If a given teaching elder did not previously take exception to BCO 58-4 in the use of "communicants in good standing in any evangelical church" but now does, should he make this known to his presbytery? Response: Yes. Adopted by CCB

Reference 6 From Philadelphia Presbytery re Complaints
Question 1: May a person charged with an offense or offenses, who is undergoing
process in a trial before a court, complain to the next higher judicatory about the
manner in which the trial is being conducted?
Response: A person may not make a complaint to a higher court until after the lower
court has acted on the complaint in accordance with BCO 43-2 and 43-3. “A
complaint shall first be made to the court whose act or decision is alleged to be
in error." (BCO 43-2) The CCB notes the right of individuals under BCO 43-1
to complain against actions taken during a trial so long as the procedures of
BCO 43-2 and 43-3 are followed.
Adopted by CCB
(6-2-0 and TE Childs requested that his negative vote be recorded)

Question 2: Do the grounds for appeal in BCO 42-3 negate the right of an accused person to complain about the manner in which a trial is being conducted? Response: No. BCO 42-3 refers to appeals and does not negate the right to complain. However, if an appeal is taken in a judicial case, no complaint is then allowable, (BCO 43-1). Adopted by CCB (6-2-0 and TE Childs requested that his negative vote be recorded)

IV. Advice to the Stated Clerk Item 1: Advice to the Stated Clerk in the matter of the role of in thesi statements. Since the adoption of the Creation Study Committee report as amended last year, I have received inquires as to the status of the report in relation to the constitution. Moreover, there are overtures this year to require exceptions for any views other than 24-hour creation days (Overture 7, 23) to allow exceptions for other view (Overture 20), and to affirm the Position of the 28th General Assembly on diversity of views on creation days (Overture 30).

My advice has been as follows:

- **a.** The Creation Study Committee Report has the status of any other study committee report, such as those on the gifts of the Holy Spirit and Freemasonry, that is, it is the thinking of a particular General Assembly on a specific subject.

- **b.** The Creation Study Committee Report, as with all other study committee reports adopted by a General Assembly, does not amend the constitution (BCO Preface, III. "The Constitution Defined" and BCO 26-1); only amendments effected by the proper constitutional procedures are actual and lawful amendments (BCO 26-2, 26-3 and 26-6).

- **C.** The Creation Study Committee Report has the status of being among those decisions of the General Assembly that are to be given "due and serious consideration by the Church and its lower courts when deliberating matters related to such actions" (BCO 14-7).

- **d.** Overtures relating to the Creation Study Committee Report would have the same status as the report, i.e. of being among those decisions of the General Assembly that are to be given "due and serious consideration by the Church and its lower courts when deliberating matters related to such actions" (BCO 14-7). Response: The CCB ratifies the advice of the Stated Clerk relative to the Role of in thesi Statements dated April 21, 2001, and offers the following additional advice: It is the purview of the lower courts to determine the suitability of men applying for reception/ordination with regard to the men's views on the matters raised in in thesi statements, subject always to proper review and/or judicial process. (BCO 13-6 and 13-9.a) (BCO 24-1) (BCO 11-3,4) Adopted by CCB

Item 2: Advice to the Stated Clerk regarding the Publication of Presbytery votes on BCO Amendments. I have received a letter of concern from an individual calling on me to "repent" of reporting the results of the BCO amendments in the spring Stated Clerk's letter. My response has been that those results are public information.

Response: The CCB advises the Stated Clerk that the committee concurs with his advice in this matter. Adopted by CCB

Presbyteries were informed by letter (dated August 29, 2000) of:

- **(1)** their right to submit evidence supporting their allegations to the SJC panel during this investigative phase; and (2) the time and place to submit evidentiary material related to the investigation. The understanding of the SJC was that further theological argument was appropriate for a trial, should an indictment have been rendered. Since no indictment was made, however, on the basis of the evidence presented by all notified parties it would have been inappropriate to try John Wood on the basis of theological arguments against matters neither he, nor the SJC, felt he supported. Had the matter moved to trial, it would have been proper for the presbyteries to make arguments for their allegations of theological error.

### 3) INQUIRY FROM THE BILLS AND OVERTURES COMMITTEE OF COMMISSIONERS

### IN RE. To OVERTURE 35:

"In the John Wood matter (i.e. a matter in which the SJC conducted a BCO 31-2 investigation but determined not to file charges), is it constitutionally permissible for the GA to amend the report of the SJC by deleting a concurring opinion?

Answer: It is the opinion of the CCB that it is not constitutional for the GA to amend the SJC report on Case 99-1 (the John Wood Matter) by deleting any or all-concurring opinions.

Reasoning:

1. The SJC manual 20-2 specifically delineates that a concurring and/or dissenting opinion of any member of the SJC is a component part of the SJC report.

2. BCO 15-5a specifically delineates that the SJC members have the constitutional right to attach concurring or dissenting opinions to any SJC decision.

3. BCO 15-5 has specifically been framed to assert that an SJC decision is the final decision of the GA. Additionally, BCO 15-5 has gone to great lengths to place into our constitution safeguards to prevent SJC decisions from being amended on the floor of GA. Unless the provisions of BCO 15-5c (one third of SJC submitting a minority report) are brought into play, there is a clear constitutional bar against any complaint, appeal, change, modification, or amendment to an SJC report.

4. While the CCB is aware that the BCO 34-1 assumption of original jurisdiction is a constitutionally unique happening, it is the advice of the CCB that the BCO 15-5 bar to amendment is still in effect. Our reasoning is as follows:

144

<a id="ga29-p147"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=147 printed_page=145 -->

- **a)** When the 28th GA referred the "John Wood Matter" to the SJC, it recognized, at least de facto, that the matter constituted a case, since BCO 15-4 seems to allow only cases to be committed to the SJC. As such, all the provisions of BCO 15-5 will apply.

- **b)** BO15-5 is the governing paragraph whenever a "case" is committed to the SJC.

1. Was a case submitted to the SJC? Yes.

2. Did the SJC make a decision? Yes.

3. Do the judges have a constitutional right to file a concurring and/or dissenting opinion? Yes (cf. BCO 15-5a)

4. Can the GA amend the SJC report of Case 99-1 to delete concurring opinions? NO (cf. BCO 15-5a) MSC

### 4) CONSTITUTIONAL INQUIRY #2 FROM TE JOHN VAN DEVENDER

The Assembly received the following Constitutional Inquiry from TE John Van Devender and referred it to CCB:

WHEREAS, SJC Case 99-1 regarding the John Wood matter is scheduled to be presented to this General Assembly; and WHEREAS, a supplemental report of a concurring opinion on this case, namely that one signed by RE Jack Williamson and others, is included in this report; and WHEREAS, this particular supplemental report purports to comment on the action of the 28th General Assembly and further to conclude that the 28th General Assembly erred in assuming original jurisdiction of the matter involving John Wood; and WHEREAS, BCO 15-4 and 5 authorizes the SJC to try and decide only the judicial cases committed to it; and WHEREAS, the SJC does not seem to have any explicit authority to comment upon or rule on an action of the General Assembly; and THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED that the 29th General Assembly directs the Committee on Constitutional Business to consider the following question and report back an answer prior to the consideration of the report from the SJC: "Does the Standing Judicial Commission have the authority to render an opinion on the legitimacy of an action of the General Assembly if not specifically asked to do so, particularly the legitimacy of an action in which the General Assembly refers business to the SJC; and BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that, if the Committee on Constitutional Business returns with a negative answer, that the 29th General Assembly move immediately to remove this specific concurring opinion from the SJC report and further that the Assembly direct members of the SJC to refrain from making such actions in the future.

145

<a id="ga29-p148"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=148 printed_page=146 -->

Answer: It is the opinion of the CCB that SJC may only address what is assigned to it. It may not render any opinion unless it is first assigned a matter. Once it is assigned a matter, the SJC may render an opinion even as to the legitimacy of an action in which the GA refers business to the SJC. MSC

### 5) RECEIVED THE MINORITY REPORT ON OPINION ON OVERTURE 19:

The undersigned respectfully disagree with the first paragraph of the CCB's response to Overture 19.

The CCB is charged with reviewing the minutes of the SJC. Yet the minutes of the SJC make no references to how the SJC handled the mandate that "representatives from the petitioning presbyteries be permitted to present their allegations before the SJC" (M28GA, p. 310). So far as we can tell, the conclusions of the majority of the CCB with regard to this matter rest solely on personal correspondence/conversations with a member or members of the SJC. But such personal contacts do not constitute the official record of the SJC and ought not to be the basis for a determination of what the SJC did or did not do. In our judgment, this matter should have been handled as the Committee on Review of Presbytery Records has typically handled matters where a presbytery's minutes do not indicate that the presbytery acted as it needed to. That is, an exception to the minutes should have been taken in the form, "The minutes of the SJC give no evidence of how or if the SJC complied with the mandate of the 28th General Assembly that 'representatives from the petitioning presbyteries be permitted to represent their allegations before the SJC (M28GA, p.310)'." The SJC would then respond formally to the apparent exception by correcting their minutes, adopting an explanatory note, etc. The CCB could have then reviewed that response, thus insuring that it was responding to the official position of the SJC.

RE Frederick Neikirk TE Morton H. Smith

### SECOND SUPPLEMENTAL REPORT OF THE

### COMMITTEE ON CONSTITUTIONAL BUSINESS

### 1) CONSTITUTIONAL INQUIRY #3:

What is the status of an SJC concurring opinion, that has been reported to the General Assembly, that has not been found by the SJC to be in "temperate language?" (SJC Manual 14-7)

Response: It is the advice of the CCB that:

SJC 14-7 indicates that the time for a determination of the temperateness of the language is prior to the concurring opinion being appended to a decision. If a concurring opinion has been appended to a decision, the opportunity to assess or reassess temperateness has lapsed.

Therefore, the status of such an SJC concurring opinion, which has been reported to the General Assembly, remains valid regardless of subsequent concerns about temperateness.

Further, the CCB observes that concurring and/or dissenting opinions are, by definition, not the opinion of the SJC. As such, they do not, of necessity, reflect the mind of the Church. They are not "... binding and conclusive on the parties who are directly involved in the matter," nor may they be appealed to in the same sense as the majority position as to any principle which may have been expressed by the concurring and/or dissenting opinion. Such concurring and/or dissenting opinions are simply the opinions of individuals. (BCO 14-7, cf. SJC Manual 18.3) Approved by CCB 4-3-0 Minority Report The CCB observes that concurring and/or dissenting opinions are, by definition, not the opinion of the SJC. As such, they do not, of necessity, reflect the mind of the Church. They are not "... binding and conclusive on the parties who are directly involved in the matter...," nor may they be appealed to in the same sense as the majority position as to any principle which may have been expressed by the concurring and/or dissenting opinion. Such concurring and/or dissenting opinions are simply the opinions of individuals (BCO 14-7, cf. SJC Manual 18.3.). The minority agrees.

However, it is the opinion of the Minority that the requirement of temperate language
cannot be left solely to the author(s) of a document. The precedent of the General
Assembly in dealing with documents which must be "couched in temperate language"
(e.g. BCO 45-5, cf. SJC Manual 14.7) is that the court itself must determine the question
of whether the language is temperate. Since the SJC, as a Commission of the General
Assembly, is the court, the SJC must itself act to determine if concurring and/or
dissenting opinions meet that standard.
147

<a id="ga29-p150"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=150 printed_page=148 -->

It is, therefore, the position of the Minority that an SJC concurring and/or dissenting opinion that has been reported to the General Assembly and that has not been found by the SJC to be temperate in language fails to meet the requirements of SJC Manual 14.7. It is not properly a part of the report of the SJC and should not be included in the minutes of the General Assembly. The only mechanism currently available for determining whether the SJC has so acted (i.e., has acted to determine that the opinion is temperate) is the CCB's review of the SJC's minutes which occurs prior to the meeting of the General Assembly.

Signed: TE Morton H. Smith, RE Frederick R. Neikirk, and RE Richard A. Springer.

### 2) CONSTITUTIONAL INQUIRY #4

Request advice on how the Assembly is to suspend our Rules of Operation: BCO, RAO, SJC Manual and Robert's Rules of Order to obey the King of the Church – Jesus Christ as He has spoken to us in His Word. What is the motion, or procedure to live by and obey God's Word when we are fenced in by our Standing Rules? Response: It is the advice of the CCB that the documents referenced in the inquiry are either part of our Constitution or are rules we have adopted as prudential applications of Biblical patterns of polity2. As such, the delegates to the General Assembly are bound by their ordination vows (BCO 21-5, 3&4 and 24-5, 3&4) to operate under these as fully and fairly as possible. Thus, for example, if a provision of Robert's Rules contradicts the BCO, the latter takes precedence and the former is set aside. Similarly, if one of the documents contains provisions for its suspension, then the Assembly may avail itself of that procedure. The absence of such a procedure in certain documents means that the General Assembly is bound to operate under the provisions of those documents unless or until they are amended.

We note this always allows those who feel that Scriptural principles have been ignored to access the means of redress available in our Constitution, including the mechanisms of BCO 45. Additionally, they (and all of us) should pray that the Holy Spirit will ultimately affirm what is correct for the Church as the Church properly follows its standards for operations and revisions in the future. Private concerns between individuals should be handled according to Matthew 18.

The presumption that we need to suspend our rules in order to obey Christ is an opinion that the CCB is not willing to affirm. If our standards are shown to be out of accord with Scripture, then there are proper procedures to follow, at each level, in order to change those standards. Approved by CCB 7-0-0

Which consists of the Westminster Confession of Faith, together with the Larger and Shorter Catechisms, and the Book of Church Order, all of which are subordinate to the Scriptures of the Old and New Testaments (Preliminary Principle III) 2 e.g., RAO, SJC Manual, Robert's Rules of Order

148

<a id="ga29-p151"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=151 printed_page=149 -->

Respectfully submitted, /s/ TE Craig Childs, Chairman /s/ TE Mark Rowden, Acting Secretary

9. That Overture 5 from Heartland Presbytery requesting to be divided so that the State of Iowa would become a separate Presbytery of the PCA effective January 1, 2002, be answered in the affirmative. Adopted

OVERTURE 5 from Heartland Presbytery (to MNA) "Divide Heartland Presbytery"

Whereas, the geographical boundaries of Heartland Presbytery are among the largest in the PCA; and, Whereas, the churches within the boundaries of Iowa now number 6 organized churches numbering 813 members; two mission; and one possible church transferring from Independency; and, Whereas, stewardship of the local churches relates to time, talent and tithes; and, with the current distances, it is difficult to maintain close fellowship due to the travel time required; and, Whereas, requests from other Presbyteries with fewer churches and members have been approved (recognizing the same difficulties as Heartland);

165

<a id="ga29-p168"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=168 printed_page=166 -->

THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED, that Heartland Presbytery be divided so that the State of Iowa would become a separate Presbytery of the PCA effective January 1, 2002.

10. That Overture 12 from Central Carolina Presbytery requesting to remove the eleven county area known as the "Piedmont Triad" of North Carolina from the Central Carolina Presbytery to form a new, Piedmont Triad Presbytery, be answered in the affirmative. Adopted OVERTURE 12 From Central Carolina Presbytery (to MNA) "Divide Central Carolina Presbytery into Two Presbyteries"

Whereas, the Central Carolina Presbytery exists for the Glory of God and the furtherance on His Kingdom here on Earth; Whereas, the Central Carolina Presbytery currently consists of Forty-Two (42) particular and mission congregations comprising more than Six Thousand (6,000) communing members within a geographical area requiring substantially more than three hours to cross; Whereas, the 16th General Assembly adopted guidelines for the multiplication of existing presbyteries into new presbyteries, which guidelines provide a set of ideals governing the development of new presbyteries; Whereas, pursuant to those guidelines, the Central Carolina Presbytery committed itself to a plan to grow into three separate presbyteries several years ago, which plan included developing three sub-regions (Metrolina, Triad, and Sandhills) within the presbytery and focusing church planting resources on developing new churches within each of these regions; Whereas, the Triad Region of the Central Carolina Presbytery has grown to Six

- **(6)** particular congregations and Two (2) mission congregations comprising more than One Thousand communing members and these churches have developed a strong sense of mutual care and potential for shared ministry and joint ministry projects; Whereas, Five of the particular congregations located in the Triad Region have communing membership in excess of One Hundred Twenty-Five, with strong prospects for continued growth in the future; Whereas, there is a commonly recognized regional identity within the Eleven

- **(11)** County area known as the "Piedmont Triad" in North Carolina which the Triad Region of Central Carolina Presbytery was formed to build upon and which does not partition any existing metropolitan areas; Whereas, the Central Carolina Presbytery believes it is consistent with the guidelines of the 16th General Assembly to form a new presbytery in the Eleven County area of North Carolina known as the "Piedmont Triad"

166

<a id="ga29-p169"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=169 printed_page=null -->

and that this multiplication of ministry would further the advance of God's Kingdom and the growth of His Church on Earth; NOW, THEREFORE the Central Carolina Presbytery hereby petitions and overtures the General Assembly pursuant to 14-6(e) of the Book of Church Order of the Presbyterian Church in America as follows:

- **(1)** To remove the Eleven County area commonly known as the "Piedmont Triad" of North Carolina and consisting of Surry, Yadkin, Davie, Davidson, Stokes, Forsyth, Rockingham, Guilford, Randolph, Caswell and Alamance Counties from the existing bounds of the Central Carolina Presbytery;

- **(2)** To erect the "Piedmont Triad Presbytery of North Carolina," establishing the boundaries of such presbytery to include those Eleven counties and the particular and mission congregations currently located within them;

- **(3)** To authorize the conduct of business by this newly established church court effective July 1, 2001, consistent with Chapter 13 of the Book of Church Order and such other provisions as may apply. It is so moved and approved by the Assembled Court of the Central Carolina Presbytery this 27th day of January, 2001. Attested by: /s/ Howie Burkhalter, Moderator, Central Carolina Presbytery

This Overture was moved, seconded and approved at a duly constituted meeting of the Central Carolina Presbytery at which a quorum was present. Attested by: /s/ David M. Frierson, Stated Clerk

18. That Overture 26 from the New York State Presbytery be answered in the affirmative (see also Communication #6). Adopted

OVERTURE 26 From New York State Presbytery (to MNA) "Redraw New York State and Ascension Presbytery Boundaries"

Whereas, the current western boundary of the New York State Presbytery includes central New York east and including Wayne, Ontario and Steuben counties; and, Whereas, the current eastern boundary of the Ascension Presbytery includes western New York west and including Monroe, Livingston and Allegany counties; and Whereas, the city of Rochester located in Monroe County and within the boundary of Ascension Presbytery has no PCA church; and Whereas, there are several families who have expressed interest in the past several years in forming a core group for the purpose of starting a PCA church in the Rochester area; and Whereas, there are some families who travel from the Rochester area to New Life Presbyterian Church in Ithaca, NY, a mission church in the New York State Presbytery, for worship; and Whereas, these same families have indicated a desire to affiliate with the New York State Presbytery; and Whereas, the New York State Presbytery would like to initiate and oversee this developing PCA work in the Rochester area as part of its vision to plant healthy and reproducing PCA churches in every major city in upstate New York; Therefore, Be It Resolved that the New York State Presbytery hereby overtures the 29th General Assembly of the Presbyterian Church in America to redraw the western boundary of New York State Presbytery and the northeastern New York boundary of Ascension Presbytery, to wit, that the counties east of and including Monroe and Livingston be transferred to New York State Presbytery, and furthermore, that the counties east of and including Steuben remain with the New York State Presbytery, to be effective July 1, 2001.

19. That Overture 29 From TE Andrew Lee of Northern California Presbytery be answered in the negative on the following grounds:

1. Regarding Items 1-4, the overture presents no reasons for requesting this review. There is no self-evident rationale for requiring this review. There are no allegations of impropriety or misuse of funds. Therefore, even the overture itself presents no reasons to proceed with an action that would require a significant expenditure of staff time.

2. Item 4 calls for an adjustment of 1990 - 1997 church planting budgets, based on a standard put in place in 1997. It is not common practice to apply a new standard to previous actions in matters such as this, and there is no rationale offered for doing so in this case.

3. This overture and its requested actions were not supported by Northern California Presbytery, the court to which they were originally presented.

4. Effective January 1, 2000, MNA discontinued the practice of assessing fees on project funds. Since that date, it has been the practice to apply 100% of every designated dollar to the project for which it is designated.

5. Regarding membership in ECFA, the MNA Committee believes that current accountability structures are sufficient to sustain the credibility of the ministry. Its annual audit by an independent accounting firm is reviewed by the MNA Committee and the General Assembly. All aspects of MNA's work are subject to the review of the General Assembly annually. MNA believes that any value gained from ECFA accreditation is more than offset by the time and expense required to maintain such accreditation. Adopted

170

<a id="ga29-p173"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=173 printed_page=171 -->

OVERTURE 29 From TE Andrew Lee of Northern California Presbytery "Direct MNA to Report Administrative Fees"

Whereas, in October 1997 the GA MNA Committee approved a policy: (a) to limit the maximum dollar amount (or percentage), of "Field Assistance and Project Development Costs" [project overhead/administrative fees] taken from funds raised for church planting projects; and (b) to disclose to select donors the existence and amounts of such costs as a percentage of donations; and Whereas, prior to October 1997, i.e., without aforementioned Committeeapproved policy, GA MNA Staff prepared and administered church planting project budgets that included "Field Assistance and Project Development Costs" [project overhead/administrative fees]; and Whereas, GA MNA heretofore has not been a member of the Evangelical Council for Financial Accountability (ECFA; www.ecfa.org) as has another PCA Committee (Mission to the World) and PCA Agency (Covenant Theological Seminary) - organizations that are also involved in fundraising (Romans 12: 17b). (It should be noted that while GA MNA's financial records are audited annually by an independent firm, and all records are reviewed by normal General Assembly processes, ECFA membership is helpful both in terms of accountability and in increasing the confidence of donors); and Whereas, GA MNA as a Committee of the PCA is accountable to the General Assembly; Therefore, Be It Resolved that the General Assembly have GA MNA report to the General Assembly on the following:

1. Written policy and limits that GA MNA Staff used to determine "Field Assistance and Project Development Costs" [and/or similar overhead/administrative fees] in preparing and administering church planting project funds in the absence of the October 1997 Committee-approved policy;

2. Written policy and practices GA MNA Staff followed to disclose "Field Assistance and Project Development Costs" [and/or similar overhead/ administrative fees] to donors and church planters in the absence of the October 1997 Committee-approved policy; 3 "Field Assistance and Project Development Costs" [and/or similar overhead/administrative fees] in: (a) dollar amounts; (b) as a percentage of; donations (cf. guidelines in the October 1997 Committee policy); (c) timing as to when such fees were taken from church plant funds with respect to project's budget plan; and

- **(d)** the implicit cost of capital that "Field Assistance and Project Development Costs" [and/or similar overhead/administrative fees] imputed to each project when netted against funding covenants. Information for items 3(a) through 3(d) to be provided for all GA MNA project budgets not covered by the October 1997

171

<a id="ga29-p174"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=174 printed_page=172 -->

Committee policy beginning from January 1990 through implementation of said Committee policy;

4. Recommended actions, if any, that should be taken for all projects in item #3 above if it is determined that "Field Assistance and Project Development Costs" [and/or similar overhead/administrative fees] were (a) lower relative to the guidelines set by the Committee's October 1997 policy; or (b) higher relative to the guidelines set by the Committee's October 1997 policy; and

5. GA MNA's current position regarding its membership in the

### ECFA.

20. That Overture 32 from the Mid-America Presbytery be answered in the affirmative (see also Communication 1, page 173). Adopted

OVERTURE 32 From Mid-America Presbytery (to MNA) "J & R of Mid-America Presbytery into North Texas Presbytery"

Whereas, Mid-America Presbytery, at times in its history having boundaries encompassing all of Oklahoma and parts of Kansas, Missouri, and Arkansas, and as many as ten churches, now, by the departure of churches and territory on several occasions to other expanding presbyteries, has been reduced to only part of the state of Oklahoma and to only four remaining churches with a combined communing membership of between four and five hundred, and Whereas, Mid-America Presbytery has the fewest churches of any of the contiguous PCA presbyteries, and Whereas, Mid-America Presbytery does not believe it currently has the resources of churches, presbyters, funds and morale most effectively to staff appropriately presbytery committees and commissions and move toward further growth, and Whereas, Mid-America Presbytery desires to gain encouragement towards future growth by being a part of a presbytery experiencing growth by church planting and the establishment of campus ministries, and Whereas, Oklahoma City and a corridor of counties connecting it to Texas are already part of North Texas Presbytery where currently, with the help of the Southwest Church Planting Network, two new Oklahoma City area church plants and a Reformed University Fellowship at the University of Oklahoma are being established, and

172

<a id="ga29-p175"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=175 printed_page=null -->

Whereas, being received into North Texas Presbytery would immediately provide our churches with the option of participating in the threepresbytery, Southwest Church Planting Network (North Texas, South Texas and Southwest); and Whereas, our four remaining churches joining with North Texas Presbytery seems the best pathway for an eventual reestablishing of a larger Oklahoma area presbytery as soon as enough particular churches are formed, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that Mid-America Presbytery – pending the consent of North Texas Presbytery to receive us – petitions the 29th General Assembly meeting in Dallas, Texas, in June, 2001, to be allowed to be joined and received, with our four particular churches, their officers and members of the presbytery, and all remaining Oklahoma counties into North Texas Presbytery, effective July 1, 2001, this action effectively dissolving Mid-America Presbytery.

Adopted at the 40th Stated Meeting of Mid-America Presbytery, on April 20,

2001. Attested by: /s/ John Owen Butler, Stated Clerk

COMMUNICATION 1 from North Texas Presbytery May 3, 2001

- **L.** Roy Taylor, Stated Clerk

RE: Mid-America Presbytery Overture to 29th GA to Join NTP

Fathers and Brothers:

At the 66th stated meeting of the North Texas Presbytery held April 27-28, 2001 at Park Cities Presbyterian Church, the Presbytery passed the following motion:

"M&P that the North Texas Presbytery inform the 29th General Assembly that it concurs with the overture of Mid- America Presbytery to dissolve and to join the NTP."

This effectively places all Indian Territory within the boundary of the NTP.

Yours in Christ, /s/ T. John Mulkey, Stated Clerk North Texas Presbytery

Whereas, the counties of Pulaski and Carroll lie geographically in the New River Valley and at the extreme northeastern end of Westminster Presbytery, closer to all the churches in New River than to those in the entire southern cluster in Westminster; and Whereas, in the formative studies of potential boundaries for Westminster and New River Presbyteries, significant consideration was given to the possibility of our two Counties being assigned to New River; and Whereas, the geographical and cultural issues involving our two churches and those in New River Presbytery have led to very positive ministry and outreach sharing, particularly between the Virginia congregations of that Presbytery and ourselves; and Whereas, New River Presbytery has indicated a desire to receive those two Counties with a notation that adding our two Counties would strengthen their presbytery without unduly weakening a stronger Westminster; and Whereas, New River Presbytery has formed an ad-hoc committee to explore with some of the churches in James River Presbytery, and our two churches, the possibility of asking the General Assembly in the future to form a new Presbytery in the west-central area of Virginia; Now Therefore, be it resolved that Westminster Presbytery herewith overtures the 29th General Assembly of the Presbyterian Church in America to redraw the boundaries of Westminster and New River Presbyteries by transferring Pulaski County and that portion of Carroll County that lies east of Interstate 77 in the Commonwealth of Virginia, and the ministers and churches therein, from Westminster to New River Presbytery, effective September 30, 2001; and Be it further resolved that the Walthall-Wood Scholarship Fund assets be transferred to the New River Presbytery with the approval of this change of boundary since they are closely tied to the Draper's Valley Presbyterian Church of Draper, Virginia. OVERTURE 36 From Central Carolina Presbytery (to MNA) "North Hills PCA in Salisbury, NC, Seeking Admission into Newlyformed Triad Presbytery"

Whereas, North Hills Presbyterian Church exists for the Glory of God and the furtherance of His Kingdom on Earth; Whereas, North Hills Presbyterian Church was admitted to the Central Carolina Presbytery in October of 1998 and has been blessed by its association with Central Carolina Presbytery and the Presbyterian Church in America; Whereas, North Hills Presbyterian Church is located in Rowan County, a county that adjoins the proposed boundaries of the Triad Presbytery; Whereas, North Hills Presbyterian Church lies in the extreme north of Rowan County next to the proposed boundary of the Triad Presbytery; Whereas, North Hills Presbyterian Church has a strong affinity to the Triad geographical region as well as to the churches in the new presbytery; Whereas, this proximity and affinity has already resulted in filial and ministry ties to the churches in the new presbytery; Whereas, official connection with the Triad Presbytery would strengthen North Hills Presbyterian Church, further its mission, and encourage its members to love and good deeds; Now Therefore North Hills Presbyterian Church hereby petitions and overtures the Central Carolina Presbytery and the General Assembly that it be allowed to join the newly-formed Triad Presbytery outside its geographical bounds effective July 1, 2001.
