The Committee adopted the following as a substitute motion:

Proposed Response of the 29th General Assembly to Communication 5 and Overture 38 From Westminster Presbytery

Dear Fathers and Brothers of Westminster Presbytery,

Greetings in the Name of the Lord. We lament the occasion of this communication, but testify to our trust that the Lord of the Church is working in all things, even these unhappy circumstances, for His glory and the good of our branch of His Church. With respect to your letter May 16, 2001 (Communication 5), this Assembly raises no question concerning your ecclesiastical and civil right as a presbytery to withdraw from the Presbyterian Church in America. However, this Assembly would be profoundly remiss in its duty to "recommend measures for the promotion of charity, truth and holiness through all the churches under its care" (BCO 14-6.k.) were it to fail to challenge Westminster Presbytery's judgment in this action. We urge you to consider again your action, and reverse your judgment. As we understand your communication, you have, by majority vote, determined to withdraw from the Presbyterian Church in America. At the same time, you ask this Assembly to make provision for erecting a new presbytery composed of the Teaching Elders and Churches that do not wish to leave the PCA. Such a request might be above reproach, if the Teaching Elders and Churches in question were just those that voted against the action of presbytery to withdraw, and who were convinced in conscience that submission to the Presbytery in this matter was sin. However, we are reliably informed that in fact a portion of those voting with the majority in favor of withdrawing from the PCA, did so with the undisguised intention of joining the new PCA presbytery. We are further informed that another portion of those voting with the majority, actually intending to depart as a presbytery, and thus claim the name and traditions of Westminster Presbytery, knew of the true intention of the aforementioned portion, and acquiesced in the matter. This circumstance, fathers and brothers, raises serious questions about the integrity of this vote, questions which, as your brothers in the Lord, we press upon you with the utmost urgency. First, with respect to the portion of the majority voting to withdraw, who did so with no intention of in fact withdrawing—please consider the following. You have apparently voted on a proposal of great moment, a proposal crying out for a principled consideration, out of mere expediency. Surely this is unworthy of the solemn privilege and responsibility of voting.

177

<a id="ga29-p180"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=180 printed_page=178 -->

Further, you apparently voted knowing that the resultant continuing Westminster Presbytery, composed of those Teaching Elders and Churches that actually do intend to withdraw from the PCA, will proclaim to the world that she, unlike the proposed new PCA presbytery, is the true, faithful presbytery, sincerely committed to the Westminster standards. Your affirmative vote makes possible this circumstance, while at the same time you cannot possibly in conscience support this allegation—for in your intention to be restored to the PCA, you profess yourselves desirous of being members of a body sincerely committed to those same Standards. Finally, you are duty bound, by your vow to submit to the government of the church, to submit to this decision of Westminster Presbytery, and withdraw from the PCA. The only justification you could have for repudiating the authority of Westminster Presbytery, would be if you in good conscience could not comply; that is to say, if it would be a violation of your loyalty to Christ for you to submit. But how can you credibly claim that it violates your conscience to do what you in fact voted in favor of Westminster Presbytery doing? Surely there are serious questions of integrity raised in such behavior. Second, with respect to the portion of the majority voting to withdraw, who did so with the intention to withdraw, and in so doing claim to be acting, not as independents, but as Presbyterians, and continuing Westminster Presbytery as she was originally constituted, to be an Old School Presbytery committed to the Westminster Standards—please consider the following. You have allied your cause with brothers whose actions are at odds with their true intentions, and at odds with your purpose, and in so doing you have made your cause dependent upon behavior of questionable integrity. Surely duty in this case required you to plead with such brethren, out of your responsibilities to them as set forth in the exposition of Scripture found in Larger Catechism Questions 140-145, not to vote in favor of the action to withdraw, unless they genuinely believed that the PCA had abandoned the biblical fidelity you suppose to be preserved at Westminster Presbytery, and unless they genuinely intended to submit to the Presbytery's action to withdraw upon its passage. Further, surely this vote is but a Pyrrhic victory for your cause: for although Westminster Presbytery has formally withdrawn from the PCA, all parties know full well that materially the action was not of the Westminster Presbytery you intend in the outcome. This action cannot, with any integrity, be said to sustain the claims you apparently intend to set before the world concerning the continuing Westminster Presbytery. That Presbytery, simply did not have the votes to withdraw, and you, and everyone else, will know it. Finally, this unhappy scheme circumvents what we suppose otherwise to have been your duty and right, not as independents, but as Presbyterians, however costly it may have been. We refer to principles from the earliest days of American Presbyterian history, set forth in the union of the Synods of New York and Philadelphia, and embraced particularly by the Old School Assembly in the controversies of a latter age. Consider their counsel:

when any Matter is determined by a Major Vote, every Mem[ber] Shall either actively concur with, or passively Submit to Such Deter[min]ation; or, if his

178

<a id="ga29-p181"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=181 printed_page=179 -->

Conscience permit him to do neither, he Shall, [after] Sufficient Liberty modestly to reason and remonstrate, peaceab[ly with]draw from our Communion, without attempting to make any Sc[hism:] provided always, that this Shall be understood to extend only to [Such] Determinations, as the Body Shall Judge indispensable in Doct[rine] or Presbyterian Gover[n]ment. (Plan of Union, Synods of New York and Philadelphia. Minutes of the Synod of New York and Philadelphia, 1758, p. 3. [Klett, ed., 1976, p. 341].)

Charles Hodge later commended this statement as laying a foundation for unquestioned principles of the Presbyterian church:

Notwithstanding, therefore, the ardent debates and mutual criminations on this subject, it appears the two parties were of one mind. They were agreed in disclaiming all legislative power in religious matters. They were agreed in the right of Synods to set down rules for the government of the church. They were agreed in the binding authority of these rules even over dissentients, except when such dissentients believed them to be sinful. They were agreed that when a member could not obey a given rule with a good conscience, it was his duty peaceably to withdraw. Finally, they were agreed that when a Synod saw that the minority were opposed to any measure, not in judgment only, but in conscience, they ought not to insist upon it, and thus necessitate a schism, unless they believed the measure to be essential to the well-being of the churches. These principles are all so plain and so reasonable, that we need not wonder they commanded the unanimous consent of both parties, or that they have remained the unquestioned principles of our church from that day to this. (The Constitutional History of the Presbyterian Church in the United States of America, part II, 1741-1788 (Philadelphia: Presbyterian Board of Publication, 1851), pp. 206-207.)

According to historic Old School Presbyterian polity it is clear that anyone who cannot in good conscience submit to the brethren in a matter, has the burden of withdrawing from the fellowship. He may well claim, that it is not he who has departed, but the majority; and he has every right to try and sustain that claim. Nonetheless, in our polity the burden to withdraw belongs to the dissident. Of course our best hope is that those disagreeing can find a way to maintain the bonds of fellowship, even in the midst of serious disputes. We are reminded of the wholesome words of Robert L. Dabney, describing the pattern of Christ-honoring thought proper to a faithful minority, and commend their careful consideration to our brothers:

We believe these measures wrong, even unconstitutional; we testify against their wrong, but we leave the responsibility of them to the majority who enacted them, and whose will must prevail in all republican bodies. Their wrongfulness does not compel us to separate from this, which we believe to be the true church of Jesus Christ, though in this matter erring. We exercise our Christian Liberty in testifying against her fault, but we go on as before, to labor for her good; for

179

<a id="ga29-p182"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=182 printed_page=180 -->

though in fault, it is Christ's bride. ("Our Position." The Central Presbyterian 2:28 (July 11, 1857): 110; reprint, Discussions by Robert L. Dabney, D.D., LL.D., edited by C.R. Vaughan (Richmond: Presbyterian Committee of Publication, 1890); reprint, Harrisonburg, VA: Sprinkle Publications, 1982), II:176-183.)

Fathers and brothers, in light of these considerations, we ask again, for the sake of Christ's glory and the good of His Church, reconsider your action to withdraw, and reverse your judgment.

Finally, this Assembly answers Overture 38 in the negative, on the grounds that:

1. this Assembly cannot countenance the action which gave rise to the request, without expressing our deepest concern for the integrity of the Presbytery in so acting, and sustaining a hope that our counsels may well be heeded by our brothers;

2. as a complaint against Presbytery's action to withdraw has not yet been heard, this Assembly should not act to erect a new Presbytery until all judicial remedies of dissenting members of Presbytery have been exhausted;

3. that the overture improperly and imprudently contemplates an action of the General Assembly of the PCA as being qualified by the actions of an anticipated ecclesiastical body with which the Assembly will have no relations; and

4. that at this time there are no churches or teaching elders qualified to make a request for admission to the PCA as a presbytery.

Should Westminster Presbytery, contrary to this Assembly's brotherly advice and sincere hope, persevere in the course set out in its action to withdraw from the Presbyterian Church in America, it is the judgment of this Assembly that at the effective date of the withdrawal, all the congregations and Teaching Elders of Westminster Presbytery will no longer be members of the Presbyterian Church in America. Should Teaching Elders or congregations find that they are unable in good conscience to continue as members of Westminster Presbytery as seceded, and by appropriate act renounce its jurisdiction, they may seek admission to the Presbyterian Church in America.

Finally, we appeal to Westminster Presbytery, if Presbytery remains determined to continue in their announced course, that, for the sake of those who may find their insurance coverage threatened by Presbytery's withdrawal, to meet and change the effective date of the action to withdraw, until the conclusion of the 30th General Assembly, so that those who desire to remain members of the PCA may immediately be admitted as a presbytery of the PCA. Adopted as amended

180

<a id="ga29-p183"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=183 printed_page=181 -->

OVERTURE 38 From Westminster Presbytery (to MNA) "Erect New Presbytery"

Westminster Presbytery hereby notifies the General Assembly of its intention to withdraw from the Presbyterian Church in America, effective at the January 2002 Stated Meeting of Presbytery; and the General Assembly be overtured to take the following action:

That the General Assembly, under the powers granted to it under the PCA Constitution to erect new presbyteries and to unite and divide presbyteries per their request, hereby established a new presbytery, in accordance with the following criteria:

Those churches and ministers which have certified to the Stated Clerk of Westminster Presbytery by the January 2002 Stated Meeting of said Presbytery that they wish to remain in Westminster Presbytery, shall be constituted as Westminster Presbytery; while those churches and ministers which have not certified to the Stated Clerk of Westminster Presbytery by the January 2002 Stated Meeting of said Presbytery that they wish to remain in Westminster Presbytery, shall be constituted as a new Presbytery, effective that date, with the same boundaries as the present Westminster Presbytery.

Adopted by Westminster Presbytery on May 15, 2001. Attested by: /s/ D. Steven Meyerhoff, Stated Clerk

Action to Withdraw and Realign Westminster Presbytery May 15, 2001

1. That, in light of:

- **a.** the declared intention of some churches and teaching elders in Westminster Presbytery to seek to continue Westminster Presbytery as she was originally constituted, and

- **b.** the advice given from the GA CCB, "Should a group of churches choose to leave the PCA in order to form a new affiliation, or to continue an affiliation that they perceive as antecedent to the PCA, then they can peaceably withdraw as a group subject to the consent of each congregation in the group..." and,

- **C.** the minutes of the Second GA where the GA of the PCA acknowledged that Westminster Presbytery reserves the right to withdraw as a Presbytery from the denomination at any time, Westminster Presbytery votes to withdraw from the PCA as of its January 2002 Stated Meeting.

2. To safeguard the integrity of the congregation's right of selfdetermination, all Sessions in Westminster Presbytery are hereby asked to consider calling a congregational meeting sometime between May 15 and the January 2002 Stated Meeting of Presbytery for the purpose of voting on whether to leave the PCA and stay within Westminster Presbytery as she leaves the PCA. This call for a congregational meeting is to safeguard the provisions of BCO 25-11 and in accordance with the advice of the GA CCB. If they vote to leave the PCA they will declare either their intent to join in the continuance of Westminster Presbytery or go to some other denomination. This action is a plea for a peaceful solution to our gridlock. This information is to be distributed to the churches of Presbytery by a letter from Presbytery's Stated Clerk, including a copy of this proposal, calling Sessions to examine these issues, consider calling a congregational meeting to vote on whether to

182

<a id="ga29-p185"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=185 printed_page=183 -->

leave the PCA with Westminster Presbytery and then to respond in writing to Presbytery by the January 2002 Stated Meeting of Presbytery. It is understood by all parties that only the congregations voting to leave the PCA and to stay with Westminster Presbytery shall have ever left the PCA. Those congregations taking no action will be understood to still be in the PCA, in a Presbytery yet to be named, with the same geographical boundaries as the present Westminster Presbytery. Any Teaching Elder(s) on the roll of Westminster Presbytery desiring to withdraw will inform the Presbytery by the January 2002 Stated Meeting.

3. Westminster Presbytery hereby notifies the General Assembly of its intention to withdraw from the Presbyterian Church in America, effective at the January 2002 Stated Meeting of Presbytery; and the General Assembly be overtured to take the following action: That the General Assembly, under the powers granted to it under the PCA Constitution to erect new presbyteries and to unite and divide presbyteries per their request, hereby established a new presbytery, in accordance with the following criteria: Those churches and ministers which have certified to the Stated Clerk of Westminster Presbytery by the January 2002 Stated Meeting of said Presbytery that they wish to remain in Westminster Presbytery, shall be constituted as Westminster Presbytery; while those churches and ministers which have not certified to the Stated Clerk of Westminster Presbytery by the January 2002 Stated Meeting of said Presbytery that they wish to remain in Westminster Presbytery, shall be constituted as a new Presbytery, effective that date, with the same boundaries as the present Westminster Presbytery.

4. That Westminster Presbytery approve the disbursal of assets between the two Presbyteries, (to be named) and Westminster, on the basis of the percentage of churches in each Presbytery as of the January 2002 Stated Meeting, the exception being the MNA funds (which are designated for the RUF/ETSU work) which shall remain in (to be named) Presbytery. This is in accordance with the advice of the GA CCB, "... There are no standards regarding continuing the name of a departing group and such matters should be left to the discretion and charity of the brothers involved. Additionally, any division of assets or attachment of corporate identity, where applicable, will need to be determined by the brothers involved."

5. That Westminster Presbytery shall continue to have the documents and minutes of her court and that the Stated Clerk, Dr. Steven Meyerhoff, shall make copies of these minutes and all her official documents for (to be named) Presbytery and shall deliver the originals, by December 31, 2001, to Mr. Brent Bradley, or a designee of his choice, as the Stated Clerk Pro Tem of Westminster Presbytery. This is in accordance with the advice of the GA CCB. "...Additionally, any division of assets or

183

<a id="ga29-p186"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=186 printed_page=184 -->

attachment of the corporate identity, where applicable, will need to be determined by the brothers involved."

6. That Westminster Presbytery ask that her Sessions discuss the controversies that raged in our Presbytery and the GA. The Sessions of each congregation shall either commit themselves as elders and a Session to:

- **a.** their present covenant obligation as part of the PCA which commits churches, Sessions and elders to either support wholeheartedly the official positions, institutions and programs of the PCA, or do all within their power to change the official positions, institutions and programs of the PCA that they cannot wholeheartedly support, or

- **b.** call for a congregational meeting to vote to leave the PCA and continue to covenant together with the other congregations to continue together as Westminster Presbytery as she was originally constituted, to be an Old School Presbytery committed to the Westminster Standards in the plain sense of the meaning of the words, or to leave to join some other evangelical denomination.

7. The following intention is set forth as the intent of some elders wishing to leave the PCA and continue Westminster Presbytery. This intention cannot bind the Presbytery (for she alone can make her own selfdetermination) and will only become the rule when approved by Westminster Presbytery, Unaffiliated. But it is the intention of these elders to propose to Westminster Presbytery, Unaffiliated, to continue Westminster in the following terms: Westminster Presbytery will declare herself at the January 2002 Stated Meeting no longer affiliated with the PCA, that she will continue the position stated in Westminster's original founding document to be an Old School Presbytery. She will remain unaffiliated with any other denomination for at least three years.

By the action of Presbytery, May 15, 2001, /s/ D. Steven Meyerhoff, Stated Clerk

### CONSTITUTIONAL INQUIRY FROM WESTMINSTER

It is the advice of the CCB in reference to the inquiry of Westminster Presbytery related to withdrawal from the PCA as a presbytery that:

There is no provision within our Constitution for a  
presbytery as a whole to withdraw. The right of an individual  
church to affiliate with whomever it will, however, cannot be  
impinged upon by a higher court (BCO 25-11; cf.11-3, 4). The  
principle of the BCO that is most closely related is that of Chapter  
25-11, which allows, "A particular church may withdraw from any

184

<a id="ga29-p187"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=187 printed_page=185 -->

court of this body at any time for reasons, which seem to it  
sufficient." Should a group of churches choose to leave the PCA  
in order to form a new affiliation, or to continue an affiliation that  
they perceive as antecedent to the PCA, then they can peaceably  
withdraw as a group subject to the consent of each congregation in  
the group. In the event of a group of churches withdrawing from  
the PCA with the consent of each church involved, those  
congregations remaining within the bounds of that presbytery that  
decline to withdraw with the departing group would stay within  
their present denomination. Those congregations not departing  
would constitute the continuing presbytery of the PCA. There are  
no standards regarding continuing the name of a departing group  
and such matters should be left to the discretion and charity of the  
brothers involved. Additionally, any division of assets or  
attachment of corporate identity, where applicable, will need to be  
determined by the brothers involved.  
Dr. L. Roy Taylor  
Stated Clerk  
April 25, 2001

"Be it further Resolved that pursuant to the above Resolution, the Presbytery of

Assembly of the National Presbyterian Church as a member Presbytery of the
National Presbyterian Church (A Corporation), with all the rights and
obligations belonging to member presbyteries as set forth in the Book of Church
Order of the National Presbyterian Church. The Presbytery of Westminster
reserves to itself the right to withdraw from said Assembly at any time under
conditions and in accordance with such rules as may be prescribed by the
Presbytery. The Presbytery reserves to itself the right of ownership of all
property of every sort, nature or description now owned or hereafter acquired.
This is not to be construed as a claim by the Presbytery upon the properties of its
constituent congregations, since the properties of congregations under the
National Presbyterian Church may not be claimed by the higher courts, except
as voluntarily given by the congregation to the said higher court.

"Done on this 20th day of July, 1974, in Stated Meeting of the Presbytery being met at Camp Evangel, Claypool, Virginia." (See M2GA, p. 124-125)

OVERTURE 1 from Missouri Presbytery (to CCB & B&O) "Amend BCO 14-1(12), Increase Number on Committees, Extend Terms to Five Years"

Whereas, the founders of our denomination, in order to minimize the concentration of power in the hierarchy of our denomination, created the structure of our General Assembly Committees and Agencies so that Committee members would be elected, in classes, for 4-year terms and are only eligible for re-election after a year has elapsed, Whereas, the responsibility and complexity of our Program Committees have grown as our denomination has grown, Whereas, it is very difficult for newly elected Committee members to function effectively until their 4-year term is almost half over, Whereas, this frequent turnover of Committee members coupled with the increased size and complexity of Committee operations tends to place more power in the hands of the permanent staff which is opposed to the intent of the founders of our denomination, Whereas, the proposed change provides for greater continuity in our Program Committees while still providing for the regular rotation of Committee members, Therefore Be it Resolved that BCO paragraph 14-1(12) in the second to the last paragraph be revised as follows: “Committee on Christian Education and Publications, Committee on Mission to North America, Committee on Mission to the World, and Committee on Reformed University Ministries shall consist of fifteen

- **(15)** men divided into five classes of three men each, with two men being TEs and one RE or two men being REs and one TE on alternate years on <del>odd years and four men each on even years</del>, elected to serve five-year terms. Committees on Christian Education and Publications, Mission to North America, Mission to the World and Reformed University Ministries shall have one ruling elder and one teaching elder as alternates to fill any vacancy that may occur during the year." Be it further resolved, that the first class of three (3) men to serve a five year term shall begin in 2003, should the 29th General Assembly approve this Overture, the consent of two-thirds (2/3) of the Presbyteries is given and the 30th General Assembly approves the same; and that each year thereafter there shall be an additional class of three (3) men who shall serve a five year term.

Adopted by Missouri Presbytery on April 18, 2000. Attested by: /s/ David R. Stain, Stated Clerk

2. That Overture 2 from New Jersey Presbytery ("Amend BCO 58-5 – Use Unleavened Bread in Communion") be answered in the negative.

188

<a id="ga29-p191"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=191 printed_page=189 -->

Grounds: There are no Scriptural grounds sufficient to mandate the exclusive use of unleavened bread in Communion. Adopted

OVERTURE 2 from New Jersey Presbytery (to CCB & B&O) "Amend BCO 58-5 – Use Unleavened Bread in Communion"

Whereas, the first paragraph of The Directory for the Worship of God, states that "BCO 56, 57 and 58 have been given full constitutional authority by the Eleventh General Assembly after being submitted to the Presbyteries and receiving the necessary two-thirds (2/3) approval of the Presbyteries,"and Whereas, Exodus 12:8, 15-20 reveals that the Passover celebration and accompanying Feast of Unleavened Bread used unleavened bread, Whereas, Luke 22:1 reveals that the Lord Jesus, when He instituted the Lord's Supper, was sharing a Passover meal with His disciples, and Whereas, 1 Corinthians 5:7 specifically states that believers are "unleavened" because Christ "our Passover" has been sacrificed, and Whereas, "leaven" is sometimes used in the Bible to denote sin, (cf. Matthew 16:6, 11-12), and Whereas, Jesus Christ is sinless, (Hebrews 4:15), Therefore, be it so ordered that the BCO 58-5 be revised by the insertion of the word "unleavened" before each occurrence of the word "bread" in the first, second, and fourth paragraphs and by adding these words at the end of the first paragraph: "If unleavened bread is unavailable, bread with leaven (yeast) may be used, but this is not to be the usual or normal practice of a congregation." The first four paragraphs of BCO 58-5 shall now read (added words are underlined): "The table, on which the elements are placed, being decently covered, and furnished with unleavened bread and wine, and the communicants orderly and gravely sitting around it (or in their seats before it), the elders in a convenient place together, the minister should then set the elements apart by prayer and thanksgiving. If unleavened bread is unavailable, bread with leaven (yeast) may be used, but this is not to be the usual or normal practice of a congregation. The unleavened bread and wine being thus set apart by prayer and thanksgiving, the minister is to take the unleavened bread, and break it, in the view of the people saying: That the Lord Jesus Christ on the same night in which He was betrayed took bread; and when He had given thanks, He broke it, gave it to His disciples, as I, ministering in His name, give this bread to you, and said, "Take, eat; this is My body which is broken for you; do this in remembrance of Me."

189

<a id="ga29-p192"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=192 printed_page=190 -->

Here the unleavened bread is to be distributed. After having given the unleavened bread, he shall take the cup, and say..."

Adopted by the Presbytery of New Jersey on May 20, 2000. Attested by: James A. Smith, Stated Clerk

3. That Overture 3 from Susquehanna Valley Presbytery ("Amend BCO 20-2 to Include Pastor in Search Committee for Assistant or Associate Pastor") be answered in the negative. Grounds: There are many ways for a church to involve a senior pastor in the search process. It is not wise to mandate a specific BCO procedure regarding senior pastor involvement in calling an assistant or an associate pastor. Adopted

OVERTURE 3 from Susquehanna Valley Presbytery (to CCB & B&O) "Amend BCO 20-2 to Include Pastor in Search Committee for Assistant or Associate Pastor"

Whereas, the Book of Church Order does not address the matter of searching for an assistant or associate pastor, and Whereas, for the peace and unity of the church it is vital that there be harmony among the pastoral staff of a church, and Whereas, any new assistant or associate pastor must be agreeable to and compatible with the senior pastor, Therefore be it resolved that the following be added to the BCO 20-2: "When a search committee for an associate pastor is formed by a congregation, the senior pastor shall automatically be a member of the committee. Before proposing a candidate to the congregation, the committee shall assure itself that the candidate is acceptable to and has the full support of the senior pastor. "In the case of a call to an assistant pastor, Session may act as the search committee or it may appoint church members as a search committee to bring a candidate for Session approval. In either case, the senior pastor shall be a member of the search committee."

Adopted by the Susquehanna Valley Presbytery on September 16, 2000. Attested by: D. F. Rundle, Stated Clerk

4. That Overture 4 be answered in the negative. Adopted as amended

OVERTURE 4 from Eastern Carolina Presbytery (to CCB & B&O) "Change Procedure for Pastoral Relationship Dissolution, BCO 23-1"

190

<a id="ga29-p193"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=193 printed_page=191 -->

Be it resolved that the Book of Church Order (BCO) 23-1 be amended as follows:

Existing provision: BCO 23-1, first two paragraphs "BCO 23-1. When any minister shall tender the resignation of his pastoral charge to Presbytery, the Presbytery shall cite the church to appear by its commissioners, to show cause why the Presbytery should or should not accept the resignation. If the church fail to appear, or if its reasons for retaining its pastor be deemed insufficient, his resignation shall be accepted and the pastoral relation dissolved. If any church desires to be relieved of its pastor, a similar procedure shall be observed. But whether the minister or the church initiates proceedings for a dissolution of the relation, there shall always be a meeting of the congregation called and conducted in the same manner as the call of the pastor. In any case, the minister must not physically leave the field until the Presbytery or its commission empowered to handle uncontested requests for dissolution has dissolved the relation."

The proposed revision of the first two paragraphs only, follows: "BCO 23-1. When any minister shall tender the resignation of his pastoral charge to Presbytery, the Presbytery shall cite the church to appear by its commissioners, to show cause why the Presbytery should or should not accept the resignation. A meeting of the congregation shall be called and conducted in the same manner as the call of a pastor, and either accept the resignation or be prepared to show cause why the Presbytery should not accept it. If any church desires to be relieved of its pastor, a meeting of the congregation shall be called to request the Presbytery to dissolve the pastoral relation, and the meeting shall be conducted in the same manner as the call of a pastor. If the pastor is agreeable to the dissolution, he shall not leave the field until the Presbytery or its commissioners empowered to handle the congregation's request has dissolved the relation. If the minister shall contest the requested dissolution, both the church and its pastor shall be cited to appear before the Presbytery to present their reasons for dissolution and reasons for contesting the dissolution. Since the bare fact that a majority of the members of a particular church desires to be relieved of its pastor is not per se a sufficient ground for dissolution, the Presbytery shall first hear from the church, then from the pastor in order to determine whether the dissolution is consistent with the Word of God in regard to the causes heard and would therefore be in the interest of both parties. In no case shall a contested request for dissolution be heard by a commission of Presbytery.

Supporting Reasons:

1. This change in the BCO is needed to make clear that a movement for dissolution on the part of a pastor or a congregation must come in the form of a

191

<a id="ga29-p194"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=194 printed_page=192 -->

request to the Presbytery and, as such, it is to be carefully weighed in the light of all the circumstances. Dissolution of a pastoral bond is within the power of the Presbytery only and is not a "rubber stamp" action based solely on the will of either the congregation or its pastor. Especially in regard to congregational requests for dissolution, there is a growing sentiment within the PCA that the will of the majority of a congregation should prevail regardless of the issues that led to the request. In other words, a congregation, like a democracy, is entitled to be relieved of its pastor simply if a majority wishes it to be so, whatever the circumstances. Such a view may be congregational, but it is not Presbyterian. The majority of a congregation may have faulty, erroneous or unbiblical grounds for wishing the removal of its pastor, and in such cases the Presbytery may deny their request in favor of a minority in the congregation who wish to continue under the ministry of a faithful pastor. A majority of Israel wished to be relieved of Moses and return to Egypt, but they were clearly in error. Had a majority returned to Egypt, Moses no doubt would have continued to pastor the faithful minority and lead them on to the land of promise. A majority of the elders, and presumably the people, wished to be relieved of Jeremiah's ministry and challenged his authority. "Thou speakest falsely: the Lord our God hath not sent thee..."(Jer. 43:2), they said; but our sympathy and support would have been with Jeremiah and the remnant who were faithful to his ministry. 2.A contested request of the congregation for dissolution of the pastoral bond is too weighty a matter to be handled by a commission of Presbytery. The Presbytery alone can authorize the formation of a pastoral bond, and the Presbytery alone should dissolve that bond. BCO 23-1 in its present form does not expressly grant Presbyteries authority to act through commissions in such serious matters although the language has been interpreted broadly. On the other hand, the present wording, "The minister must not leave the field until the Presbytery or its commission empowered to handle uncontested requests for dissolution has dissolved the relation", could be said to suggest that only uncontested requests are appropriately handled by a commission.

3. There is need in the PCA to set in place a clear rule of discernment and judgment especially in matters of contested dissolution requests. To say that the majority of the congregation is entitled to its wish without regard to the circumstances and without evaluating the cause of the majority in the light of Scripture, is neither wise nor safe. To "save" a church by yielding to a majority in rejecting a faithful pastor without legitimate grounds may be to sacrifice a faithful minority to an unfaithful majority. This is not to save a church in the true sense of the word, for the blessing of God may be withdrawn from a church in such circumstances. If the congregation rejects one appointed by Christ to serve, may it not be viewed by the Head of the Church as a rejection of Him? This principle is illustrated in the words of God to Samuel: "They have not rejected you, but they have rejected me" (I Sam. 8:7). When the prophets were

192

<a id="ga29-p195"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=195 printed_page=193 -->

refused, God was refused; and history often revealed the divine displeasure. "Touch not mine anointed, and do my prophets no harm" (Psalm 105: 15). When Paul's apostleship was not acknowledged, Christ was not acknowledged. Examples of churches left to themselves after rejecting a faithful undershepherd of Christ may be found in every age.

This is not to suggest that the Presbytery should never dissolve the pastoral bond between a faithful pastor and a congregation in cases of contested requests for dissolution. There may be circumstances in which a pastor not accused of any personal fault in life, doctrine or ministry should step aside. Such actions warrant Presbytery's most careful deliberation in the light of Scripture and sound reason.

The changes proposed in this overture are offered in the interest of providing a mechanism for Presbyteries to carefully address these important and often difficult matters. May the King and Head of the Church be pleased to assist us in promoting His revealed will for the governance of His Church.

Adopted at the Fall Stated Meeting of Eastern Carolina Presbytery, on October 21, 2000. Attested by: /s/ Austin Leake, Stated Clerk

5. That Overtures 7 from Calvary Presbytery, #20 from New River Presbytery, and #23 from Mississippi Valley Presbytery [dealing with exceptions to the length of creation days] be answered in the negative. Grounds: It is the prerogative of the lower courts to determine if a man's view is an exception to the standards. Adopted

Minority Report (Overtures 7, 20, and 23)

We the undersigned respectfully disagree with the majority report of the Bills and Overtures Committee on the matter of Overtures 7, 20 and 23, and offer the following Minority Report as a substitute:

"Handling of views of Creation regarding our Confessional Standards"

Whereas, the Presbyterian Church in America is a confessional church based upon the Scriptures and certain doctrinal statements as interpreted in the Westminster Standards; and Whereas, the Scriptures in Genesis 1, Exodus 20:11 and Exodus 31:17 teach that God created the heavens and the earth, the sea and all that is in them in six days; and Whereas, "[b]y faith we understand that the universe was formed at God's command, so that what is seen was not made out of what was visible" (Hebrews 11:3, NIV); and

193

<a id="ga29-p196"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=196 printed_page=194 -->

Whereas, our Confession of Faith states that God created the universe "in the  
space of six days" (WCF 4.1; WLC 15, 120; WSC 9, 58 and 59); and  
Whereas, the 28th General Assembly affirmed that "a diversity of views on  
creation days...is acceptable" thus, in essence, invalidating any definitive  
creedal statement; and  
Whereas, many in the denomination interpret the decision of the 28th General  
Assembly as removing the right of the courts of original jurisdiction to  
determine the acceptability of a man's particular view, as long as his  
view is one of those numerous addressed in the Report of the Creation  
Study Committee; and  
Whereas, the words "in the space of six days" are reasonably and normally  
interpreted to mean six consecutive days of normal duration and any  
alleged ambiguity to the words "in the space of six days" is clarified by  
the growing historical and scholarly evidence that demonstrates the  
intent of the Westminster Assembly to define the "space of six days" as  
days of normal duration; and  
Whereas, integrity compels a man to make known his particular views to the  
courts of original jurisdiction, especially when such views differ from  
our Confessional Standards; and  
Whereas, the courts of original jurisdiction ought to examine a man and to  
determine whether his particular views are consistent with or differ from  
our Confessional Standards (BCO Preliminary Principle III; BCO 26-1);  
Therefore, Be It Resolved, that the 29th General Assembly of the PCA  
acknowledge, with charity toward all our members, and with integrity  
regarding our Confessional Standards, that the Westminster Standards'  
phrase "in the space of six days" means that the six days of creation were  
days of normal duration with evening and morning; and  
Be It Further Resolved, that, for the peace of the church, any man who holds a  
view which may differ with the above meaning of the phrase "in the  
space of six days" shall inform the court of original jurisdiction of such  
view for its consideration and determination; and  
Be It Finally Resolved, that courts of original jurisdiction make all  
determinations on the acceptability of a man and his views with care,  
charity, honesty, and impartiality.

Signed, RE Mark A. Buckner RE Fredrick T. Greco TE Carl W. Bogue RE Dennis W. Baker TE Paul Honomichl TE G. Brent Bradley TE Jerry I. Maguire RE M. Dale Peacock RE Andrew J. Webb TE Byron Snapp

OVERTURE 7 From Calvary Presbytery (to CCB & B&O) "Require Exceptions for Views Other Than Six 24-Hour Creation Days"

Whereas, the Presbyterian Church in America is a confessional church based upon the Westminster Standards; and Whereas, our Confession of Faith states the time frame of God's original creative activity with the phrase, "in the space of six days" (WCF 4:1); and Whereas, growing historical evidence demonstrates the intent of the Westminster Assembly was to define the six creation days as 24-hour calendar days (At least 13 Westminster divines have been identified as attesting to a 24-hour creation day in their writings and recorded sermons; while none has been documented as holding to other time frames.); and

195

<a id="ga29-p198"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=198 printed_page=196 -->

Whereas, the official position of Calvary Presbytery states that the doctrine of  
the Confessional standards of the Presbyterian Church in America  
explicitly asserts that the world was created by divine fiat, literally "in  
the space of six days". Because the Confession's teaching on creation is  
unassailably grounded in Scripture, we joyfully proclaim that our  
preaching and teaching should conform to its content and emphases.  
(Adopted October 24, 1995); and  
Whereas, the 28th General Assembly affirmed that "...a diversity of views on  
creation days...is acceptable" thus, in essence, invalidating any definitive  
creedal statement; and  
Whereas, it has been our historic practice during elder examinations to note any  
differences from our standards as exceptions to be discussed by the  
church court;  
Therefore Be It Resolved, that the 29th General Assembly of the PCA declare  
that, with charity toward all our members, and with fidelity to the  
original authors of our confessional standards, and until evidence to the  
contrary is found, we understand the Westminster divines intended the  
phrase "in the space of six days" to specify that the six days of creation  
were days of normal duration with evening and morning; and  
Be It Further Resolved, that, for the peace of the church, any future candidates  
who differ with this original meaning should request an exception to the  
sense of the Confession unless documentation that the Westminster  
divines held other views is firmly established or unless the Standards are  
duly amended; and  
Be It Finally Resolved, that courts of original jurisdiction make these future  
determinations with care, charity, honesty, and impartiality.

Adopted by Calvary Presbytery on January 27, 2001. Attested by: /s/ Charles E. Champion, Stated Clerk

OVERTURE 20 from New River Presbytery (to B&O & CCB) "Allow Exceptions on Length of Creation Days"

Whereas, the 28th General Assembly rejected the unanimous recommendation of the Creation Study Committee to wait two years before taking any action on the subject of the interpretation of the length of the days of creation in Genesis 1 and 2; and Whereas, the 28th General Assembly gave approval to an action which, while described by the Moderator as simply 'pious advice', is being perceived by many in the denomination as pressure to approve candidates for office without regard to their views on these issues, therefore, BE IT RESOLVED, that New River Presbytery, voting at its 80th Stated Meeting in Roanoke, Virginia on November 10, 2000, hereby encourages and requests the 29th General Assembly of the PCA to take

196

<a id="ga29-p199"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=199 printed_page=197 -->

the following actions as additions and further explanation of the Assembly's response to the Creation Study Committee report:

- **A.** While the PCA recognizes both a historic and current diversity of views in the area of the length of creation days described in Genesis 1 and 2, it remains the primary and original responsibility of Presbyteries and Sessions to examine their candidates and determine if their views, no matter how diverse, are in accord with the Constitution of the church, and to determine if such views are exceptions.

- **B.** Presbyteries and Sessions who define any other view than the 24 hour day view as an exception to the standards in this area, in keeping with the actions of the 14th General Assembly, Section 143-52, Report of the Committee of Commissioners on Judicial Business, are to make the determination as to whether the teaching of these defined exceptions may or may not be allowed.

- **C.** Presbyteries and Sessions are counseled that, until such time as a view other than six, 24-hour solar day creation is adjudged to be out of accord with the fundamentals of the system of doctrine of the church through a change to the constitution, a final action in a judicial case, or the approval of a recommendation by a study committee, no officer should be refused ordination based on that exception alone. Adopted by New River Presbytery on November 10, 2000, at its 80th Stated Meeting. Attested by: /s/ Don K. Clements, Stated Clerk

OVERTURE 23 From Mississippi Valley Presbytery (to B&O &CCB) "Require Exceptions for Views Other than Six 24-Hour Creation Days"

Whereas, the Bible, in Genesis 1, Exodus 20:11, and Exodus 31:17 teaches that God created the heavens and the earth, the sea and all that is in them in six days, and Whereas, our doctrinal standards (WCF 4, LC 15, and SC 9) affirm that it pleased God, by the word of his power, to create the world and all things in the space of six days, and all very good. Therefore, Be It Resolved, with charity toward all members and with fidelity to the original authors of our confessional standards, our understanding is that, unless evidence to the contrary is found, the Westminster Standards' phrase "in the space of six days" means that the six days of creation were days of normal duration with evening and morning. Accordingly, for the peace of the church, any future candidates who differ with this original meaning should request an exception to the Confession, unless documentation that the Westminster Assembly meant otherwise is firmly established. We also pledge to make these future determinations, with care, charity, honesty and impartiality.

197

<a id="ga29-p200"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=200 printed_page=198 -->

Adopted at the Stated Meeting of Mississippi Valley Presbytery on February 6,

2001. Attested by: /s/ Roger G. Collins, Stated Clerk

6. That Overture 30 from North Georgia Presbytery ("Affirm Position of 28th Assembly on Diversity of Views on Creation Days") be answered in the negative. Grounds:

1. It is the responsibility of the lower courts to examine and determine if a man's views are in accord with the constitution, not the man himself, not the General Assembly, except in cases of judicial process.

2. Using general revelation to determine doctrine is contrary to WCF 1.6. Adopted OVERTURE 30 From North Georgia Presbytery (to B&O) "Affirm Position of 28th Assembly on Diversity of Views on Creation Days" Be it Resolved, that the North Georgia Presbytery overtures the 29th General Assembly of the Presbyterian Church in America to affirm the position of the 28th General Assembly, allowing a diversity of creation views, and likewise, with charity toward all our members, declare liberty-of-opinion concerning the intent of the Westminster divines in their use of the phrase "in the space of six days." Be it Further Resolved, that the 29th General Assembly recognizes that, within the church body, there are strongly held views concerning the days of creation; and, the Assembly acknowledges that for a creedal-based church, positions of diversity-of-view and liberty-of-opinion are not permanently satisfactory. Therefore, Presbyteries, Sessions and individual church members are encouraged to explore ways by which the scientific evidence of general revelation can be objectively studied and validated so that the church can move toward a unified understanding of how God created the universe and brought the earth into existence. Meanwhile, let us rejoice in our bonds of brotherhood and the hope we share in the reformed faith until our knowledge of His truth is more fully developed.

Adopted by North Georgia Presbytery on April 17, 2001. Attested by: /s/ Dwight Allen, Stated Clerk

7. That COMMUNICATION #4 from Western Carolina Presbytery be received as information, and spread upon the minutes of the 29th General Assembly. Grounds: We appreciate the concern and call for purity, peace, and unity in the denomination. Adopted

198

<a id="ga29-p201"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=201 printed_page=199 -->

COMMUNICATION #4 From Western Carolina Presbytery (to B&O) "A call for Purity, Peace and Unity of the Church"

Fathers and Brethren: Two years ago, Western Carolina Presbytery initiated inquiry into the question of a woman preaching at the Cedar Springs Presbyterian Church of Tennessee Valley Presbytery, and also into the views of the Rev. John Wood on the subject of women preaching. Our concern, shared by many throughout the denomination, was that a woman should not be allowed to preach in a PCA pulpit. Tolerating false doctrine and false practice is one way in which other denominations have degenerated in the past. We believe that failing to express our concern would not have fostered the purity, peace and unity of our Church. It has been our wholehearted desire to encourage and promote the peace of the church. While we confess that we have been far from perfect in that quest, we believe that we can, with clear conscience, testify to the fact that we were earnest and sincere in all of our actions with regard to the John Wood matter. It was never our intention or desire that the Cedar Springs Presbyterian Church should leave the PCA. We wanted to know the facts. Our hope all along was for this congregation and its pastor to conform to the obvious teaching of Holy Scripture with regard to female preaching. With the events that have transpired since that time, and the departure of the Cedar Springs Presbyterian Church from the PCA, Western Carolina Presbytery desires to issue a call to the whole PCA to bring closure to this matter and to endeavor to pursue together both the purity, peace and unity of the Church. A Committee of Western Carolina Presbytery interviewed members of the Standing Judicial Commission regarding various reports that had been circulated and found that the investigative committee of the SJC found and reported that there were no discrepancies in the testimony of witnesses. Mr. Wood acknowledged that the testimony of the witnesses was accurate, and he stated before the panel "he should have been more careful to articulate his belief that women should not be ordained to the teaching or ruling eldership and that they should not be permitted to 'preach' in the traditional sense of authoritative teaching from the word of God, and teaching elders are called and ordained to do." Though one may differ with the finding of the SJC, the WCP Committee found that the SJC had a full and frank deliberation of the investigating panel's report and voted unanimously that "the investigation has not resulted in a strong resumption of guilt on the part of TE John Wood... and therefore judicial process should not be instituted against TE John Wood for his expressed views regarding women." We accept the decision of the SJC. The WCP investigation found that the SJC followed the Manual of Operations in determining to disqualify any one of the SJC members from participating in the deliberation.

199

<a id="ga29-p202"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=202 printed_page=200 -->

It is because of all the controversy and alleged irregularities surrounding the John Wood matter that we, once again, found ourselves duty-bound to raise the question of possible impropriety when reports were circulated that one or more members of the SJC had deliberately sought to protect John Wood at the Vision 2000 Caucus, but had not recused themselves from debating and voting. The WCP Committee investigated these allegations, and are happy to report that we have not been able to confirm them. In a statement made to two members of our Presbytery, RE John White, Chairman of the SJC, stated that he had not tried to advocate any particular course of action for the Assembly to take prior to the meeting of the Assembly itself. Mr. White indicated that at a meeting of the Vision 2000 Caucus several months prior to the 2000 General Assembly, he had set forth what he thought was the Constitutional position, viz., that the Assembly could not overturn the SJC's determination in the John Wood matter. We hereby report Mr. White's recounting of the facts, in the hope that the rumor that one or more SJC members have engaged in improper lobbying regarding the John Wood matter can now be put to rest. As we come to closure on the John Wood Judicial Matter, we hope and pray that all of us in the Presbyterian Church in America have learned from it. Perhaps the foremost lesson is that in order to maintain the bond peace (Ephesians 4:3-6), which we all desire, there must be genuine unity; and that, in order to have proper unity, humility (Eph. 4:2, Philippians 2:1-22) is the necessary foundation. Of course unity can only be maintained between differing brethren when there is a genuine respect for the integrity of all parties, a gentle patience that bears with one another (Eph. 4:2). For whatever the reason, there seems to have been a general breakdown of trust across the denomination. The biblical way to restore trust is for individuals to pursue each other to resolve differences and clear up misunderstanding and miscommunication (Matthew 5 and 18). We pray that the Lord may be pleased to restore peace to us and maintain purity, peace and unity among us. Again, we urge that the John Wood matter be put to rest by this year's General Assembly, recognizing that she must handle the several questions that have been raised by Ascension and Calvary Presbyteries. We trust that we can now move forward as a denomination, in the bonds of purity, peace and unity in which we can all rejoice.

Adopted at a called meeting of Western Carolina Presbytery on May 8, 2001. Attested by: /s/ Skip Gilliken, Stated Clerk

8. That Overture 8 from Calvary Presbytery ("Condemn Action of SJC in Judicial Matter 99-1 (re. TE John Wood)") be answered in the negative with reference to Communication 4, which states our grounds. Adopted

OVERTURE 8 From Calvary Presbytery (to B&O) "Condemn Action of SJC in Judicial Matter 99-1 (re. TE John Wood)"

Whereas, the 28th General Assembly instructed the SJC to hear from the  
Presbyteries concerned in the charges against John Wood; and  
Whereas, the SJC nor its panel of three men gave the Presbyteries an  
opportunity to speak to the theological and constitutional issues involved  
in the John Wood case; and  
Whereas, the SJC made theological interpretations without hearing from the  
Presbyteries; and  
Whereas, the SJC was instructed to determine Mr. Wood's views, in their report  
they do not focus on his views but that he has not agitated for the view  
that women may preach in the church; and  
Whereas, in the report of the panel there is a conflict between the testimony of  
Drs. Smith and Pipa and that of Mr. Wood with respect to Mr. Wood's  
definition of preaching and there was no opportunity for cross  
examination; and  
Whereas, there is a conflict between the report of Mr. Wood's position in the  
SJC ruling and his expressed position in his letter of October 2, 1999;  
and  
Whereas, such conflict can only be resolved through a trial with cross  
examination; and  
Whereas, in its spring meeting in 2000 the SJC would not allow its members  
who were from the Presbyteries that brought the original overtures to the  
SJC to vote on the issue, even though it was pointed out that in cases of  
original jurisdiction no member of the court was required to recuse  
himself.  
Therefore Be It Resolved, Calvary Presbytery overtures the 29th General  
Assembly of the Presbyterian Church in America to condemn the report  
of the 28th Assembly through the SJC (not to draw up charges against  
Mr. Wood and proceed to a trial).

9. That Overtures 9 and 11 from Evangel Presbytery ("Procedures on Assuming Original Jurisdiction") be answered in the negative. Grounds: The concept of original jurisdiction is strong and dear to the denomination and must be preserved. However, the proposed changes to the BCO lead to the possibility of the court of original jurisdiction becoming the court of exclusive jurisdiction. The details of the proposed administrative procedures produce more difficulties than benefits in dealing with spiritual problems. Adopted

OVERTURE 9 From Evangel Presbytery (to CCB & B&O) "Procedures on Assuming Original Jurisdiction Over Church Members"

A New BCO 33-1 Process against all church members, other than ministers of the Gospel, shall be entered before the Session of the church to which such members belong, except in cases of appeal. This principle of original jurisdiction is designed to protect the right of the Session to investigate and adjudicate matters of sin within its bounds. Additionally, this principle of original jurisdiction is designed to protect the church member against judicial charges from those outside the Session who do not necessarily have access to the facts or access to the right of investigation. However, if there are other sessions in the same Presbytery which are not satisfied with how the Original Jurisdiction Session (OJS) has dealt with a matter of allegation against one of its members, then the following process shall be followed:

1. Those other sessions in the same Presbytery must formally request the OJS to conduct a BCO 31- 2 investigation of allegations against or reports surrounding this member within the OJS's jurisdiction.

2. If the OJS conducts a BCO 31-2 investigation, then the matter will remain totally within the jurisdictional bounds of the OJS, subject, of course, to BCO provisions of complaint appeal, review and control.

3. If these other sessions in the same Presbytery (which followed step one above) do not believe that a BCO 31-2 investigation has taken place within a reasonable time period. these other sessions may request their Presbytery to assume original jurisdiction.

4. If at least two of these other sessions in the same Presbytery (who followed step one above) make such a request for their Presbytery to assume original jurisdiction, the matter shall be dealt with at the next stated meeting of the Presbytery at which time a commission will be appointed to conduct a preliminary hearing as to whether or not the OJS has conducted a BCO 31-2

202

<a id="ga29-p205"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=205 printed_page=203 -->

investigation prior to the time of the commission's preliminary hearing. The commission may consider written briefs and oral presentations from the OJS and the two (or more) accusing sessions. The only question to be considered at this hearing is this: At the time of this commission's preliminary hearing, has the OJS conducted a BCO 31-2 investigation of the alleged behavior or belief of its member.

5. If the commission determines that the OJS has conducted the BCO 31- 2 investigation, then the commission shall rule that the OJS has acted to exercise its right of original jurisdiction.

6. If the commission determines that the OJS has not conducted the BCO 31-2 investigation (even though it has been properly asked to do so and has had sufficient time to do so), then the commission shall rule that the OJS has forfeited its right of original jurisdiction, shall rule that Presbytery has assumed the right of original jurisdiction and shall try the case as the court of original jurisdiction.

Grounds/Rationale:

- **A.** The controversy at our 28th General Assembly surrounding the John Wood matter engulfed our Standing Judicial Commission, our GA Stated Clerk, our Committee on Constitutional Business, our Bills and Overtures Committee of Commissioners, and our floor of the General Assembly in a constitutional quagmire because the existing BCO 34-1 does not adequately answer several questions:

1. What does "refuses to act" mean?

2. Who gets to decide what "refuses to act" means?

3. Does the Stated Clerk of the GA give this BCO 34-1 matter to the SJC for adjudication or route it directly to the GA via the Bills and Overtures Committee of Commissioners?

4. How can we balance the concerns between the need to protect the doctrinal purity of our church and the need to protect our principle of original jurisdiction which serves in turn to protect our ministers from judicial charges from those who may not necessarily have access to all of the facts or access to the right of investigation

- **B.** BCO 34-1 is amended, then BCO 33-1 must also be amended so that there is a consistency in our constitutional principles as they apply to our Presbyteries and our Sessions.

Approved at the Stated Meeting of Evangel Presbytery on Tuesday 23 January

2001. Attested by: /s/ Dr. Richard Trucks, Stated Clerk

OVERTURE 11 From Evangel Presbytery (to CCB & B&O) "Amend BCO 34-1 on Assuming Original Jurisdiction of Ministers"

203

<a id="ga29-p206"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=206 printed_page=204 -->

A New BCO 34-1 Process against a minister shall be entered before the Presbytery of which he is a member. This principle of original jurisdiction is designed to protect the right of the Presbytery to investigate and adjudicate matters of sin within its bounds. Additionally, this principle of original jurisdiction is designed to protect the minister against judicial charges from those outside the Presbytery who do not necessarily have access to the facts or access to the right of investigation. However, if there are other presbyteries which are not satisfied with how the Original Jurisdiction Presbytery (OJP) has dealt with a matter of allegation against one of its member ministers, then the following process shall be followed:

1. Those other presbyteries must formally request the OJP to conduct a BCO 31-2 investigation of allegations against or reports surrounding this minister within the OJP'S jurisdiction.

2. If the OJP conducts a BCO 31- 2 investigation, then the matter will remain totally within the jurisdictional bounds of the OJP, subject, of course, to BCO provisions of complaint, appeal, review and control.

3. If these other presbyteries (which followed step one above) do not believe that a BCO 31- 2 investigation has taken place within a reasonable time period, these other presbyteries may request the General Assembly to assume original jurisdiction.

4. If at least two of these other presbyteries (who followed step one above) make such a request for the General Assembly to assume original jurisdiction, the matter shall be referred immediately by the GA Stated Clerk to the GA Standing Judicial Commission for a preliminary hearing as to whether or not the OJP has conducted a BCO 31- 2 investigation prior to the time of the SJC preliminary hearing. The SJC may consider written briefs and oral presentations from the OJP and the two (or more) accusing presbyteries. The only question to be considered at this hearing is: At the time of this SJC preliminary hearing, has the OJP conducted a BCO 31-2 investigation of the alleged behavior or belief of its member minister?

5. If the SJC determines that the OJP has conducted the BCO 31-2 investigation, then the SJC shall rule that the OJP has acted to exercise its right of original jurisdiction.

6. If the SJC determines that the OJP has not conducted the BCO 31-2 investigation (even though it has been properly asked to do so and has had sufficient time to do so), then the SJC shall rule that the OJP has forfeited its right of original jurisdiction, shall rule that General Assembly has assumed the right of original jurisdiction, and shall try the case as the court of original jurisdiction.

Grounds/Rationale:

And our floor of the General Assembly in a constitutional quagmire because the existing BCO 34-1 does not adequately answer several questions:

1. What does "refuses to act" mean?

2. Who gets to decide what "refuses to act" means?

3. Does the Stated Clerk of the GA give this BCO 34-1 matter to the SJC for adjudication or route it directly to the GA via the Bills and Overtures Committee of Commissioners?

4. How can we balance the concerns between the need to protect the doctrinal purity of our church and the need to protect our principle of original jurisdiction which serves in turn to protect our ministers from judicial charges from those who may not necessarily have access to all of the facts or access to the right of investigation.

- **B.** If BCO 34-1 is amended, then BCO 33-1 must also be amended so that there is a consistency in our constitutional principles as they apply to our Presbyteries and our Sessions.
