operation. Dominic Aquila will continue to serve as editor on a part-time basis. Other support staff and services will operate out of the AC offices.

VI. Strategic Planning The project was approved by the Twenty-eighth General Assembly. The Strategic Planning group has met twice since the last General Assembly. They are meeting again during the week of General Assembly. They are in preliminary stages of planning and will make a more detailed report to the next General Assembly.

VII. General Assembly Arrangements The Hyatt Hotel at DFW Airport, the scheduled site for the Assembly meeting, cancelled our contract due to the Airport Authority's plan to demolish one of the hotel towers to build a new concourse. We were able to secure alternative arrangements with the Adams Mark Hotel in downtown Dallas due to diligent efforts by the AC staff and the Local Arrangements Committee. North Texas Presbytery is sponsoring a preassembly convocation dealing with the topic of doctrinal subscription. The convocation will be held Tuesday, June 19, 12:30-4:30 p.m. MNA was willing to forego their usual pre-assembly seminars in order to have the convocation. The cancellation of the contract by the Hyatt was the second such occurrence (the first being planning the 14th GA in Philadelphia) in the history of our denomination. This brought to the fore the need for some procedure to deal with such situations. The only present possibility is BCO 14-3, which deals with an emergency meeting of the Assembly. The AC recommends that the "RAO" be amended by the addition of a new provision to cover extraordinary events and unusual circumstances (see recommendation 6).

VIII. PCA Office Building The Twenty-eighth General Assembly approved the sale of the 1852 Century Place Office Building in Atlanta and authorized the purchase of land and construction of new office buildings (M28GA, pp. 368-371, 264-265). Accordingly, the 1852 Century Place Office Building was sold to Micron Optics, a growing company located in an adjacent building. A building site has been purchased near the intersection of I-85 and Sugarloaf Parkway in Gwinnett County, Georgia, approximately eighteen miles northeast of the Century Place Building. Ground breaking was held in January 2001. The complex was named the Cassels Ministry Center in honor of Mrs. Rosalie O. Cassels, a benefactor of many PCA causes. Two buildings of approximately 25,000 square feet each are under construction. MTW offices will be housed in one building; AC, CE&P, RUM, IAR, PCAF, MNA offices will be housed in the other building. There is room on the site for future expansion for both. The total costs of the building and relocation project are approximately $6,800,000. With the proceeds (approximately $2,880,000) from the sale of the Century Place Building, together with contributions and pledges received thus far, we need only about $500,000 to be able to move into the Ministry Center without a long-term debt. Development efforts are under way to reach that goal so that funds that would have had to be used for debt retirement may be used for the ministries of the various committees and agencies. In keeping with the General Assembly action MTW will have title to their section of the site and their building. The

### ATTACHMENT A

### BIBLICAL CONFLICT RESOLUTION

Preface As we continue to seek to become a church holy before God, the manner in which we respond to sin and conflicts in the body, and gently shepherd those caught in sin, will reflect our commitment to the authority of God's Word and the spirit of love which should define all of our actions and relationships. Biblical peacemaking is one of God's highest priorities (Matt. 5:23-24; Rom. 12:18; Gal.6:1); therefore, it must be one of our highest priorities. The Book of Church Order (BCO) reflects our commitment to following God's procedure for reclaiming those going astray. It says, "Scriptural law is the basis of all discipline because it is the revelation of God's Holy will. Proper disciplinary principles are set forth in the Scriptures and must be followed" (BCO 27-5). It also says, "An injured party shall not become a prosecutor of personal offenses without having tried the means of reconciliation and of reclaiming the offender, required by Christ" (BCO 31-5). The purpose of this appendix is to provide guidance through the steps of biblical peacemaking required as pre-conditions to judicial process in cases of personal offense (BCO 31-5), and for use whenever possible in cases of general offense (BCO 31-7).

Each presbytery should endeavor to have several elders trained in the methods of "Christian conciliation" (including mediation and arbitration), and available to serve as Christian conciliators in cases that could and should be resolved privately before judicial process is initiated. We would do well to follow the wisdom of those who have considered the importance of this matter. For example, Elder Edmond Clowney states, "Discipline...is not first an exercise of negative judgment, a matter of church courts and censures. It begins with the care of friends with whom we strive to follow Christ" (Clowney, E.P., The Church, IVP, 1995).

The Biblical Steps of Discipline as they Relate to Biblical Peacemaking

BCO 27-5 outlines the proper principles for the exercise of church discipline. This BCO section emphasizes that the steps indicated, (a) through (d), must be followed in proper order. The steps are:

- **a)** Instruction in the Word;

- **b)** Individuals' responsibility to admonish one another (Matt. 18:15; Gal. 6:1);

- **c)** If the admonition is rejected, then the calling of one or more witnesses (Matt. 18:16);

- **d)** If rejection persists, then the church must act through her court unto admonition, suspension, excommunication and deposition. This appendix addresses the first three steps, (a) through (c), by providing an expanded discussion of the implications raised by Scriptural direction for a complete process at each

382

<a id="ga29-p385"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=385 printed_page=383 -->

step. Step (d), formal church discipline, is addressed by Part II of the Book of Church Order, The Rules of Discipline.

1. The first step - Instruction in the Word. Many Christians do not fully understand the emphasis God places on living at peace and in unity with others ( Eph. 4: 3). Preaching and teaching should regularly address this emphasis and the purposes for church discipline as set forth in BCO 27-3 and BCO 27-4. Attention should be drawn to the fact that the main procedural passage related to church discipline, Matthew 18:15-20, is set forth in the context of two powerful parables teaching the extent and depth of God's love in reclaiming those who have strayed (Matt. 18:10-14), and the vast measure of His forgiveness and the expansive forgiveness He expects from His children toward one another (Matt. 18:21-35). The extent of instruction on reconciliation provided to church members in "new member classes" and regular preaching from the pulpit will have a significant bearing on the extent to which a church member understands the benefits of church discipline and has consented to ecclesiastical jurisdiction (which is helpful for the church if it is to avoid legal liability for the proper exercise of church discipline).

Teaching God's Word concerning sin and conflicts that result from it, and how Christians should respond biblically to conflict, will equip church members to become peacemakers themselves. Peacemaking has always been one of a Christian's most important ministries. As we are reminded in 2 Corinthians 5:18, God "reconciled us to himself through Christ and gave us the ministry of reconciliation." One of the most powerful ways that we can encourage reconciliation with God is to model reconciliation among people. When others see us resolve our differences in a loving and biblical manner, they are inclined to give more weight to what we say about the Lord (John 13:34-35; 17:20- 23). On the other hand, when they see Christians embroiled in disputes, they tend to write God's people off as hypocrites and dismiss the claims of Christ (Rom. 2:21-24; 1 Cor. 6:1- 8).

The Bible sets forth a process for resolving personal and substantive disputes in a constructive manner. This process is sometimes referred to as "Christian conciliation" and it may be used to resolve everything from minor personal differences to church divisions or lawsuits involving church members. As indicated in passages such as Proverbs 19:11, Matthew 5:23-25 and 18:15-20, 1 Corinthians 6:1-8, and Galatians 6:1, conciliation involves three basic steps: (1) when Christians are involved in a conflict that is too serious to overlook, the first thing that they should do is meet together privately and in person to try to resolve their differences; (2) if this effort is unsuccessful, they should ask one or more other Christians to meet with them and help them to seek reconciliation and a voluntary settlement of their differences (a process sometimes referred to as mediation); and (3) if they cannot arrive at a voluntary settlement, they should ask one or more other Christians to hear both sides of the matter and render a biblically based decision that both sides are obligated to accept (a process sometimes referred to as arbitration).

There are many benefits to resolving disputes through Christian conciliation. It prevents a public quarrel that would dishonor the Lord Jesus Christ and diminish the credibility and witness of His church. Conciliation also allows Christians to demonstrate

383

<a id="ga29-p386"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=386 printed_page=384 -->

their faith in Christ and their confidence in His teachings (John 13:34; 14:15; 17:20-23). In addition, conciliation encourages forgiveness and promotes reconciliation, which can help to preserve valuable relationships and strengthen the church (Eph. 4:29-32; Col. 3:12-17). Conciliation also helps people to identify and deal with the root causes of conflict, which may include such things as pride, selfishness, fear, vengeance, greed, bitterness, or unforgiveness (see Matt. 7:3-5). This allows people to make changes in their lives so that they will enjoy more peaceful relationships in the future (Eph. 4:1-3, 22-24).

Christian conciliation is especially beneficial for people who sincerely want to do what is right and are open to learning where they have been wrong (Prov. 15:31-32). Conciliators can help them to identify improper attitudes or unwise practices, to understand more fully the effects of their decision and actions, and to make improvements in their lives that will help them to honor and serve the Lord more effectively in the future (1 Peter 2:12).

Teaching and Ruling elders are encouraged to learn all they can about Christian conciliation and develop local ministries that will equip members under their care to respond to conflicts in a manner that reflects the power of Christ working in their lives. The more church members understand these concepts and benefits, the more likely they will be to apply biblical principles when conflicts occur.

2. The second step - An individual's responsibility to admonish another (Matt. 18:15; Gal. 6:1). Scripture warns against making a premature judgment about a matter (Matt. 7:1-5). By first going personally and in private to those who have offended, we provide the opportunity for clarification of misunderstandings and avoid premature judgment. This step includes the three responses of personal peacemaking as follows:

Overlook an offense: An individual may overlook an offense of another if it is minor in nature and it has not significantly dishonored God, damaged a personal relationship, or hurt other people (including the offender). "A man's wisdom gives him patience; it is to his glory to overlook an offense"(Prov. 19:11).

Discussion: When personal wrongs are too serious to overlook, the parties are required to seek to resolve them privately through loving confrontation and confession. "If your brother has something against you...go and be reconciled" (Matt. 5:23-24). "If your brother sins against you, go and show him his fault, just between the two of you" (Matt. 18:15).

Negotiation: When a substantive issue related to money, property, or other material issues or rights divides Christians, a process of biblical negotiation should be followed that will meet the interests of all those involved. "Each of you should look not only to your own interests, but also to the interests of others" (Phil.2:4).

Privately responding to conflict early, before it escalates, through the means of these three forms of personal peacemaking will often result in reconciliation and no need for further peacemaking attention. Successful personal peacemaking is usually based on at least one parties willingness to accept responsibility for how they have contributed to the conflict and by being willing to humble themselves for the greater goal of God's glory through "making every effort" (Eph. 4:3) to keep the unity of the spirit.

384

<a id="ga29-p387"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=387 printed_page=385 -->

3. The third step - If private admonition is rejected, then calling of one or more witnesses (Matt. 18:16; 1 Cor. 6:1-9). Involving others is a serious escalation of a conflict and should be considered only after the elements of step two have been fully exhausted. Step three includes the three assisted peacemaking responses as follows:

Mediation: If a dispute cannot be resolved through personal peacemaking, the parties should ask one or more other Christians to meet with them to help the parties communicate more effectively and explore possible solutions. The mediators may give advice but have no power to impose solutions. They may later act as witnesses in formal church disciplinary proceedings should mediation fail due to hardness of heart or the unrepentant sin of one or both parties. "If he will not listen, take one or two others along, so that every matter may be established by the testimony of two or three witnesses." (Matt. 18:16).

Arbitration: When two parties to a conflict cannot come to a voluntary agreement on a substantive issue, one or more arbitrators may be appointed to listen to the arguments and evidence of each side and render a binding decision. "If you have disputes about such matters, appoint as judges even men of little account in the church" (1 Cor. 6:1-8).

Church Discipline: Formal church discipline, pursuant to the procedures of BCO Part II, is reserved for those cases where the person who professes to be a Christian refuses to be reconciled, repent of personal sin, and do what is right. Church leaders bearing ecclesiastical jurisdiction over such persons should formally intervene to promote justice, repentance, and forgiveness. "If he refuses to listen, tell it to the church" (Matt. 18:17-20).

Application of the Principles

Judicial cases that come to the attention of church courts frequently begin as
personal disputes between two or more individuals. Typically, when one side feels they are
not getting what they want, they bring charges of sin against the other side. In this manner,
sessions and presbyteries are drawn into conflicts that would better be resolved at a personal
level through Christian conciliation. Of course, when conflicted parties refuse to be
reconciled, the accountability afforded by formal church discipline should be used to further
the goals of purity in the church, the rebuke of offenses, the removal of scandal, and the
spiritual good of offenders (1 Cor. 5:5). Every effort should be made, however, to resolve
the conflict through repentance, confession, forgiveness and reconciliation before formal
charges are entertained by a church court. The intent of the relevant BCO provisions is to
encourage Christian unity before the formal provisions of church discipline are brought to
bear on a situation. Of course, not every situation will lend itself to Christian conciliation.
However, every effort should be made to utilize private confrontation, mediation, and
arbitration in order to reserve the use of formal church discipline, and the time of church
courts, for those matters related to the purity of the church and the keeping and reclaiming
of disobedient sinners (BCO 27-3). Many of these ends will be realized through the
processes of Christian conciliation and, therefore, should be viewed as prerequisite
procedures to the formal disciplinary process.

385

<a id="ga29-p388"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=388 printed_page=386 -->

Failure to Follow the Steps

Churches unwilling or unable to instruct their members completely in the full
breadth of the steps of conciliation and discipline encourage resorting to unbiblical, worldly
responses to conflict. The escape responses of denial, flight, and even suicide can be
expected if church members are not positively directed to the biblical processes of Christian
conciliation. Others, when not given the hope of having matters responded to within the
body of Christ, will resort to civil litigation, verbal and physical attack, and possibly even
murder to remove an opponent where there is no avenue for a just resolution.

Moving a case too quickly to formal church discipline can build barriers that could otherwise be dealt with in mediation or arbitration. Every church and presbytery is encouraged to equip elders and mature members with the skills of Christian conciliation, and to exhaust conciliation processes and remedies before moving to formal church discipline.

Use of Conciliation Clauses in Membership Documents

One significant way church members can be educated and prepared for biblical conflict resolution is through the use of a conciliation clause in the membership covenant or other agreement signed by new members when they join the church. The recommended language for this clause is set forth below. It should be noted that signing this clause cannot be made a condition for membership, but may be encouraged as a voluntary biblical commitment. It should be clearly offered as an optional statement for the resolution of any disputes that may arise.

Christian Conciliation Members are encouraged but not required to make this additional commitment.

If I ever have a dispute with the church that cannot be resolved through its own
internal procedures, I agree to resolve the dispute according to biblical principles (such as
those set forth in Matthew 5:23-25 and 18:15-20, and 1 Corinthians 6:1-8) by submitting
the matter to mediation and, if necessary, arbitration, according to the Bylaws of this church
and the Rules of Procedure of the Institute for Christian Conciliation. I understand that
arbitration is a legally binding process, and that judgment upon an arbitration award may be
entered in any court otherwise having jurisdiction.

### THIS AGREEMENT IS SUBJECT TO ARBITRATION PURSUANT TO THE [STATE]

### ARBITRATION ACT, TITLE ##, CHAPTER #, [STATE] CODE ANNOTATED.

[The Institute for Christian Conciliation is a division of Peacemaker Ministries. For a copy of the Rules of Procedure, see www.His Peace.org or call (800) 711-7118. Other conciliation clauses for use in employment, construction, and service contracts are also available.]

Amend Church Bylaws to Allow Continuing Church Jurisdiction

The following clause is recommended for inclusion in local church bylaws to allow the continuing ecclesiastical jurisdiction over a member who may otherwise simply flee from the church to avoid biblical discipline:

Members may be removed from membership at their own request by informing the Session of their intention to withdraw and the reasons therefore. If a member requests to withdraw because of specific problems or disappointments with the church, the Session shall attempt to resolve those matters so that the member may remain in the church and enjoy greater fruitfulness and personal spiritual growth. If the Session is unable to resolve those matters, it shall offer to assist the member in locating a church of like faith and practice that can respond more effectively to his gifts and needs. If it appears to the Session that a member has requested removal merely to avoid church discipline, that request shall not be given effect until the disciplinary process has been properly concluded.

Use of this clause will also help the church avoid serious legal liability for following through with all of the steps of church discipline. Members should be informed of its provisions and carefully taught the Scriptural basis for continuing shepherding and pastoral care especially when caught in sin (see also BCO 38-3 and 38-4).

Conclusion

The courts of the church are encouraged to employ the means of Christian conciliation whenever possible. That is, churches and presbyteries are encouraged to defer judicial action until all other remedies have been exhausted. Peace, unity, and the mission of the Church can be furthered through careful and complete attention to every step of the process as set forth in BCO 27-5 as understood through the expanded guidance concerning Christian conciliation as set forth above.

### RESOLUTION

Whereas, in the providence of Almighty God, in 1982 He brought Mrs. Laurel De Bert to labor in the administrative offices of the Presbyterian Church in America, and

Whereas, the church at large, the General Assembly, Presbyteries, individual churches and members have all benefited from her heart for the concerns of the Church, and Whereas, her energy, enthusiasm, experience, expertise in meeting planning, and sacrificial service have resulted in the smooth, timely and efficient functioning of numerous Assemblies, committees, and meetings for the past 19 years, and

Whereas, over the course of these years her ability to get the job done with limited financial and personnel, and

Whereas, providing leadership as Administrative Assistant to the Stated Clerk year in and year out during the tenure of three Stated Clerks and working alongside and supervising many different staff members and volunteers has meant the effective operation of the Stated Clerk's Office, and

Whereas, she has performed the many complex and demanding tasks with diligence, perseverance and cheerfulness, and Whereas, her caring concern, graciousness in the midst of transition, and example as a sister in the Lord have ministered to countless members of the Body of Christ, therefore

Whereas, she now find it necessary to leave her position in the Stated Clerk's Office – Administrative Committee, therefore

Be It Resolved that the members of the Administrative Committee, meeting in Dallas, Texas on Tuesday, June 19 do hereby UNANIMOUSLY thank Mrs. Laurel DeBert for her labor of love these many years and for her service in support of the work of the Church of the Lord Jesus Christ, and commend her to this 29th General Assembly of the Presbyterian Church in America.

Adopted at the Administrative Committee Meeting, June 19, 2001,

### ATTACHMENT C

### REPORT OF THE

### PCA HISTORICAL CENTER

### TO THE

### ADMINISTRATIVE COMMITTEE

Our Mission: Since its establishment in 1985, the PCA Historical Center has sought to preserve and promote the record of what God has done and is doing through the people of the PCA. We do this by: Preserving the official records of the PCA, its agencies and committees. Collecting the personal papers of key individuals in the PCA. Promoting the writing of church histories by our local congregations. Working to develop in the people a deeper appreciation of the value of our legacy. Our New Home: September of 2000 saw the completion of work on the newly expanded J. Oliver Buswell, Jr. Library, where the Historical Center is located. Over the course of that month, some 2000 boxes were moved into place, some on shelving but most set on the floor, awaiting the purchase and installation of high-density moveable shelving. The Historical Center's new facility consists of a 440 sq. ft. Reading Room and behind that another room where the Center's collections are stored, measuring approximately 1500 sq. ft.

The new facility has a much more visible location on the Covenant Seminary campus, and as a result, the number of visitors to the Center has greatly increased. I have estimated that we have thus far seen a 400% increase in patronage overall, including requests coming in from our web site.

The one thing lacking at this point is that we still have not been able to raise all of the needed money to purchase the shelving, so the boxes are still on the floor, though neatly arranged in rows. Sufficient funds were raised and have been spent on the installation of the track and deck that the shelving will set on; all that remains is the purchase and installation of the shelving itself. We urge you to pray with us for God's provision of this great need, that we might properly preserve our legacy and better serve our people.

Website: At the time of last year's General Assembly, a major revision of the Historical Center's web site took place. Finding aids (indexes) to most of the collections were posted, along with many other resources. The greatly increased size of our site also resulted in a new and simpler address: www.pcanet.org/history. Then as 2001 began, we were able to begin uploads directly from our St. Louis location. This has meant that we are now able to keep the site up to date, with frequent additions of new content. A web journal page has been added which allows visitors to keep up on the latest news of activities and new acquisitions.

394

<a id="ga29-p397"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=397 printed_page=395 -->

Statistics have indicated that the site has roughly 1000 visitors and 8-10,000 "hits" per month.

Requests for services have come from South Africa, Wales and Australia, among others.

The Administrative Committee has authorized the Historical Center to pursue its own separate web site, using an address such as www.pcahistory.org. Such a move is still under consideration, but for the time being, the existing address seems to be working well for us and costs the Center nothing. The latter point is important, given our very modest operating budget.

Publications: Two new brochures have been published in the past year. Researching the Archive: A Guide to Its Resources is a basic introduction to using the facilities of an archive or manuscript repository. The other brochure, Should I Donate My Papers?, speaks to the common questions frequently asked by those considering a donation of documents to the Historical Center.

Records Processing: Due to the ongoing construction this last year, processing of collections slowed considerably. Almost all of our boxes had to be wrapped in plastic to protect them from dust and other construction hazards, and so I was only able to work with a few select collections. Much of my time was spent in moving the boxes to one location or another to stay ahead of construction crews. Now that the move to the new facility is more or less complete, processing has resumed.

Collections Development Notable materials received in the last year include the Papers of the Rev. B.I. Anderson, Stated Clerk of Mississippi Valley Presbytery and an almost complete bound set of Minutes from Mississippi Valley Presbytery, donated by TE Roger Collins. Also received were the Papers of the Rev. Dr. Frederick W. Evans, Jr. The latter collection is important to the Historical Center's effort to document something of the whole of the conservative Presbyterian movement in the 20th century. Rev. Evans was one who left the PCUSA in 1955 to independency and only late in life did he transfer his credentials to the PCA. Nonetheless, his life is an important witness to the larger story of the Continuing Presbyterian Church and a testimony to God's covenant faithfulness displayed across the generations of a family. His father, Frederick, Sr., is said to have been the last true evangelical to serve as moderator of the PCUSA; his son John is a PCA missionary in Zambia and his oldest son William is a professor at Erskine [Bill Evans was also the ARP fraternal delegate to our General Assembly in 1999]. Lastly, there was a substantial addition to the Papers of the Rev. Henry G. Welbon, donated by TE Stu Sherard upon the final dissolution of Rev. Welbon's estate and we have just received a major addition to the Papers of the Rev. Dr. R. Laird Harris.

Some 200 of our PCA churches are currently participating in the Local Church History program. Of these, about 150 actually have an appointed church historian who writes

395

<a id="ga29-p398"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=398 printed_page=396 -->

and submits an annual account. The remaining 50 or so simply send newsletters or other materials. Beyond these numbers, the Historical Center has some sort of file on about 600 PCA churches. In some cases we may only have a single Sunday bulletin to represent all that we know of a church's history. In a few cases we have several large boxes of materials. Most of our collections average perhaps a dozen file folders each. One goal for the coming year is to greatly increase the number of churches reporting information to the Center.

Staff: As of September 1, 2000, RE Wayne Sparkman has been moved to full-time status as Director of the Historical Center. Mrs. Florence Graham, who has worked here as a volunteer almost since the inception of the Historical Center, was unable to work in the Center this past year because of the construction work on the Library. She does anticipate returning to her volunteer duties soon. Additional volunteer workers will be recruited in coming months from among the Covenant Seminary students, now that the Center is situated in its new facility. M.Div. students will be able to earn a portion of the Field Education requirement by working in the Center.

New Endeavors: In May of 2000, I was pleased to be awarded a scholarship which substantially undercut the cost of attending a conference in Philadelphia. Hosted by the Conservation Center for Art and Historic Artifacts (CCAHA), the conference provided training in the preservation of architectural records. A number of our PCA churches have historically significant buildings and several are on the National Historic Register. Among the more notable of these is First Presbyterian Church in Augusta, Georgia, whose building was designed by Robert Mills, architect of the Washington Monument and other significant structures. Thus far, the PCA Historical Center had not ventured into this area of preserving architectural records. It is my hope that we can now more fully assist our churches in the preservation of all of their records, including the record of their "built environment." A brochure will soon be prepared which will allow me to share with our churches something of what I learned at the conference.

Historical Center Subcommittee: The Historical Center Subcommittee continues to faithfully provide guidance and oversight for the operations of the Center. It is a distinct honor to be able to work with these men and women of God. Members of the Subcommittee are: Dr. David Calhoun Dr. Donald J. MacNair Dr. Will Barker [newly elected] Dr. Frederic Mau Miss Lannae Graham Mr. John Spencer Mr. Edward S. Harris Mrs. Shirley Duncan

TE L. Roy Taylor and TE John Robertson are ex-officio members of this committee.

Respectfully submitted, /s/ RE Wayne Sparkman, M.A.R., M.Div. Director, PCA Historical Center

### ATTACHMENT D

Donald J. MacNair 1922-2001

The PCA Historical Center Committee lost one of its valued members this year, Dr. Donald MacNair. Don born in 1922, was born again in 1936. He enrolled graduated from Rutgers University, as a mechanical engineer. He was called into the ministry in 1944, the same year he was married to his childhood sweetheart, Evelyn, and attended Faith Theological Seminary from which he graduated with a B.D. degree in 1949.

He served the Bible Presbyterian Church of Coatsville, PA 1944-1953. Donald accepted the call of the First Bible Presbyterian Church in St. Louis, in 1953 following the ministry of Francis Schaeffer. The Bible Presbyterian Church changed its location to Town and Country and adopted a new name, The Covenant Presbyterian Church, where Don served from 1953 to 1964. During that time, the congregation grew to over 400.

In 1955, Don and five other men formed the Board of Directors for a new college and a new seminary, both called Covenant. Covenant Church and the MacNair home served as centers for these institutions, as well as the denominations and Synod of which they were a part. Don became president of the National Presbyterian Missions Committee of the Bible Presbyterian Church, General Synod

In 1962, Executive Director of NPM.

- **I.** In 1982 Don held a firm belief that denominations of like doctrine should merge, and was a leader in the formation of the Reformed Presbyterian Church, Evangelical Synod and in 1982 the RPCES joined with the Presbyterian Church in America. Don organized Churches Vitalized, Inc, a consulting firm, in 1972. In 1982, Geneva College awarded Don an honorary doctorate for his "ability to combine a behavioral engineering approach with the ministry." He authored seven books and continued to teach courses in practical theology at Covenant Seminary, where his life experiences and wisdom prepared students for the realities of the pastorate. He had a keen interest in the history of the conservative Presbyterian and Reformed movement in North America.

In 1974 Don was asked to serve on the Board of Directors for Life Care Retirement Facilities. He also served on the boards of Friendship Villages, West and South, and on the PCA Historical Center Committee until his death, March 3, 2001.

### BUDGET PHILOSOPHY

The budget is built primarily on the job description of the Stated Clerk in the RAO, which determines the services that are to be provided by the Office of the Stated Clerk to the churches, presbyteries, committees and agencies, and to the General Assembly.

### GENERAL COMMENTS

Many of the activities and responsibilities of the Administrative Committee are directly affected by the size and growth of the PCA, which in turn are reflected in annual budget increases for many line items. The economic inflation rate also affects most budget items and is applied to most line items, except as noted in the Economic Assumptions shown below.

The budgets are presented in a format to comply with the standards for not-forprofit organizations adopted by the Financial Accounting Standards Board (FASB). The FASB standards provide a definition of "supporting activities" which they call "management and general". Therefore, compensation for the Stated Clerk and his staff is allocated according to the estimated time spent by each person in "program," administration, and fund raising areas.

### CHRISTIAN EDUCATION & PUBLICATIONS

### PROPOSED BUDGET 2002

Philosophy: CE&P's ministry program is driven by the Strategic Faith Plan. The plan defines CE&P's mission, goals, strategies and programs. The proposed budget is a "program-based" budget and represents the resources needed to adequately fund the planned activities, which have been approved and/or directed by the Permanent Committee and the General Assembly.

Summary: The proposed 2002 expense budget represents a total increase of $140,960 or 5.20% from the 2001 budget. CE&P's contribution need increases by $75,960 or 4.51%. These increases are detailed and explained below.

Assumptions: Underlying assumptions include: 1) the PCA will grow between 3% and 5%; 2) the consumer price index or inflation rate will be approximately 4%; 3) Occupancy cost will remain at $14 per square foot (unless the building capital campaign raises the remaining balance); and 4) health insurance premiums are expected to increase 10%. Both the approved budget for 2001 and the proposed budget for 2002 are based on 24.55 full time equivalent employees. Currently, CE&P is not fully staffed so no increase is anticipated.

Notes:

Other Revenues (line 2) for 2002 are anticipated as follows:

Bookstore Sales/Postage $725,000 Seminar/Conference Fees $182,000 Subscriptions and Advertising $88,000 Video Library Memberships $50,000 Reimbursements (travel, postage, etc.) $45,000 Total $1,090,000

Training, Conferences and Consulting (page 2, line 3) represents a sustained increase that began in 1999 with a conference schedule of more than 15 conferences and 50 seminars and continues into 2001 with the Mercy Ministry conference. CE&P anticipates meeting the growing demand for training through regional multi-purpose conferences and a full complement of specialized training events. The Regional Trainers become more strategic in extending CE&P's reach to the local church. The Women in the Church (page 2, line 4) is anticipated to increase at a higher than average rate due to increased size and scope of the annual training meeting for women in leadership. Also, CE&P has recently added ten trainers to help multiply the denominational WIC ministry.

404

<a id="ga29-p407"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=407 printed_page=null -->

CE&P continues, in a limited way, to help local churches that request assistance in developing Men's Ministries (page 2, line 5). Currently, most of CE&P's ministry to men occurs through officer training events and consultation. Multi-cultural ministries (page 2, line 6) remains the same as the 2001 budget as CE&P believes it would be most effective to contract with various consultants who have expertise working with different ethnic groups. The significant increase in Youth Ministries (page 2, line 7) represents CE&P's assimilation of Presbyterian Youth of America. The expenses associated with CE&P's management of these conferences are offset by a corresponding increase in Revenue (page 2, line 2). This increase is likewise represented in Meeting Facility, Special Events, Travel and Honorariums (page 1, lines 33, 38, 22, 35.) CE&P will continue to develop the network of regional youth trainers and anticipates additional participants in the internship program. While CE&P has always provided training to those who work with children, CE&P is committed to establishing a Children's Ministries department (page 2, line 8) with a staff person to assist PCA churches in training workers, staffing positions and identifying resources available to them. The slight decrease is due to reevaluation of staffing needs for this department. Publications and Curriculum (page 2, line 9) includes the periodicals Equip for Ministry and the Bulletin Supplement and a portion of the WIC Resource Letter. It also includes the costs associated with developing and producing other annual materials for Stewardship season, PCA Week of Prayer and Christian Education Sunday as well as other video series and training manuals. The Bookstore (page 2, line 10) is the largest portion of the proposed budget. The increase of the Bookstore budget represents additional resources needed to further enhance the Bookstore's product offerings, services and related promotion. Management and General (page 2, line 12) is anticipated to increase as there will likely be unanticipated expenses associated with the office relocation which were not included in the 2001 budget and will need to be addressed in 2002. The decrease in Fund Raising (page 2, line 15) is due to the decision of CE&P to not renew the contract with a marketing consulting firm and instead pursue a plan of regionalized development representatives. Also see Professional Services (page 1, line 21). The 2002 budget represents two individuals being in place along with current CE&P staff development efforts. Though CE&P has temporarily been relieved of the responsibility of funding a portion of the PCA Foundation (page 2, line 16 and page 1, line 30), CE&P's management earnestly desires to participate in this program once again if funds are available. The Coordinator, his assistant and related expenses are allocated to the various expense categories as follows: Training 20%, Fund Raising 10%, Administration 10%, Bookstore 15%, WIC 10%, Men's Ministry 5%, Youth Ministries 10%, Publications and Curriculum 20%.

### COVENANT COLLEGE

### PROPOSED BUDGET 2001 - 2002

The college uses the NACUBO (National Association of College and University Business Officers) definitions of revenue and expense categories. This insures that the college will be able to directly compare various ratios with other colleges and assess our effectiveness in accordance with our assessment systems. While the categories do not exactly parallel the definitions used by the Accounting and Financial Reporting Guide for Christian Ministries, there is some similarity. NACUBO categories including Instructional, Academic Support, Library, Student Services, Public Service and Student Aid could be broadly considered "Program Services." Maintenance of Plant and Institutional Support could be considered "Supporting Activities." Several major accounting changes were made in 1996-1997 in accordance with changes in standards published by the Financial Accounting Standards Board. Included in these are two that have significantly changed the figures shown from previous years and made comparisons with those years unproductive. Therefore, the proposed budget spreadsheets show only years 1996-1997 and following. First, depreciation is now an operating expense rather than an expense only in the plant fund. The requirement to fund depreciation comes from a variety of directions. Funding depreciation is a good thing for an organization as it provides funds to repair and replace facilities as they age without additional fund raising. Generally accepted accounting principles also require depreciation to be accounted for as an operating expense and these rules must be followed to obtain an external audit in good standing. Finally, the accrediting body in which Covenant participates requires a balanced bottom line for continued accreditation, including depreciation. For these three reasons, the college must actually fund the depreciation expense from increased revenues. Due to this change, tuition will rise 3% more than otherwise would be the case for the next several years. These tuition increases will fund depreciation, allow Covenant to show a net positive bottom line and reduce pressure on future capital campaigns by providing funds for facility and equipment replacement and repair. This expense is shown on the expense spreadsheet divided between Maintenance of Plant Depreciation, representing the depreciation costs of the facilities used for educational purposes, and Auxiliary Depreciation, representing the depreciation costs of the residence halls, food service and for-profit facilities. Second, since capital gifts are shown as revenue in the year they are used for construction, but the construction expense only appears over time through depreciation, capital projects tend to positively overstate the operating results of the college. In order to show the results more clearly, the operating net results for the college are shown on the expense budget at the bottom of the page on the line titled "Increase (Decrease) in Undesignated Net Assets." This line will show a negative figure until the completion of funding the depreciation expense through the tuition increases mentioned in the previous paragraph.

### COVENANT THEOLOGICAL SEMINARY

### NEW BUDGET HIGHLIGHTS

FY 2001-02

- **I.** Revenue:

- **A.** Tuition and Fees:

1. Tuition in most programs will increase from $250 per credit hour to $260. This 4% increase is a little more than last year (3.3%) and the second lowest since at least 1990. Because we plan to discontinue the discount for any hours over 14 in a semester, the annual tuition for a student taking a full 30 hours would be $7,800. Tuition will pay about 41.9% of the cost to educate a seminarian. This is down from 42.2% this year.

2. We are projecting enrollment in the Fall of 2001 to be 4 full time equivalents higher, although head count will be down.

- **B.** Endowment: Earnings used after management expenses are budgeted to be 7.2%. This is up from 6.63% actually experienced for FY99-00 and the same as was budgeted for FY00-01. Endowment income in all areas (unrestricted, apartments, and student aid) will increase by $35,000, versus $223,600 for this year and $396,000 the year before.

- **C.** Gifts & Grants: The Gifts & Grants goal (PCA Partnership Share) will increase from $1,760,000 to $1,785,000. This is an increase of 1.42% and follows an increase of $30,000 or 1.73% for this year. This gifts & grants goal is an increasingly smaller percentage of the total operating budget compared to other typical seminaries. We are projecting Restricted Gifts of $233,000 for next year, up from $215,000 for this year. The increase is for Art @ The Institute, a program of the Francis Schaeffer Institute.

- **D.** Student Aid: This source of income is expected to remain flat at $219,400. These funds come from Endowment earnings.

- **E.** Other Income: We expect this source of income to decrease to $182,350 in the new year from $207,350 in the current year. Most of this decrease is from lower interest income due to funds held for the Youth In Ministry Institute, as those funds are expended. The interest income is unrestricted.

- **F.** Auxiliary Enterprises: Rents for the apartments will see smaller increases this year, as shown below. This follows about a 3% increase for this year.

Single student housing will be increasing about 3% for single occupancy and 4% for double occupancy. The additional income from all rents will be about $7,370. We are making a conscious effort to keep our rents marketcompetitive, while minimizing overall costs to our seminary students.

II. Expenditures:

- **A.** General:

1. The budget assumes overall salary increases of 3% for staff and 8% for faculty.

2. Medical Insurance premiums will change July 1, 2001. Preliminary quotes reflect a 15% increase, which has been the experience of other local employers.

3. General expenses (where appropriate) were held flat. The tight budget will mean that departments will have to reduce usage overall to allow for expected price inflation of about 3%

4. The Youth in Ministry Institute (YIMI) expenses are not shown in the budget since they are covered by restricted gifts also not shown.

- **B.** Educational & General:

1. President & Trustees: A small provision is made to help the President deal with the lack of equity build-up in a home, since his family resides in seminary housing that would be relinquished at his retirement.

2. Instruction - General Budget:. A full year's salary and benefits are reflected for a new professor to be added in July. A part-time faculty secretary position shared with D.Min. is converted to full-time. Faculty increases average 8%, due to the higher salaries now prevalent at similar institutions.

3. Instruction - Doctor of Ministry: Reflects salary increases and a portion of the faculty secretary position just described above.

4. Instruction - Master of Theology: Provision is made for 1 more class.

5. Instruction - Evening Program: Budgeted for 17 3-hour classes at $725 per credit hour.

6. Instruction - Extension Program: Increases for printing and computer hardware

7. Instruction - Counseling: Provision is made for professional advancement and furnishings for new counseling rooms.

8. Instruction - Francis Schaeffer Institute: Increases reflect the parttime person administering Art @ The Institute, which is covered by restricted gifts.

9. Instruction - Church Planting: Reflects increases in salaries and benefits.

10. Registrar's Office: Provision is made for fabrication of new graduation hoods.

11. Library: Provision is made for some additional staffing.

12. Student Services: Normal increases

414

<a id="ga29-p417"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=417 printed_page=415 -->

13. Family Nurture: Normal increases

14. Student Aid:

- **a.** Administration – Normal increases

- **b.** Scholarships – Normal increase, considering enrollment projections and this year's experience.

15. Development: Normal increases

16. Public Relations: Unchanged

17. Gift & Estate Planning: Normal increases

18. Admissions: Provision for staffing changes

19. Electronic Media Production: Retirement provision for new director; a reduction in expenses for media production equipment

20. Business Office: Some staffing changes and a higher provision for legal services

21. Computer Services: A reduction in staffing and an increased provision for new network servers

22. Physical Plant: Increases include more student labor for housekeeping due to the new library, and higher utilities and insurance expenses based on experience.

- **C.** Auxiliary Enterprises:

1. Operations: Increases for utilities

2. Student Apartments: Increases for utilities and insurance

3. Tape of the Month Club: Normal adjustments

- **D.** Transfers:

1. Educational & General:

- **a.** Money is annually transferred to the Plant Fund so that we can replace the President's auto every four to five years. Also, $13,410 is transferred to Renewal and Debt to amortize the expenses associated with the Administrative Software Project. This project will be fully amortized in July, 2005.

2. Auxiliary Enterprises:

- **a.** $36,000 is set aside as reserves for future apartment repairs.

- **E.** Contingency: The provision is for $12,000.

### INSURANCE ANNUITIES, AND RELIEF

### PROPOSED BUDGET 2002

Statement of Purpose The purpose of the Board of Trustees of Insurance, Annuity and Relief Funds of the Presbyterian Church in America is to glorify God through serving His servants who minister in the Church by offering financial products to provide for the health and welfare, retirement and relief needs of the denomination's ministers, missionaries, lay church workers and their families, and to serve the churches. committees and agencies of the PCA and related organizations by sponsoring and endorsing a denominational property and liability insurance program.

This budget reflects the costs incurred to administer the trust funds for Insurance, Retirement, and Relief. This budget does not reflect the financial activity in those trust funds. (Complete financial activity in the trust funds may be found in the IAR Annual Report, which includes audited financial statements.) The 2002 budget reflects an increase of 17.95% over the 2001 budget. 2000 actuals are unaudited. The increase in the Retirement portion of Support and Revenue is a more accurate representation of the allocation of expenses between supporting activities. The increase in the Relief portion of Support and Revenue reflects costs associated with moving the Relief virtual office back to the PCA building and transition costs for hiring and training a new Relief Representative. The total number of staff budgeted for in 2002 is 10 FTE. Currently, ten of these positions are filled. An overall net increase of 9.6% in salaries and benefits is assumed in 2002. Budgeted positions include a 4% average salary increase and a 10% health insurance increase. This increase does not include the positions discussed in the next bulleted item.

Because the Director and the Relief Representative will retire at the end of 2002, we have budgeted salary and benefits for the new Director at three months overlap and for the new Relief Representative at five months overlap. An overall net increase of 39.33% in rent is assumed in 2002 due to the additional square footage utilized by IAR in the new facility. An overall net increase of 20% in board meeting expense is assumed in 2002. Due to the building relocation, IAR board meetings will no longer be held at the current or the new PCA building. We also anticipate increased travel expense based on the probable composition of the Board of Trustees.

### MISSION TO NORTH AMERICA

### PROPOSED BUDGET 2002

The MNA Mission:

This budget reflects our continuing emphasis on regionalization – assisting and working with presbyteries to develop church planting in local areas.

Due to the impending transition of Reformed University Ministries to separate committee status, the budget for 2002 is being presented without the revenue and expense associated with campus ministries. This is creating a decrease of 9.4% compared to the 2001 budget which included campus ministries.

While the total revenue and expenses will decrease 9.4% compared to the 2001 budget, the portion included in the "partnership share" will decrease only 2%. These decreases are the result of Reformed University Ministries' budget being removed from the overall GA/MNA budget. The Partnership Share only decreases by 2%, because a lesser portion of the RUM budget is covered by Partnership Share than the GA/MNA budget. The remainder of the RUM budget is covered by affiliated campus transfers.

An overall net increase of 5% in salaries and benefits is assumed. That is an aggregate of cost of living, merit increases and health insurance costs.

The total number of multicultural missionaries budgeted for is 4. Between 59 and 77 projects are budgeted to receive direct support in church planting, multicultural church planting and urban and mercy ministries.

The total number of full-time equivalent staff budgeted for in the 2002 budget is 30-1/2, which is the same as in the 2001 budget. Twenty-nine and one-half of these positions are currently filled. The unfilled position is for an assistant coordinator for church planting.

The cost being charged by the Administrative Committee for office space is assumed to be at $14 per square foot; more square footage will be occupied in the new building. The complete and separate 2002 budget for Reformed University Ministries (MNA Campus Ministries and the affiliated presbytery campus committees) is provided.

### MISSION TO THE WORLD

### MTW DOCKET MEMO

TO: Finance/Management Subcommittee

### FROM:

Roger R. Kooistra

### DATE:

February 13, 2001

### SUBJECT:

Mission to the World Proposed Budget for 2002**

The proposed Mission to the World Consolidated Operating Budget for the calendar year 2002 is presented on the following pages. The consolidation includes career missionaries and projects, MTW/IMPACT, the Home Office, the Medial Insurance Fund (MIF) and the Endowment Fund.

The Presbyterian Church in America Administrative Committee has scheduled the review of budgets to take place March 15, 2001.

RECOMMENDATION: That the Proposed Consolidated 2002 Budget for Mission to the World, including MTW/IMPACT, the Medical Insurance Fund and the Endowment Fund be approved for the calendar year 2002 in the amount of $37,696,015 for expenses and the MTW Capital Budget be approved for the calendar year 2002 in the amount of $90,000 for presentation to the PCA Administrative Committee.

RRK/jm

### MISSION TO THE WORLD

### PROPOSED CONSOLIDATED 2002 BUDGET

- **I.** Methodology and Background: The 2002 budget is proposed from an analysis of key factors that influence the income and expenses of Mission to the World operating in a global context with a rapidly changing global economy. We reviewed the results of 2000 and extended these indicators into 2001 and 2002. The year 2000 saw the US dollar remain relatively strong through out the year gaining slightly against the Euro and the Yen. For mission work this can sometimes be helpful. Our overseas missionary expenses in US dollars ended the year at approximately ninety nine percent of budget, which included some expansion to program content. However, we saw a faltering US economy

III. Projection Base for 2002:

Projections have been made regarding the number of missionaries, home office staff, annual income and annual expenses. In making these projections the following assumptions have been used:

We anticipate that continued efforts to recruit missionaries in 2001 will show additional results during 2002. The number of career missionaries is projected to grow to 545, two-year missionaries to 155, internship missionaries to 300 and two-week missionaries to 7000.

We will have limited home office staff increases in 2002 for the ministry initiatives that have recently started and for growth in our short-term missions programs.

We anticipate that the US dollar will continue at its current value level. We expect other global economic factors to be unstable, with higher inflation than here in the US, but somewhat offset by currency devaluation.

Income has grown from $7.8 million in 1985 to $36.2 million in 2000 and is projected to be $38 million in 2002. Income projections have assumed a continuing strong support for missionaries from churches and individuals in a reasonably stable US economy and in a gradually growing PCA denomination. We have projected the support requirements of missionaries, adjusted for inflation, as a basis for future income. For expenses, the combined effect of salary adjustments, growth and currency value, using historic trends indicates an increase of approximately 5 percent for 2001 and 4 to 5 percent for 2002.

Missionary support accounts with deficit balances continue to remain low. Total deficits for all missionaries have gone from $400,000 in 1994 down to only $73,015 in 2000 indicating the strong support of MTW's ministry partners.

Partnership share giving for the home office grew from $300,000 in 1994 to $1,107,000 in 2000 and is projected to grow to $1,200,000 in 2002. We have assumed that good church relations and increased services to churches will allow a gradual annual increase in partnership share giving.

Project and field income is calculated as a part of the support requirements of missionaries and we expect a 4 to 5 percent growth in 2002.

Investment income projections assume that interest rates will remain stable near their current levels. In 2002, we will see some endowment earnings available as needed in the general fund and the church-planting center (Global Training & Development) to cover operational costs. In addition, the GTD has set aside funds for the next two years operations.

The 2002 proposed budget for IMPACT is based on a summer program of 7000 students, an internship program of 300 persons and a two-year missionary staff of 155 missionaries. The following major factors form the basis for projecting the income and expenses for IMPACT:

- **A.** Office Staff—The cost in the home office reflect several changes and new staff added during 2000. Four additional full-time equivalent positions are added for 2002.

426

<a id="ga29-p429"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=429 printed_page=427 -->

- **B.** Expanded programs in most areas will generate both higher income and expenses that are being designed to stay in balance.

The medical insurance fund (MIF) had an above average expense year in 2000. We expect that costs will increase slightly faster than inflation. The operating capital reserve showed a slight loss in 2000 and will produce very little investment income in 2002.

With the income from partnership share giving leveling off at about 25% of the requested amount, we project that the fixed monthly administrative assessment charge per missionary will start increasing in future years. We anticipate that this will be based on the South Consumer Price Index rate each year.

Major programs that will influence expenses in 2002 are the church-planting movement with training and mentoring, the StreetChild ministry, mercy/medical ministry and the continued growth of the summer two-week program.

There are three tables showing the consolidated income and expenses budget proposed for 2002. The first table presents a historical perspective showing 2000, 2001 approved at General Assembly and 2002 information. The second shows a functional breakdown between program, administration and fund raising. The third table shows changes in budget from 2001 to 2002.

In addition to the income and expense budget, the capital expense budget is presented on the last table in the amount of $90,000. It assumes all major facility changes for the new building will be completed in 2001. The major items to be purchased relate to information technology, improved telecommunication and some office reconfigurations to maximize space utilization for staff growth.

### PRESBYTERIAN CHURCH IN AMERICA FOUNDATION, INC.

### 2002 PROPOSED BUDGET SUMMARY

### GENERAL COMMENTS:

The PCA Foundation has shown significant growth in the last several years due to the reengineering that took place in 1997-1998. Also, as a result, the Foundation successfully achieved self-supporting status in 2000. Gifts, distributions and total assets have increased considerably. This has resulted in actual and projected increases in Support and Revenue. Likewise, the expenses necessary to operate the Foundation and implement new initiatives have and will continue to increase accordingly.

NOTES TO NATURAL EXPENSE STATEMENT - (Notes generally relate to notable comparisons of 2002 Budget to 2001 Budget.)

### SUPPORT & REVENUE

UNDESIGNATED EARNINGS (line 1) - These are earnings on funds held by the PCA Foundation, mainly from Advise & Consult Funds and the PCAF Endowment, which help underwrite the Foundation's operating expenses. The 2002 Budget of $455,000 represents a 30% increase over the 2001 amount budgeted. This increase is primarily the result of the past and projected future growth of A&C Funds.

C & A SUPPORT (line 2) – General Assembly mandated support from the four remaining Committees and Agencies (Covenant College, Covenant Theological Seminary, Mission to North America, and Mission to the World) was eliminated in

2000. Their mandatory support in 1999 was $15,000 each, for a total of $60,000, having been reduced from $30,000 each in 1998, $34,000 each in 1997 (after a $10,000 refund to each), and $44,000 each in 1996. The Foundation has now successfully achieved self-supporting status.

FEES (line 3) – There are two components of the 2002 budgeted fees: 1) Administrative fees charged on funds held for long term administration such as Charitable Remainder Trusts, Endowments, Annuities, Designated Funds, etc., and

2. Investment management fees on the accounts held by the Foundation. The 2002 budgeted increase ($67,000) over the 2001 Budget is warranted due to an expected increase ($7,000) in administrative fees resulting from an increase in the number of charitable remainder trusts and endowments and new, first time, investment management fees ($60,000) anticipated to be received beginning in

2002. The Foundation's lead bank presently provides investment management services for those Foundation accounts held in custody at the bank and those accounts are charged accordingly. The PCAF anticipates that, beginning in 2002,

430

<a id="ga29-p433"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=433 printed_page=431 -->

it may begin performing the investment management of these accounts itself, and accordingly, the PCAF operating fund would then receive the investment management fee income. In the event that this occurs, there would be an offsetting operating expense associated with performing this function and, accordingly, the 2002 Budget also includes $60,000 for investment management expense. CONTRIBUTIONS (line 6) - Gifts made to help underwrite the Foundation Operating Budget. The budgeted amount of $150,000 is due primarily to a $60,000 matching challenge contribution and the corresponding matches for a period of 10 years. These contributions helped provide the resources necessary for the Foundation to successfully achieve self-supported status in 2000.

### OPERATIONS EXPENSES

STAFF WAGES & BENEFITS (line 8) – 2002 Budget reflects compensation increases of 5% and the recent hiring of an individual for the position of VP- Development. The 2001 Budget reflected expenses relating to a development position as part of Professional Services expense (line 10).

TRAVEL EXPENSES (line 9) – 2002 budgeted increase compared to 2001 Budget is primarily due to travel expenses associated with the new VP-Development position, and monthly payments for a new automobile for President (present automobile provided to President is fully paid for and will be used by VP- Development in 2002).

PROFESSIONAL SERVICES (line 10) – 2002 Budget includes $60,000 for investment management expenses not previously budgeted, but which may be incurred beginning in 2002. These costs to be funded by new investment management fees budgeted in Support and Revenue. (See explanation for Fees – line 3 above.)

2002 Budget does not include $61,000 for development expense fees, which had been budgeted on this line in 2001. (See explanation for Staff Wages & Benefits – line 8 above.)

PROMOTIONAL EXPENSES (line 11) - 2002 budgeted increase primarily due to the use of a marketing consultant, not budgeted for in 2001 Budget.

RENT (line 15) – 2002 Budget increase due to increase in space rented in new PCA Building (occupancy estimated in August, 2001). Space is budgeted at $14.00/sq. foot, the same rate used in the 2001 Budget. The actual charge per square foot may be less, depending on final results of the campaign to obtain funding for the new PCA Building.

### REFORMED UNIVERSITY MINISTRIES

### PROPOSED BUDGET 2002

The RUM Mission:

Reformed University Ministries has the goal of building the church now and for the future by reaching students for Christ and equipping students to serve. This is accomplished by supporting the RUF works of presbyteries and churches in the areas of administration, finance, development, intern program, training, conferences, recruiting, and general ministry operation.

This budget reflects our continuing growth as we assist and work with presbyteries and churches to develop new RUF works on campuses nationwide. For 2002 we project to be on 72 campuses with well over 100 field staff, including 58 interns.

The total expense growth of 36.6% can be attributed to ministry support growth, new staff additions, permanent committee formation and new building rent increase.

The total number of full-time equivalent staff budgeted for 2002 is 10. This is two more than in the 2001 budget. Eight of these positions are currently filled. The unfilled positions are an Assistant Coordinator and a receptionist.

An overall net increase of 5% in salaries and related adjustments to benefits is assumed for all existing staff positions. This is an aggregate of cost of living and merit increases.

Permanent Committee formation costs make up most of the 46.4% expense increase of Support Services. This includes significant additions of such items as printing, postage, equipment, database maintenance, supplies, General Assembly relations and committee expenses.

The cost being charged by the Administrative Committee for office space is assumed to be at $15 per square foot; more square footage will be occupied in the new building.

The 201.5% increase in budgeted Contributions is partially attributed to the loss of transfers from MNA of $100,000.

The 2002 Budget for the entire ministry, including affiliated committees is included in the RUM General Assembly report for information.

### RIDGE HAVEN CONFERENCE CENTER

### PROPOSED BUDGET 2002

Introduction Though the Ridge Haven budget has continued to expand reflecting our growth in ministry and service, our partnership share needs have continued to decrease since 1999. From our perspective these two trends seem an unlikely pair, thus worthy of note and praise to the Lord. This phenomenon certainly reflects the Lord's blessing both in an increasing awareness of the value of the ministry and opportunities that Ridge Haven is providing to the PCA and Christian community at large, and how by His protection, good stewardship of all resources, and the spreading of fixed costs over a greater number of users, we are able to control expenses. The 2002 budget reflects our trust in Him and His continuing blessing.

We would be negligent however, if we did not express our continuing need for the churches of the PCA to support Ridge Haven! The opportunities available and the ongoing needs continuing to face us are not less but greater. The mandate of the State of North Carolina for the upgrading of our water system (estimated to be $300,000), the need for facility renovations (estimated to be a minimum of $200,000), and our desire to provide new and enlarged facilities to serve the growing opportunities (especially a new cafeteria), are only a part of our needs. A review of the 2000 budget verses actual figures (especially line items 30, 34, 35, 40, 44, and 45) shows that in some areas of maintenance, improvements, and ministry the money is not there to spend due to the partnership share not being met. From the human perspective it is extremely difficult if not impossible for us to meet these needs with partnership share giving that since 1999 has continued less than 25%, the lowest of all the Committees and Agencies. As the 2002 Ridge Haven budget is considered, we ask the Church to join us in praying for the Lord to open the windows of heaven and pour out a blessing that cannot be contained, not only a blessing for Ridge Haven but on all of the Presbyterian Church In America.

Notes

1. Line 2, C/C (Camps/Conferences) Facilities – During 2000 this category was discontinued with the income being added/included into the C/C registrations category, line 1. In future budgets the line item will disappear all together.

2. Line 5, Resident Leases - This category includes income from lot leases, lot lease interest, lot lease maintenance fees (the administrative amount we charge for keeping all lot information on file and current), water hookups, water usage fees and road maintenance fees. The amount projected for 2002 is the actual amount expected without lot sales or water hookup fees of which we have no guarantee or expectation of income. The budgeted amount for 2001 should also have been $23,474.

437

<a id="ga29-p440"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=440 printed_page=438 -->

3. Line 6, Other Contributions – The category includes contributions from WIC groups, other groups, and individuals toward the daily operations of Ridge Haven.

4. Line 7, Non-medical Reimbursements – The category includes amounts paid to Ridge Haven by individuals or groups for the use of Ridge Haven postage, office copier, vehicle parts, fuel, pay phones, etc.

5. Line 13, Sale of Assets – The category reflects the liquidation of material items no longer needed. The amounts reported are unpredictable. There is no certainty of income from the sale of assets from year-to-year.

6. Line 17, Other Salary/Benefits - Beginning in 2000, payroll taxes (also line 22) have been included in/with salaries and benefits. In future budgets the line item will disappear all together.

The Ridge Haven staff consists of a total of 9 year-around employees. The Administrator, Administrative Assistant, Ministry Director, Maintenance Superintendent, and Food Service Director are salaried, full-time employees. The Accounting Manager, Food Service Assistant Director, and two House Keeping staff are all year-around part-time hourly paid employees. In recent months we have had a part-time office assistant and maintenance assistant. The present (2001) budget allows for both of these positions to be full-time as employees are available. The present (2001) budget also includes temporary food service staff and allows for the addition of a year-around but part-time Resident Manager. The amount provided in the 2002 budget reflects the addition of a Camps Director (intern status), increased compensation for the Maintenance Superintendent bringing him up to the average compensation level for employees in comparable positions in other area camps and conference ministries, for the Food Service Assistant Director to become a full-time salaried position, and a 3% cost-of-living increase for all other employees.

7. Line 19, Counselor and Camp Support Staff - The budgeted figure provides for an amount needed to allow us to remain competitive in compensating counselors and support staff and adding additional counselors and support staff for larger camps and a junior counselor program.

8. Line 21, Workers' Comp - The amount reflects the corresponding cost for increasing compensation and added staff identified in the line 17 note.

9. Line 22, Payroll Taxes - Beginning in 2000 payroll taxes were included in/with salaries and benefits with the exception of one employment position that has now been discontinued.

438

<a id="ga29-p441"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=441 printed_page=439 -->

10. Line 23, Other Fees - This category includes North Carolina Fees (usually a small amount), Miscellaneous fees (also usually a small amount), Solid Waste Fees, Pool Fees (the amounts we pay for county inspection at the beginning of each season), etc. The 2000 Actual amount was inflated by a one-time loan-origination fee created by the establishment of a line of credit to finance the water system upgrades approved by the 2000 General Assembly.

11. Line 25, Planning/Promotion/and Recruiting - This category includes all printing costs.

12. Line 34, Equipment/Furnishings - We continue to need additional equipment and furnishings for several of our buildings. These items are purchased as the money becomes available.

13. Line 35, Grounds - We have several erosion and landscape projects we are seeking to implement. The amount indicated will allow us to do these as the money comes in.

14. Line 40, Vehicles - Ridge Haven owns and operates a fleet of 8 vehicles. The budgeted amount allows for us to repair and/or replace aging and/or failing vehicles as the money comes in.

15. Line 45, Facilities Renovation - All 21 of the Ridge Haven buildings/facilities need renovations from time-to-time that are not otherwise provided for in the day-to-day maintenance category. The amount provided in this category reflects renovations for 9 different buildings that could use immediate attention. The renovations desired were professionally estimated.

16. Line 46, Water System - The decrease in the budgeted amount reflects the actual projected cost of maintenance for the water system once the Assembly's approved $300,000 upgrading project mandated by the State of North Carolina is complete.

17. Line 47, Water System Loan - This budgeted amount will allow us to repay the money borrowed in the event that contributed funds are not sufficient to cover upgrading costs as they are progressing.

18. Line 48, New Programming - The addition of new conferences and/or other similar ministries requires an upfront investment of about $10,000-$12,000 per conference. It takes approximately three years for a conference to reach the "break-even" point. At least two new conferences are being planned for 2002.
