## APPENDIX D

### CHRISTIAN EDUCATION AND PUBLICATIONS

REPORT to the

### 29TH GENERAL ASSEMBLY

### INTRODUCTION

As we present this report to the 29th P.C.A. General Assembly, we are more aware than ever of the challenge and urgent need for God's people to be trained and equipped in the Christian faith. We are aware that in our North American culture there is no distinctly Christian mind to help us navigate the pluralistic, even secular and postmodern, waters. Our culture communicates so many uncertainties. More and more choices of more and more things are being offered to people who are not that equipped in the truth to make the best choices. Church attendance is beginning to decline for the first time in fifty years and the dropout rate of the older teenagers is alarming.

The Presbyterian Church in America does not exist in a cultural vacuum; and, as part of the Church of Jesus Christ, it is not supposed to. The Bible describes the church as the "ground and pillar of truth," and yet its influence is being marginalized either by withdrawal and isolation from the world or by becoming too much like the world. Either extreme neutralizes the potential effectiveness of the church. Somehow, even in the more evangelical churches, people have either lost their connection between what the Bible teaches and how they live their daily lives, or they never saw the connection in the first place. Our own surveys, as well as other studies are revealing that the younger generation is not impressed with a church that chooses either of the two above extremes.

One of the things that has concerned the Christian Education and Publications committee and staff is the lack of cohesion and unity that is being demonstrated by the church in general and often our own denomination. We are both aware of and involved in the General Assembly's strategic planning process, which will hopefully serve to unify the PCA as we are moving further into the 21st century.

As the heart of God's kingdom, the church has a growing challenge to prepare and equip its people to be Kingdom people. The church has a key role in actually coordinating the training and learning process. Failure to do that only evidences the tendency for one part of the kingdom activity to work against another. This is definitely true in the area of education and training. The church, the home, and the school should have a well-coordinated strategy where each part mutually benefits from the efforts of the other parts.

442

<a id="ga29-p445"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=445 printed_page=443 -->

Starting from the Kingdom of God perspective, which is all inclusive of God's reign and realm, it is important that the church step up to the plate to coordinate these activities. No one of the Kingdom entities can rear covenant children alone. But, how do the various parts come together in a mutually supportive way? In seeking to be a biblically reformed church, by taking the great truths of our reformed tradition and dealing with them contextually, the PCA from its beginning has been committed to a quality of excellence in educating the church's covenant people, youth, children, and adults.

CE/P's prayer and desire is that we might continue challenging and assisting the churches in challenging, training, and equipping our people to think and live like Kingdom of God people—to live with a biblically reformed worldview. We believe that part of the church's present day shallowness and lack of effectiveness are attributed to a sub-standard of training and learning. The people are therefore not as equipped for ministry and not as prepared to live in this kind of world as they should be.

As our summary mission statement says, CE/P exists in the PCA for the purpose of assisting its people to:

know the Lord, know the Word, know the world, and know themselves;

Through our diversity of programs, we target churches and families in general, and children, youth, and adults specifically. CE/P is committed to that task.

People often ask, "Who is CE/P and what do you do?" The answer is both simple and complex. We are the PCA's agency of resources and training. Our resources (curriculum, books, media, and variety of other publications) are available to churches and individuals from CE/P and our training services, made up both of events and consulting, are also available. When the Apostle Paul said, "The church grows and builds itself up in love as each part does its work," he preceded those words with the reminder that God has given to the church those who are to train and equip those people for ministry and Kingdom service. He has also instructed us to pass on His Gospel truth, his story, to the next generation that they might know the wonder and power of God.

It is both our challenge and privilege to be a part of this ministry in the PCA. It is our humble joy and delight to connect our churches, large and small, rural or urban, metropolitan and inner city with peoples and resources to help them be more effective in their ministry. We have experienced in many ways the blessings of God as we have coordinated events, resources, and meetings with local church leaders as well as key lay people across the PCA, some of which you will read about in this report.

443

<a id="ga29-p446"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=446 printed_page=444 -->

According to reliable polls, the church is losing some of its authenticity and integrity with the rising generations. That must not be. There are two kinds of people that motivate us to move forward: those who need to be ministered to and those who need to see us (the church) ministering to those in need. The late Francis Schaeffer, to whom the PCA is deeply indebted, said that if the young people do not see the church being and doing what the church is suppose to be and do, "they will not listen" and "they should not listen."

Our ministry previewed and summarized in this report represents CE/P's desire to help the church, particularly the PCA, create a vision of Kingdom consciousness in order to see the challenge of the moment and to develop, expand, and network a more effective ministry in the PCA, as we seek to make the best of training and resources available to our churches.

The body of this report will be focused on our two main areas—resources and training.

### RESOURCES

We have two categories of resources that we make available to the PCA and other interested churches. First, there are the resources that we publish and produce, and second, the resources that others have developed and made available to us. The CE/P bookstore and video library are the center of our resources in the area of education and training.

1. Bookstore

The CE/P bookstore serves around 90% of the PCA churches. Materials can be purchased using the Internet or our toll free number. Not only does the bookstore carry the materials produced by CE/P but also the official documents of the PCA, and general tracts, and brochures on various topics. Discounts are available to PCA churches and customers. Satisfactory working arrangements with various publishers and distributors enable the bookstore to quickly process orders and respond to customer needs.

The bookstore personnel are a key to linking churches and people to resources, and linking CE/P program staff to churches and people, particularly in the area of recommending resources. Children and youth materials are available, as well as materials for women in the church, men in the church, and other leadership training resources.

From the bookstore Website, customers can link to other CE/P services in education and training. Also, through the bookstore ministry, CE/P has helped numbers of churches develop their own book tables or has provided some churches with books to make available at retreats and various events. The CE/P staff attempts to stay abreast of the <del>444</del>

<a id="ga29-p447"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=447 printed_page=445 -->

best resources, past, present, and future. A bookstore catalogue is printed annually to make local churches more aware of the variety of resources available to them. As the committee assigned to provide Christian education resources for PCA churches, the CE/P bookstore is committed to meeting and expanding its services and resources in the future. In many ways, all the other services and ministries of CE/P grow out of this central ministry resource.

2. Video Library

The CE/P Video Library annually services over four hundred churches with over six hundred titles including training and educational titles. The video lending library not only provides videotapes to local churches, but also offers counsel as to how best to use videos in education and training. Like the bookstore, the video library publishes a catalogue of available titles. CE/P is planning to expand this resource so that we can serve more churches.

3. Equip for Ministry

The CE/P bi-monthly publication Equip for Ministry is one of the three communication centerpieces to keep ideas, resources, and other educational and training needs (especially good books) before the readership. Equip for Ministry circulates some 11,000- 12,000 copies bi-monthly, either by individual subscription or by bulk subscription to local churches. Equip for Ministry seeks to selectively advertise good resources that can serve PCA churches in a variety of ways. Plus it contains some general information about the PCA that is not available from other sources. CE/P provides a one-year subscription to those who participate in our various training events. Equip for Ministry focuses on the whole of God's covenant family while giving special attention to those in leadership roles in the home, the church, and the broader Kingdom.

4. Website

The CE/P Website is the second of the two major centerpieces. The Website is easily accessible and regularly visited by people in the church. Materials, resources, and other needs are listed on the Website. There are a number of links to other ministry resources on the net, as well as to other sections of our own site. From the Website a church or individual can learn of conferences and seminars, and print out the registration forms. They can learn of other CE/P resources such as the CE/P regional trainers for youth, children, and adults, as well as for the women in the church ministry. The Website, www.pcanet.org/cep quickly provides information on a variety of things consistent with CE/P's and the PCA's purpose.

445

<a id="ga29-p448"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=448 printed_page=446 -->

5. WIC Resource Letter

The Women in the Church ministry department of CE/P produces a quarterly WIC Resource Letter that is mailed to local WIC presidents and pastor's wives. This is the third communication centerpiece for CE/P. The Resource Letter, along with a quarterly WIC Bulletin Insert, is used to keep the ministry of WIC before the people in the local church. The resource letter contains helpful information and ideas for women's ministry in the local church. Soon we will begin to distribute this communication piece to the local diaconal chairmen.

6. Other publications

The monthly Bulletin Supplement is designed to share ministry ideas across the denomination and encourage creative thinking in local churches. Some 40,000 copies are printed and circulated to over 300 subscribing churches.

7. Great Commission Publications

Through its 26-year partnership with the Orthodox Presbyterian Church, CE/P, representing the PCA, shares joint ownership of Great Commission Publications, a publishing ministry of the two denominations. GCP primarily publishes Sunday school curriculum for all ages, the Trinity Hymnal used in many PCA churches, and church bulletins. Through the GCP curriculum, Sunday after Sunday PCA people have the opportunity to study the truths of God from a biblically reformed and redemptive historical perspective. The joint venture also enables both denominations to serve a growing number of non-PCA and non-OPC churches as well. CE/P regional trainers, mentioned below, are trained to assist churches with the use of this curriculum.

### TRAINING

The second half of CE/P's ministry comes under the category of training. Training includes both events (conferences and seminars) and consulting (working directly with church leadership).

1. Trainers

Along with our fulltime staff, we have regional trainers across the country to help minister to the needs of our growing denomination. We presently have thirteen regional trainers, eight regional youth trainers, and eleven WIC trainers. CE/P has been committed to multiplying our ministry in the most effective and efficient ways possible. Carefully selected and trained regional trainers are a part of CE/P's ministry of multiplication. Using regional people allows CE/P to meet the needs of local churches in a cost effective way, to give CE/P a personal presence across the church, and to assist local churches in an ongoing consulting relationship. 446

<a id="ga29-p449"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=449 printed_page=447 -->

Regional trainers are equipped to do things such as teacher training, particularly (but not exclusively) for those churches using our GCP curriculum. Many churches ask CE/P for help with teacher training. As a part of that service, we can also help a church evaluate its Christian education and training program and work with local personnel to develop a more effective ministry in that area. The trainers also link local churches to available resources. Together with the CE/P staff, regional trainers served over one hundred churches during the past year.

2. Leadership

Most of the leadership training, including officer training and general consulting, is handled by the fulltime CE/P staff. Other more specialized categories such as conflict management, small group training, worship, strategic planning, cultural awareness, etc. are also generally done by the CE/P staff.

3. Equip Conferences

CE/P also works in coordination with local churches and presbyteries for larger conference called Equip conferences. This past year three conferences were held in North Carolina, New Hampshire, and Mississippi with several hundred people participating.

4. Children and Youth

CE/P has conducted its third annual conference for children's ministry staff in local churches. One hundred people attended the March 2001 conference in Atlanta. CE/P also serves as a clearinghouse and resource center for individuals and churches regarding their needs in both youth and children's personnel.

In February 2001, CE/P and North Georgia Presbytery hosted an Equip conference for youth workers. Nearly one hundred youth workers and volunteers from several neighboring states came together to discuss the family and church roles in ministering to the millennial generation.

Presbyterian Youth of America is part of CE/P's leadership training teenagers. Two conferences are held each summer, one in Colorado, and one at Covenant College. Around two hundred teenagers come together annually for intensive Christian leadership training. Plans for other regions of the PCA are being considered.

5. Mercy Ministries Conference

The big conference of the year was the mercy ministry conference (The Call of the Gospel: Sharing Christ, Showing Mercy), which was jointly sponsored by CE/P and Mission to North America. Six hundred PCA men and women came together in Atlanta 447

<a id="ga29-p450"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=450 printed_page=448 -->

for a challenging and inspiring weekend. In addition to plenary speakers and workshops, several local church ministry examples were highlighted. This conference built on the mercy ministry training CE/P has included in our Equip and WIC conferences. The unique thing about this conference was that it brought together men and women to discuss this vital ministry. In the PCA, MNA has a mercy ministry department and oversees the "deed" aspect of that ministry and CE/P has the "word" or training aspect. This was a timely and strategic opportunity for both agencies to co-host such a conference.

6. Women in the Church

One hundred and eighty women attended the annual Women in the Church leadership training seminar for local church and presbytery WIC leaders, which was held in conjunction with the mercy ministry conference. The new regional WIC trainers were introduced, and the new WIC Bible Study Series, published by CE/P, was announced. Dr. Morton Smith brought the message at the seminar's closing worship service.

6. Other conferences

In addition to the training mentioned above, CE/P conducts conferences in a variety of areas. "Partners in Ministry" is designed primarily for pastors, youth pastors, and their wives. Two were conducted during the past year in Augusta, Georgia, and Ocean City, Maryland. CE/P has been facilitating music and worship conferences since the early 1980's. This past year two events were conducted: one in Atlanta with over 130 participants and a conference in Dallas, co-sponsored with Park Cities PCA (scheduled for April 2001).

CE/P also works with Ridge Haven, Mission to North America, Mission to the World, and to co-sponsor the annual YOWAW (Youth World Awareness Weekend) conference for high school students. Over two hundred students came together at Ridge Haven for this conference in February. Plans are being made for the 2002 conference.

7. Audio/Visual Training

In addition to their central position as resources, the Video Library and Bookstore also play key roles in training through the medium of audio and video materials. CE/P seeks to make the best of training available through all of its resources, hence the video library, the bookstore, and the availability of staff and trainers are key to the success of the training programs. Audio and videotapes of CE/P conferences and events are available through the video library and bookstore.

448

<a id="ga29-p451"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=451 printed_page=449 -->

### CONCLUSION

The heartbeat of CE/P is training and equipping God's people to live for Him in this pluralistic postmodern world. Our strategy is to challenge and assist local churches in training their people to think, to live biblically, and to know how to effectively pass on the Christian faith to the next generation. Because of who we are as the covenant people of God, and because we realize that God has placed us here at this moment in time to serve His purpose to this generation, our present thrust is to encourage adults to reach out and into the lives of the younger generation. The church, as we have known it, is changing. We believe our role is to help steer a course through that change process and help churches apply biblical truth to today's world in a way that respects the past, that builds upon it by presenting that truth to today's world, and that hopes for the full and soon coming of the Kingdom of God –"reformed and always reforming."

4. That the Women in the Church be thanked for their generous support of the 2000 Love Gift for Mission to North America. (The 2001 Love Gift is directed to Ridge Haven, and the 2002 to CE/P).

## APPENDIX E

The 1999-2000 Institutional Effectiveness Report Covenant College Office of Planning

Introduction

Assessment, as we know it today, has been a part of higher education for the last 10 – 15 years. Assessment methods continued to evolve during that time. In the early days of assessment, the process was more concerned about the inputs to the educational process. Therefore, measurement items include student/faculty ratio, the percentage of faculty with earned doctorate, and faculty teaching within their field of discipline. Over time, assessment became more concerned with the results of student learning than the inputs of the educational process. The items of greater concern became student results on standardized tests such as the Major Fields Achievement Tests, reporting a student's ability to get into graduate school, and general student learning as measured often through value-added tests.

In the Spring of 2000, a major but subtle change occurred in the evolution of assessment. A test project, co-sponsored by the Carnegie Foundation for the Advancement of Teaching and the Pew Forum for Undergraduate Learning, was developed and implemented. This survey examined students' behaviors that show correlation with student learning. This shift begins a change of focus back to inputs. But, rather than the inputs of facilities, faculty, and finance, it addresses the behaviors of student learning. Covenant College participated in this pilot program of the National Survey of Student Engagement (NSSE) in the spring of 2000. A more detailed review of the results of that program will be presented later in this report.

In light of the change that seems to be taking place in assessment, again giving consideration to the inputs of education, the format of this year's Institutional Effectiveness Report has been somewhat modified. Within each major section, issues of input can be found in italic type while issues of outcomes can be found in bold type. It is hoped that this change will more clearly identify actions taken by the college to improve student learning and effectiveness of the institution. You will find over 135 inputs identified and over 95 outcomes identified throughout the report.

The report is divided into six major sections: Academic Affairs; Student Affairs; Planning and Research; Financial Affairs; Advancement; and the new Three-year Plan 2000-2003. Each section contains information which provides evidence of the health of the institution. Some of that evidence is in the form of student outcomes, some as inputs, and some as results of various performance indicators.

450

<a id="ga29-p453"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=453 printed_page=451 -->

The Academic Affairs section includes information about students, academic assessment, faculty, and academic support functions. The student information provides both student outcomes and student profiles. Both types of information give evidence of the type of student attracted to Covenant College and the results of their academic experience. Faculty information provides input evidence of the college's efforts to provide a quality educational opportunity for the students. Academic support information demonstrates additional input evidence of an atmosphere conducive to learning.

The Student Affairs section presents evidence of services provided to our students by the Student Development Department. This information includes both input and outcome evidence.

The Planning and Research section includes the activities and findings of the planning and research functions of the college as they impact changes.

The Financial Affairs section of the report furnishes evidence of institutional financial stability and how resources were used to provide students with learning opportunities. All financial aid information is included in this section.

The section on Advancement includes all financial development and new student recruitment and fund raising information. While this evidence tends to be input in nature, it also demonstrates the commitment of new students and donors to the institution.

The sixth, and final, section of the report is a copy of the new 2000-2003 Three-year Plan, which was completed this year.

It is our hope that this new format will provide a clearer picture of what Covenant College has been doing over the last year to ensure a high quality Christian education for its students. The results as seen through both institutional and student outcomes are driven by the mission of the college.

The following excerpts of the Covenant College Mission Statement should provide a basis upon which the college is driven.

Covenant College is a Christ-centered institution of higher education emphasizing liberal arts. It is the college's purpose to help students make significant progress toward maturity in the following areas:

This union and commitment should lead to an understanding both of one's sin and of one's significance as a person redeemed by Christ, resulting in a growing awareness of purpose. This awareness of purpose should facilitate the development of goals, priorities, and practices that foster spiritual effectiveness and

### Student Retention

Covenant was again ranked in the top tier of regional liberal arts colleges in the South according to the 2001 issue of the U. S. News and World Report Best Colleges. The college moved up from a tie for twenty-fourth position last year to a tie for nineteenth position this year. The average freshmen retention level for those recognized as the Best Regional Liberal Arts Colleges in the South (33 schools) was 73.4%. Covenant's freshmen retention rate was 80%. Only one college in the first tier (Fisk University) had a better rate of retention (87%) than Covenant College.

Retention rates continued to increase this year. While the junior to senior rate dropped by 4% (further study will be done to see if a cause can be found), all other classes improved. Last Summer, orientation for new students was quite different than in the past. Students spent time with professors in their first college academic experience as part of their orientation to college life. This early introduction to the rigors of college study might have better prepared students for their freshman year and account for the 2% rise in retention. College-wide retention rose from 82% last year to 85% this year.

### Graduation Rate

The college experience is intended to lead to graduation from the four year of college study. The graduation rate measures how many students in any given freshman class graduate within 150% of the planned time. Since Covenant offers baccalaureate degrees based on a four-year curriculum, the graduation rate is based on a six-year period. To be considered in the graduation rate, students who came to Covenant as first-time freshmen in the Fall of 1994 (n=169) must have graduated from Covenant by August of 2000.

### Academic Assessment

A variety of measures and assessments have been collected to provide evidences for reflection of past performance and direction for future action. Both quantitative and qualitative apparati have been employed in an effort to synthesize a holistic picture of collect performance in the academic arena. A caution regarding the limits of evidence needs to be considered as assessments are reviewed. While the data gathered here is not a complete picture, nor are we free from bias, the following information has something to say to us.

There is much to thank God for in these data. Generally the health of the college as a faithful learning community is strong according to many measures relative to both internal and external standards.

### Traditional Program

The integral presentation of faith embedded in academic disciplines continues to be a strength of the college. The reformed perspective of the college is evidenced in the variety of assessments and measurements.

The following results were noted for the 1999-2000 academic year:

<a id="ga29-p461"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=461 printed_page=459 -->

Confirmations: High scores on the social problems essay including reasoning 4.0, worldview 4.1, biblical themes 4.1, responsibility 4.0, and historical/structural considerations 3.4. All scores on a five-point scale. High scores on the faith statement of showing growth in all areas. Scores on a fivepoint scale from 1 = falling away to 5 = significant growth were: relationship with God 4.9, relationship with others 4.5, and relationship with creation 3.6. Senior integration projects received a mean rating of 6.3 on a scale of 1 – 8 for faith integration. Measurements from departmental assessments indicate a high satisfaction of faith integration from information gathered from focus groups. Professors received a mean rating of 4.0 on a five-point scale for their ability to bring a Christian perspective to their teaching.

Content Mastery – Traditional Program

1. Covenant College is dedicated (as shown in the Mission Statement goal 2. on page 3) to presenting an academically rigorous program which challenges students to excel in scholarship based on biblical principles.

Confirmations Sophomores took a biblical literacy test which was designed by the members of the Biblical Studies Department and achieved a mean score of 90% on the objective portion of the test. This was the first administration of the test and no previous benchmarks have been established. Senior integration projects received a mean rating of 6.3 on a scale of 1-8 for scholarly content. Students are able to communicate well on SIPs as indicated by ratings of 6.2 and 6.4 on eight-point scales for written and oral expression respectively. Major Field Achievement Tests (MFATs) scores had a weighted mean in the 75th percentile, indicating that our average student taking the test ranked at the threshold of the top quartile of similar college graduates. Departmental assessments indicate student responses and performance which is consistent with these confirmations.

Concerns Some departmental MFAT scores need further study. Perhaps the recommendation of the biology department to statistically correlate results with GPAs would be a helpful step in assessing our assessing. Various departments have made specific recommendations involving slight adjustments of course offerings or delivery systems what may have positive influence on achievement of these goals.

459

<a id="ga29-p462"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=462 printed_page=460 -->

Instructional Effectiveness - Traditional Effective teaching is described in the faculty manual as

...[including] concern for the learner, the learning process, the subject matter, teaching methodology, and the teacher. For the process to be called Christian, it must occur in the context of viewing each of the above dimensions with biblical insight. Such biblical insight can then lead to a Christian practice.

Students are made in the image of God and are called to participate in God's work and reflect His character. This means that students are created to be active, creative, productive, purposeful beings who make sense of ideas and experiences in order to exercise some control over the world around them. They cannot be allowed to be merely passive recipients of information. Rather, they must be challenged to think and conceptualize, make judgments, discern the implications of ideas, and act upon their knowledge for the glory of God and benefit of humankind. Instructional practices must foster the development of these characteristics in the students.

Classroom instruction is assessed through various means at the college. In the traditional program, it is the backbone of the college accounting for one half of the evaluation of professors. Student course evaluations are distributed and the dean of faculty and peers of professors perform observations. Indications strongly support a positive performance in this area college-wide.

Confirmations Course evaluations by students indicate a high regard for the instruction offered. Mean ratings near or above 4 on a five-point scale are achieved in all measures. Students (n=1743) consistently rate all areas of instruction high. Focus groups reported in departmental assessments also give high praise for classroom instruction and the role of professors in the instructional process. Observations by the dean of faculty give further attestation to the high quality of instruction. The National Survey of Student Engagement (NSSE) mean ratings for relationships with professors and encouragement to think critically are statistically significantly above peer institutions.

Concerns Both course evaluations and the National Survey of Student Engagement indicate a need to investigate student involvement in the learning process through projects and groups work. Course evaluations tend to focus on more senior level courses (an average of second semester sophomore, first semester junior) when appreciation for leaning may be at its best. A distribution of ratings that would follow more core courses and students who are earlier in the college career may be helpful.

460

<a id="ga29-p463"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=463 printed_page=461 -->

### New Initiatives - Traditional

As new programs are initiated or former programs are changed significantly, a comprehensive assessment is applied. This year, a delivery system for Self in Society I was implemented during orientation and the first semester of the freshman year, creating a "freshman experience" for new students. The students were placed in small groups with professors who would also serve as their advisors. The experience was assessed through course evaluations, student focus groups, and a faculty questionnaire. The assessment resulted in the following recommendation:

The delivery system will remain largely intact for the coming year. Attention for improvement will be directed toward the content of the course. There is a significant group of faculty who would like to see the course become a foundational introduction to the distinctives of the college and leave discussions of social science to introductory courses within the disciplines. The curriculum committee of the faculty is currently addressing this issue.

Quest The Quest program continues to be the largest department of the college and continues to make positive changes in curriculum and delivery resulting in positive ratings by current students and recent alumni. The Quest program has grown much in the past few years to the point that this past year Quest leased and maintained classroom facilities in downtown Chattanooga and Cleveland, Tennessee, Dalton and Canton, Georgia. The program is in the process now of leasing space at Floyd College in Rome, Georgia, for a new program that is preparing to begin there this year. There are several curricular

463

<a id="ga29-p466"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=466 printed_page=464 -->

changes that have also taken place during the last year and are being piloted as this next year begins. The Business Communications course has been rewritten and upgraded; Divisional Research module has been revised to become Applied Decision Making (using resource principles to improve students' decision making skills by including primary and secondary data in the process); and the original Creative Problem Solving course has been integrated into the new Applied Decision Making course, it's place in the curriculum taken by Managerial Marketing.

In an attempt to ensure that Quest stays on the cutting edge of programs of this type, we have recently met with members of the Information and Computer Science faculty to plan a pilot program which will allow offering the current Quest degree in Organizational Management with a two- to six-course emphasis in Information Management. These changes would help the program line up better to prepare graduates for MBA programs which require marketing and a better understanding of the role of information management.

In May 2000, the Quest program graduated 156 students. This was a new record number of graduates for the program. The Quest program also had a record enrollment providing the largest revenue to date.

A one-year post-graduation survey was conducted in May 1999 to determine how the graduates' Covenant education has contributed to their work performance, career/personal development, and world view. Concepts taught in the program affecting their career/personal development resulted in positive scores ranging from 92% to 98%. 85% of the students reported that Philosophy of Culture has a positive impact on their world and life view, with 92% reporting this impact for the Old and New Testament courses, also.

Master of Education Program The Master of Education program continues to receive high marks relative to a number of internal and external measures. Faculty Profile As mentioned in the introduction, the NSSE begins a shift in assessment practices to look at inputs that are closely tied to student learning. Faculty members play an important role in engaging students in the learning process. Faculty at a college are becoming more than lecturers. They not only bring first-hand content knowledge into the classroom, they also model to students the process of educational engagement. Students have the opportunity to see their professors engage in the learning process as they often work together and become a community of learners. These opportunities may come through faculty preparation for class, pedagogical engagement techniques, or collaborative learning projects. Therefore, an examination of the teaching faculty at Covenant provides the first evidence of student learning potentials.

The Covenant College faculty have long held a strong commitment for providing a strong liberal arts core curriculum. The Academic Bulletin states that "the core curriculum is based on the faculty's belief that a liberal arts education should be broad and inclusive, introducing students to ideas and values of continuing concern and providing them with historical and spiritual perspectives on the complex problems of our society."

This year the faculty voted to make some changes in the core curriculum that will further enhance a broad and inclusive educational experience. The freshman course, Self and Society, has been replaced with the teaching of The Christian Mind and a distribution course in the social sciences. The two-hour course on microcomputer applications has been lengthened to three hours, allowing for the inclusion of Christian perspectival dimensions of technology. This should provide a more uniform approach to

465

<a id="ga29-p468"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=468 printed_page=466 -->

that portion of the course that attempts to help students to examine their educational experience through the "spectacles of the Scripture" and permit students to select an area of interest within the humanities.

Another evidence of quality in the examination of the faculty is the progress of individual faculty members moving through the academic ranks and receiving tenure at the college. The length of contract offered to a faculty member at Covenant College is dependent on quality of teaching, the longevity of service, and a scholarly presentation which demonstrates integration of the discipline and the Christian faith. The Board of Trustees approves a five-year contract (tenure) when faculty have demonstrated a high level of quality over a period of time. Following is a table showing the current status of faculty.

Academic Support

Diversity Scholarship Recipient Program (DSR) During the 1999-2000 academic year, the DSR Program provided $311, 125 in financial assistance for seventy-three students. Forty-six students were projected to return as scholarship students for Fall 2000. Of the remaining 27, 16 graduated, 5 did not reapply, and six are not returning.

Of the sixteen graduating DSR seniors in 2000, nine took the MFAT; the other students were majors in disciplines which did not offer the test. Five students had scores above the mean department score at Covenant. Three others had scores within eleven points of the mean department score.

The DSR program developed a new leadership format this year which involved providing training for 10 upperclassmen who would serve as mentors to fellow DSR students. These mentors were able to help students and also track their progress in terms of academic, social, and spiritual adjustment at the college. Also, the new director of the program, Daphne Haddad, held a weekly tea time on campus to provide a more convenient way for students to make contact with each other and with her.

Library This past year, a new three-year plan was completed which will guide the college through the years 2000 to 2003. The entire plan can be found in Section 6 of this report. One of the major objectives in the plan is to "dramatically increase the prominence and usefulness of Library resources and space to provide the campus with a center for serious research and collaborative inquiry." While the Library has grown much this year in a variety of ways, both inputs and usage, there are still major strides that need to be made to bring it to the level of effectiveness desired. Some of the tactics in the plan include an increase of $35, 000 each year for the next three years to increase the library print materials, additional periodical subscriptions in both paper and electronic form, and the hiring of an additional professional librarian and technical support staff.

Library circulation for this past year totaled 32,955 items. This is almost double the circulation of the previous year, partly due to a new statistical report by the automated

467

<a id="ga29-p470"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=470 printed_page=468 -->

system. Use of on-line databases also increases every year as more and more databases become available. Request by faculty for classroom presentations of library research methods have also increased resulting in much more intelligent use of our existing library resources. Total items in the library are now 129,881. These items include books, periodical subscriptions, microfilm reels, microfiche cards, records and compact disks, audio and video tapes, films, slides, and computer media. However, when compared to several different sources, our library seems to have many major holes that need to be filled in both physical and virtual areas. The most recent comparison was done with Choices Outstanding Academic Books, 1992-1997. That list contains 332 titles that should be held by undergraduate and graduate libraries of our size. Our library has only 83 of those titles, or 25%, when we should be at 75%. While the physical resources still need major improvement, the virtual library has been growing. GALILEO now contains 87 databases. In addition to those databases, it contains 18 subject category links to sites on the worldwide web. During this past year, phase one of JSTOR was completed. This phase contains the complete run of 124 scholarly journals, with many individual journals and full-length articles available.

Student ranking of the importance of library resources and services has been very high over the last three years. However, their satisfaction has been low enough to rank this area as the number one issue needing attention according to the Student Satisfaction Inventory. Details of this research can be found in Section 3 of this report.

Over the last three years, the Master of Education students and seniors writing their Senior Integration Papers were asked to rate the library resources and services. Sixty to eighty percent agreed or strongly agreed that the services and resources were adequate. The apparent incongruity between these two surveys may demonstrate the difference between planned research needs and short-term resource needs. However, comments and focus groups from the participants demonstrate a strong desire to see library resources and services improved.

Audio Visual Services The workload for AV Services steadily increases each year, and 1999-2000 was no exception. Courses such as CHOW Art and Music, Christ and Culture, the film course, and Self and Society (now The Christian Mind) were heavily dependent upon technology. Technology Services/Instructional Technology/Telephone The 1999-2000 academic year was very busy for Technical Services. Search for a campus-wide database system began in the fall of 1999 resulting in the selection of SCT's Banner. Sufficient progress was made to allow the Accounting and Purchasing offices to begin using Banner Finance on July 1, 2000.

Technology Services was also kept busy upgrading and installing new computers throughout the campus. Faculty and staff were provided with 29 new or upgraded computers. The student labs received 47 new computers for student use.

There are now four student computer labs and three computer clusters in the residence halls providing 133 computers for student use. The labs are open to students, faculty, and staff, except when a class is scheduled in the lab. The hours of operation are 8:00 a.m. to 12:00 midnight, Monday through Thursday, 8:00 a.m. to 6:00 p.m. Friday and 8:00 a.m. to 12:00 midnight on Saturday.

A new Remote Access Server was implemented for faculty allowing them to access the campus network from home. The Telephone Department added a new Y2K compliant voice mail server giving all students access to voicemail. Because of the large number of potential students accessing the college web site (http://www.covenant.edu), it was given a new "look and feel" better complimenting other promotional materials produced by the school.

Two (2) new "smart classrooms" were added. This now provides three classrooms equipped with a high level of multi-media equipment for teaching. A "mobile smart cart" was also equipped which can be moved into other classrooms. This provides portability of multi-media equipment similar to that found in the "smart classrooms."

Additionally, Technology Services/Telephone installed and upgraded over 47,000 feet of cable. A Microsoft Proxy Server and Trend Micro's virus scanner were installed providing greater security from outside attacks and email viruses installed on the firewall enabled scanning of all inbound and outbound email messages. CyberPatrol's Internet filter was also installed, enabling blocking of pornographic sites on campus.

The Instructional Technology department continued their efforts to ensure faculty and staff are well trained in the use of all technology currently available to them. On-site training for implementation of the Banner line of products was held for various offices throughout the spring and summer.

Section 3: Planning and Research

Planning Office

Three-year Plan Process The work on developing the new Three-year Plan was completed this year. Five faculty members spent much of their time helping in this process to ensure the plan would reflect the academic needs of the college. The final plan with goal statement, strategies, objectives, and tactics was presented to the Board in March 2000. Since then, the planning committee has prioritized initiatives totaling almost $120,000. They include additional academic operating supplies, academically focused work study positions, outside speakers, additional library book and periodical acquisition, library support staff, and a minority recruiter.

Institutional Research

National Survey of Student Engagement Covenant College participated in the first year of the National Survey of Student Engagement (NSSE) in the spring of 2000. There were a total of 276 participating fouryear colleges and universities involved in the study. There were 151,910 first-year and senior students participating. The study was co-sponsored by the Carnegie Foundation for the Advancement of Teaching and the Pew Forum for Undergraduate Learning and supported by the Pew Charitable Trust.

In October 2000, national benchmarks of good educational practice will be released based on the results from the NSSE 2000. This study will probably play an important role in the discussions regarding what educators will consider to be good educational practice. They may eventually play an important role in national rankings of schools. A brief profile of the nearly 152,000 participants follows:

Class: First-year Students 49% Seniors 51% Gender: Women 67% Men 33% Enrollment Status: Full-time 86% Part-time 14%

There were four major areas of the survey. The first was College Activities, which included: academic, intellectual, and social experiences; reading and writing; nature of exams; character of mental activities and weekly activities. The second section was Educational and Personal which included knowledge, skills, and personal development. The third section was Opinions About Your School, which included institutional emphasis, quality of relationships, and satisfaction. The fourth section consisted of questions designed by the Council of Christian Colleges and Universities (CCCU).

473

<a id="ga29-p476"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=476 printed_page=474 -->

The survey report gives information for our first-year students and senior students and compared those results with the CCCU and National means. Another piece of data given is the Effect Size. This is the indicator of the "practical significance" of the magnitude of the difference between the means. In essence, this is a process to determine if the Covenant average, as compared with other averages, is of any significance. An Effect Size between.2 and.5 is considered rather small,.5 to.8 is moderate, and.8 and higher is large. Therefore, when viewing Effect Size, one should take notice of anything that is.6 or.7 and above. That Effect Size shows some significant difference between Covenant and the other schools of comparison. The data that is reported in the remaining portion of this section is intended to demonstrate benchmarks which will later be compared with future NSSE reports.

There were six areas in the NSSE results which showed some level of statistical difference between Covenant students, the students of the Council for Christian Colleges and Universities (CCCU), and the national sample. These areas were academic, intellectual, and social experiences; reading and writing; knowledge, skills, and personal development; institutional emphasis; quality of relationships; and three questions posed by the CCCU.

There were three responses within the area of academic, intellectual, and social experiences that were slightly lower at a small or moderate level of statistical significance. When compared to the mean scores of CCCU schools or the national pool, our students were below the norm concerning working with other students on a project in class or a faculty member on a research project. The issue of working with a student on a class project moved from a small significance for freshmen to a moderate difference among the seniors. The mean score for our seniors was also below the mean for CCCU schools and the national schools at the small level of significance in the area of coming to class prepared. However, the use of e-mail to communicate with an instructor or other students was higher at both the freshman and senior level when compared to both groups.

An area of strength for Covenant students was thinking critically and analytically. Our seniors demonstrated a moderate level of difference when compared with the CCCU and national schools. While our freshmen responses resulted in a small negative difference in the issue of "understanding people of other racial and ethnic backgrounds," the seniors did not show any difference. It appears that time spent at Covenant College helps students in this area.

The largest positive differences were in the issues of relationships. Our seniors' responses demonstrated a moderate level of statistical significance when compared to the national mean in the area of "helping you cope with your non-academic responsibilities," "providing the support you need to thrive socially," and "relationships with administrative personnel and offices." "Relationships with other students" and "faculty members" were also ranked at a small level when compared with the national group.

474

<a id="ga29-p477"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=477 printed_page=475 -->

Two responses among the CCCU questions gave our students a small positive level of statistical significance. The freshmen mean score was higher than other CCCU schools on the statement: "This college has challenged me to critically evaluate and reconsider values that I have always held." The senior responses demonstrated the next step in this personal identification with Christ as their mean score ranked at a statistically higher score than the other CCCU schools to the statement: "The way I do things from day to day is often affected by my relationship with God."

These two responses are very important pieces of information. Our students are better prepared to meet the mission of the college when they are able to claim their value system as their own and then see how their relationship with God affects their action.

### Student Satisfaction Inventory

This past year ended a three-year period of researching student satisfaction at Covenant. The purpose of the study was to examine many areas of service based on the student's rankings of importance and satisfaction. Results include comparisons of the mean scores of our students and that of two other groups - other four-year private colleges and CCCU schools.

The survey examined areas of academic advising, campus climate, campus life, campus support services, concern for the individual, instructional effectiveness, recruitment and financial aid, registration effectiveness, responsiveness to diverse populations, safety and security, service excellence, and student centeredness. Students were asked to give two responses to each question - one rating their view of the importance of the issue and the other their satisfaction with the issue. The difference between importance and satisfaction is termed the performance gap.

Covenant's ranking is higher (meaning a lower performance gap) in all 12 of the areas listed above when compared to public colleges and 11 of the 12 when compared to the private colleges.

### There are five questions that have been fairly consistently ranked with a high level of importance and a low level of satisfaction.

The largest performance gap we had over those three years was question dealing with the "adequacy of the library resources and services". Covenant's average performance gap over those three years was 3.32, while the national average at CCCU schools was only 1.34, ranking it fifth. This indicates that there is a major concern among our

students in both importance and satisfaction, and it is more isolated at Covenant than it is at other schools. This issue now holds a very high priority in use of time and funding in the new Three-year Plan.

The question that seeks information about our students' perspective on the "core curriculum" is the number two issue of concern. It is worth noting that during these years, the student leadership gathered student's opinions about the core – specifically Self and Society and made some recommendation. The faculty recently made modification in that course (as reported on pages 11 and 12) which should improve the core.

Two questions that ranked third and fourth in a high performance gap dealt with the ability to register for classes with few conflicts and the variety of classes offered. It does appear that this is a common problem in a small Christian school and that we share it with other CCCU schools.

Our students ranked the adequacy of financial aid as the fifth greatest concern over the three-year period of study. It is interesting to note that our performance gap of 1.81 compares very favorably to 1.61 of the average CCCU school. The 1.61 would rank this concern as the number one issue among CCCU schools, where it is only fifth at Covenant.

Section 5: Advancement

Admissions The 1999-2000 academic year provided a great change for the manner in which the Admissions office was managed. An Admissions Self-Managed Team (ASMT) was organized to provide all managerial oversight for admissions functions. Each team member was assigned various responsibilities, such as training, campus preview weekend, hiring, office management, etc. As they continued to improve the process of being a self-managed team, several members have taken on additional administrative responsibilities in conjunction with the needs of the office and the college.

The team is seeking new strategic relationships and further the development of current relationships within the PCA. They are also seeking to increase visibility in targeted regions. With the addition of a diversity recruiter, there are now six team members traveling to represent the college at various college fairs, schools, churches, and inhome visits. This year was also the first year when a large number of inquiries and applicants were received via the internet. This is a rather new method of recruiting for Covenant College, causing the ASMT to seek better ways to communicate the mission to those students inquiring about Covenant College through the worldwide web.

While the goal of converting 40% of applications into matriculants was met, the number of new students fell short of budget projections. There were several factors contributing to this small new student count. The 1999-2000 recruitment year was the first year that the college awarded financial aid using a financial leveraging system. This type of system attempts to meet 100% of the financial need for the more qualified students as defined by the merit index point system. Index points are awarded based on academic, spiritual, and leadership characteristics. Financial aid from other sources such as Church Scholarship Partnership (CSP) program, and state or federal programs are not affected by this system.

Those students receiving the highest level of index points and those in the CSP program were awarded first. Awarding then continued in the second group. The students in the second group who had extremely high need were awarded last within that group. This ensures that a larger number of qualified students can be awarded 100% of their need before the financial aid funds are depleted. The process continued, meeting 100% of the need for those students awarded, until the institutional financial aid budget was expended. The major difference between this system and the systems used in previous years was the percentage of need met of those students who were awarded was higher. While fewer students were awarded from this particular fund, those students who were awarded received close to 100% of their need.

Past experience has shown that meeting a smaller portion of need for a great quantity of students did not serve either the students or the college well. The financial aid leveraging system attempts to provide financial assistance at a higher level to those students who are best qualified to enter Covenant College. Because of the change of

480

<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=483 printed_page=481 -->

awarding system, 39 students were placed on a waiting list for financial aid. Research shows that most schools that shift to financial leveraging suffer a drop in applications the following year while the matriculation percentage increases. This is evidenced in the figures below:

Section 6: Three-year Plan 2000-2003

The Plan for 2000-2003

GOAL: Strengthen the College's academic culture with its Reformed emphasis, to serve Christ, His church and His world.

Covenant College—its Board of Trustees, faculty, staff and students—serves as an agency of the PCA for the purpose of preparing God's people to extend Christ's ministry to the church and the world. This preparation necessarily requires both spiritual and intellectual development. As an academic institution, the unique task of this agency is to teach people to think christianly and to serve as an intellectual resource. This plan builds on the College's historically strong commitment to academic training informed by our Reformed heritage. The College's purpose statement spells out the essential character of the Reformed academic culture we seek to strengthen: fostering an environment that encourages a zeal for God's truth submissive to God's Word and a spirit of love and humility. Zeal for the truth involves both joyfully searching for it in every area of life, and confidently defending God's truth by critiquing those forms of thought and life antithetical to it. Christ-like love and humility require that these activities be characterized by gentleness and respect for others. Cultivating this attitude about the truth and the ability to apply it to Christ's service requires that concern for intellectual development inform every aspect of the College's operations. An environment that encourages this kind of cultivation requires a campus-wide commitment. Not only must the curriculum foster a delight in academic rigor and intellectual engagement, but the atmosphere outside of class must promote it as well. This plan seeks to focus the College's energy for the next three years on reviewing all our efforts with this end in mind. The following ten objectives will be implemented during that time to help us better serve the mission of the college.

483

<a id="ga29-p486"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=486 printed_page=484 -->

1. Become more intentional about continuously improving the quality and breadth of both teaching and learning and the strength and coherence of the academic program. Develop a comprehensive long-range academic plan. Establish new Procedures and Criteria for the regular review of academic (and administrative) departments and the overall college curriculum. Establish or identify the appropriate body to be responsible for the oversight and coordination of the Core Curriculum. Direct the attentions of the faculty development process to the mentoring of good professional skills for new and continuing faculty. Become more proactive in recruiting potential faculty candidates. Establish an honors program. Increase the visibility of the college's academic programs.

2. Cultivate a campus climate that encourages academic excellence. Add more academically oriented work study positions Help students with work loads and financial pressures by raising work study Encourage and recognize staff contributions to the academic climate Change presidential scholarship point system to encourage primacy of academic tasks Establish additional outside speakers programs Establish a hiring policy which increases diversity Continue to develop and deepen freshman orientation's focus on academic tasks Strengthen departmental identity among faculty members and students in the disciplines

3. Enhance the overall coherence of each student's Covenant experience. Establish an institutional-wide policy concerning complete and uninterrupted daytime access for students to all offices that provide student services. The student senate will collaborate with the appropriate faculty committee to develop a document that specifies the "Expectations and Priorities of the Academic Culture." The teaching faculty and the residence life staff will work cooperatively to ensure that the residence policies support and enhance instruction and learning. The Career Development office will collaborate with the appropriate faculty department to develop discipline-related life experience opportunities for students. Explicate the chapel and practical service graduation requirements rendering them coherent with the academic program. Develop a college philosophy for academic support services and establish procedures regarding reasonable accommodation and access to academic instruction. The office of academic affairs will coordinate and promote an enhanced schedule of on-campus scholarly exchanges and performances.

484

<a id="ga29-p487"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=487 printed_page=485 -->

Evaluate the college's national athletic affiliation and propose actions that are consistent with the college's purpose and objectives for its athletic program.

4. Nurture a climate of genuine spiritual vitality, consistent with our identity and role as a Christ-centered college, that is characterized by godly relationships, effective communication and mutual trust. Increase understanding of and commitment to the proper role and witness of faculty, administration, and staff in nurturing a climate of genuine spiritual vitality at Covenant. Various methods of assessment will be developed by the Chapel committee to evaluate the current climate of spiritual vitality on campus. These methods should be generally narrative and descriptive rather than quantitative. Students, faculty, and staff will be offered opportunities to learn and grow in the area of biblical conflict resolution, in the effective and edifying use of personal and electronic communications, and in mutual accountability. Following an audit of all print and electronic sources of official on and off campus communications, a review should be made of the overall coherence and effectiveness of these products with respect to the distinctive academic and spiritual climate of the college and the need for complete and timely communication on important issues.

5. Explicate Covenant's educational philosophy and organizational values. Develop a process leading to action on a consensus educational philosophy document that is commonly understood by most faculty regarding its meaning and uses. Develop a consensus organizational values document that is commonly understood by employees of the college regarding its meaning and uses. Also, develop tools that help examine the consistency of institutional decisions with that document.

6. Evaluate and address faculty privileges and load responsibilities for teaching, advising, research, and committee service; and nurture the faculty as a collegium of teacher-scholars whose scholarship enriches the classroom, engages their disciplines, and provides visible intellectual resources for Christ's church and his world. Expand the existing faculty "load" mechanism beyond contact hours in class with students in order to include faculty responsibilities in the core areas of advising, scholarship, committee work and (otherwise uncompensated) service to the college. Using this mechanism, identify a normal faculty "load." Reward faculty for service above and outside their normal responsibilities. Provide practical encouragement for faculty collaboration in research, pedagogydevelopment, and publication. Offer at least two faculty-led educational services directly to PCA churches (weekend seminars on current issues, distance-learning opportunities for RUF students, pastor's wives, missionaries, homeschoolers).

7. Dramatically increase the prominence and usefulness of library resources and space to provide the campus with a center for serious research and collaborative inquiry. Purchase additional periodical subscriptions in paper form for each academic major as recommended by faculty. Purchase electronic periodical subscriptions from Project Muse. Explore a pilot joint venture with the Center for Christian Studies at the University of Virginia. Raise $10, 000 per student in designated funds to support newly recruited diversity students.

10. Develop a long range Financial and Campus Master Plan that will enable the college to grow to full potential while safeguarding the academic culture of the college.
