## APPENDIX F

### REPORT OF

### COVENANT THEOLOGICAL SEMINARY

### TO THE 29TH GENERAL ASSEMBLY

### OF THE PRESBYTERIAN CHURCH IN AMERICA

We are delighted and humbled to report that the Lord has again graciously provided for future generations of ministers and Christian workers "faithful to the Scriptures, the Reformed faith and the Great Commission" by blessing this year's ministry of Covenant Theological Seminary. Our Savior reminds us that, "unto whomsoever much is given, of him shall be much required" (Luke 12:48). What God has given is the enlargement of our boundaries, provision for our needs, and the great joy of sensing that his hand is upon us. While it is our responsibility and privilege to recount those blessings again this year, we want to begin by telling you how we are responding in gratitude to the mercies of our God. Since our Lord requires that we make good use of his gifts, we are attempting to identify opportunities to serve his Church more effectively and to proclaim his name more broadly among the nations.

- **I.** New Opportunities to Serve Our Church

Covenant Worldwide Extension Program: Covenant Worldwide is the extension training and media ministry program of Covenant Seminary that is taking an accredited degree and lay training resources around the world with new technologies. This past February marked the beginning of a new era in Seminary Extension Training. We were already offering external Master of Arts degrees in four cities across the country (as well as offering accredited course work in dozens of cities across this nation and internationally). Now we have received approval to offer a fully-accredited Master of Arts degree any time, anywhere. This degree is offered through a combination of audio and visual resources, phone support, three one-week residencies – all enhanced by internet resources and support. We are one of only two accredited seminaries in North America that has permission to offer this extension degree in such a format. Now we will be able to serve church leaders throughout the world who want advanced seminary training but are not able to move to a seminary. Elders, deacons, youth and campus workers, Sunday School teachers, Christian school teachers, missionaries, and devoted lay persons from all walks of life will be able to obtain the highest quality seminary training both in this degree program and through a variety of non-degree, media resources. While we do not plan to offer the Master of Divinity through this program, students preparing for the ministry will also be able to earn significant portions of their degrees through Covenant's Worldwide Extension Training. We are firmly committed

488

<a id="ga29-p491"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=491 printed_page=489 -->

to a residential training program for pastoral training that involves interaction in community with peers, professors and local churches. Still, we want to share with our church and world the wonderful resources that God has given us to defend and spread faith in the inerrancy of his Word and the wonder of his grace. Already we have the Master of Arts curriculum available for extension students. This program will be upgraded and expanded over the next three years with nearly one million dollars in additional funding. Dr. Brad Hough (Ph.D. in Instructional Technology from Vanderbilt), Vice President for Enrollment and External Programs Kevin Vanden Brink, and our experienced External Program Director Dan Gilchrist are providing excellent leadership for this exciting new ministry opportunity.

Youth in Ministry Institute: Last year we told you that that Covenant Seminary had also been awarded a $1.2 million grant from the Lilly Endowment to develop our Youth in Ministry Institute

### (YIMI).

The Youth in Ministry Institute first seeks to provide high-school-age youth with seminary resources to think in a deeper way about vocational ministry. Second, the Youth in Ministry Institute provides new academic programs to prepare seminarians (and those presently ministering to young people) for youth ministry in the PCA and beyond. This program is off to a wonderful start. We have conducted three institutes in various regions of the country. We have offered three youth ministry courses. And we are seeing new students coming to Covenant for a focus in youth ministry. We presented an extraordinary report to the Lilly Endowment regarding these efforts and it has offered us the opportunity to apply for increased funding for this important program that is so vital for the future of our Church's youth and youth pastors.

Francis Schaeffer Institute: The mission of the Francis Schaeffer Institute is to help Christians address the concerns of our culture with the claims of Christ. We help students and fellow believers learn to bring the light of the Gospel to areas of culture that traditionally challenge our efforts to honor the Savior. Through a variety of special lectures, courses and art exhibits the Schaeffer Institute has become one of the Seminary's primary means of equipping students attitudinally as well as intellectually to reach the diverse culture around us. The major lecture series of the Schaeffer Institute this year were: Time, Money and God: Does Faith Make a Difference Gender and Faith: An Examination of Women's Roles in Society Visiting lecturers also addressed the following: Perspectives on Presenting the Gospel in Russian Society Islam and Christianity Apologetics from an African-American Perspective Loving Those Who Hate the Church The popular Friday Nights at the Institute, where students and professors address topics at local bookstores, continues to be an effective way of speaking to persons

489

<a id="ga29-p492"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=492 printed_page=490 -->

outside traditional church circles. A number of churches around the country have taken up the model begun at Covenant Seminary as a way of reaching the unchurched in their communities. Topics addressed on Friday nights this year have included: The Yearning for Spirituality in Pop Music Have Missionaries Really Been Bad for Culture? Restoration in the Inner City As part of the spring Schaeffer Lecture Series we again invited PCA Women in church staff positions across the nation to attend to a conference to discuss how to serve the Lord biblically in their settings. We have received words of great appreciation from these women for this opportunity to share ideas and challenges with one another.

Archaeology Institute: Through the marvelous provision of caring donors we have received endowed funds that will allow Dr. David Chapman to succeed Emeritus Professor of New Testament Dr. W. Harold Mare as Curator of the Mare Institute for Biblical and Archaeological Studies. This provision will enable Covenant to continue providing students with archaeological evidence and explanation for the truth of Scripture, as well as providing a consistent, Evangelical voice in the field of Biblical Archaeology. Dr. Mare will continue his supervision of the Archaeology Institute as Dr. Chapman "learns the ropes" both here and at the Abila Project excavations in Jordan.

Field Education: Increasingly we are cooperating with local churches in the training of students for ministry. We require Covenant Seminary students to "do theology in the context of the church" in order to receive our degree. We see as increasingly important the requirement that every ordination-track student have at least 300 hours of field education in a local ministry supervised by a local pastor or session. Earning an M.Div. from Covenant Seminary means more than simply doing well in class. We are more than a graduate school. In addition to training students under professors of the highest academic credentials, we believe that it is necessary for students (and professors) to be integrally involved in the life of the local church. Preaching, teaching, visitation, session meeting involvement, evangelism, and mentoring by mature church leaders are now vital components of student ministry preparation. Having students in community with peers, professors and pastors creates a vital matrix that we believe is necessary for training the next generation of leaders with the very best resources and wisdom that this generation of leaders can provide. Our goal is to engage heart as well as mind, and to use church experiences as well as academic challenges to instill wisdom regarding God's Word and love for his people.

II. God's Gifts and Blessings:

Enrollment: In this twelfth year of consecutive record enrollments, the Lord brought 935 students from 47 states and 16 nations to Covenant Seminary for the fall semester.

490

<a id="ga29-p493"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=493 printed_page=491 -->

Over 1,172 students throughout the entire year were registered in Covenant Seminary classes. Not only are we thankful for the increased number of students but also for the increasing support of PCA churches as indicated by student referrals. The number of incoming students referred to us by churches and pastors doubled in the last two years.

Finances: God enabled Covenant to finish this fiscal year in the black. This has been our consistent report through the last decade. Our God is great and greatly to be praised for so faithfully providing for his Church and her future servants. Through the Lord's wonderful provision we are typically able to provide at least half of the tuition through financial scholarships for each PCA student in the ordination track and under care of his presbytery. Placement: We praise God for his extraordinary blessing in providing placement for our growing number of graduates. Every M.Div. graduate seeking placement in an ordained ministry position and having Seminary recommendation was placed this year (100% placement rate for the second consecutive year). Over the past eleven years, over 98% percent of Master of Divinity graduates with Seminary recommendation seeking ordained placement have secured ministry positions. Additionally, since the first class graduated in 1995, 97% of the graduates of the Master of Arts in Counseling program have also been placed. We are very grateful for the confidence the churches of the PCA have shown in our ministry-training focus as is evidenced by their reception of our graduates.

Pastor/Scholar Faculty: For over forty years, the faculty of Covenant Theological Seminary has sought exceptionally gifted pastor/scholars to defend and communicate the historic Christian faith. In January 2001, the Board of Trustees approved Dr. David Chapman to join our faculty to teach New Testament and Biblical Archaeology. Dr. Chapman completed his doctorate at Cambridge University after years of college campus ministry. The Board also approved the Rev. Zachary Eswine, senior pastor of Grace Presbyterian Church (PCA) in Hudson, OH, to join the Homiletics faculty. Rev. Eswine is a gifted preacher and musician who is completing a doctorate in Speech Communication at Regent University. Both of these gifted teachers reflect the pastor/scholar profile that Covenant seeks in our faculty, combining high academic achievement with significant ministry experience. Significant contributions to the following works have been made by our Faculty this year: Rev. Jerram Barrs The Heart of Evangelism (Crossway) Women of the Word (Crossway) Dr. Hans Bayer New Testament Introduction (Baker) Commentary on Mark (R. Brockhaus)

491

<a id="ga29-p494"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=494 printed_page=492 -->

Dr. Bryan Chapell Holiness by Grace (Crossway) Commentary on Titus (Crossway) Dr. David Chapman "Perceptions of Crucifixion Among Jews and Christians in the Ancient World" (Tyndale Bulletin) Dr. Jack Collins The God of Miracles (Crossway and IVP-UK) Old Testament editor for the English Standard Version of the Bible Dr. Dan Doriani Putting the Truth to Work (P&R) Dr. Donald Guthrie A Life-long Call to Learn (Abingdon) Dr. Robert Peterson Hell Under Fire (Zondervan) Knowing God Our Heavenly Father: What the Bible Teaches about Adoption (P&R) Dr. David Jones "The Posture of the Theological School" in Aims and Purposes of Evangelical Theological Education (Eerdmans) Dr. Richard Winter "A Biblical and Theological Perspective on Grief and Bereavement" (Journal of Psychology and Christianity) Dr. Robert Vasholz Commentary on Leviticus (Christian Focus)

In addition to writing pursuits and their full-time teaching duties our professors remain engaged in many avenues of ministry. For example: Dr. Phil Douglass (Church Planting and Renewal Professor) continues to pastor Emmanuel Presbyterian Church in a renewal ministry that uses many seminary interns, and serves as a church planting consultant to various churches. Dr. Nelson Jennings (World Mission Professor) continues to conduct mission trips for seminary students and others (countries visited this past year include Ghana and Peru). Dr. Hans Bayer (New Testament Professor) will minister in Germany, the Ukraine, and Hungary this year. Dr. Dan Zink (Biblical Counseling Professor) directs the New Hope Counseling Services of Chesterfield Presbyterian Church.

Facilities: The most visible fruit of the $16 Million "Jewel of Grace, Fire for Ministry" capital campaign is the completed construction and tripled size of Covenant's J. Oliver Buswell, Jr. Library. We are reveling in the expansive space for books, the beautiful surroundings for student study, the vastly upgraded technology resources, multiple conference centers, and a new home for faculty offices. We had a glorious day of dismissed classes as students and professors joined to move books and offices to the new facility. We were pleased that supervisors of the professional library moving company (that helps hundreds of libraries with such transitions) said that they had never seen the kind of student and faculty support that we had involved in this library move.

492

<a id="ga29-p495"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=495 printed_page=493 -->

The Library expansion also provided additional space for the PCA Historical Center Archives, and an internet-enhanced Resource and Information Center that pastors and alums can use from remote locations.

Administrative Blessings: In light of the growing technology pressures and opportunities in higher education we have added a Chief Technology Officer to our President's Cabinet. Dr. Brad Hough, from our Nashville PCA church family, came this past fall to lead our technology efforts. He received a Ph.D. in Instructional Technology from Vanderbilt University, and also holds a Master's Degree in School Administration and a Bachelor's in Interactive Media Design. Dr. Hough is an author and speaker on the use of technology in education and has developed and provided custom technology training for a number of universities and schools. Mr. Dave Wicker will serve as Covenant's new Vice President for Seminary Advancement. This is a new position for the Seminary that includes both the traditional fundraising responsibilities of our chief development officer, as well as the new responsibilities of coordinating all of the Seminary's church relations, public relations, media and publications. Mr. Wicker comes well prepared for these responsibilities having spent 25 years in marketing and management for some of our nation's leading retailers and client relations firms.

### CONCLUSION

On March 3, 2001 the Rev. Dr. Donald J. MacNair went to join his Maker and Savior after a lifetime of faithful service to the Church of Jesus Christ. Don MacNair was one of the chief architects of the Joining and Receiving of the RPCES and the PCA. He remained one of the staunchest and most articulate advocates of bringing together these like-minded bodies committed to biblical Presbyterianism even when he knew that the consolidation would require that he leave his position as head of his denomination's church planting arm. Dr. MacNair was far more concerned for the advancement of the Kingdom than he was for his own personal advantage. Don MacNair's commitment to Kingdom purposes was displayed over and over as this visionary and humble man met with a few other pastors and layman at his desk 45 years ago to plan the organization of Covenant College and Seminary. He even helped string the land survey chains when the boundaries of the original campuses were marked. He led the construction effort of the flagship Covenant Presbyterian Church in St. Louis, and also was the visionary leader behind the now-large, Christian retirement community known as Friendship Village. An author of seven books on the care and feeding of the local church, Don MacNair poured his last years into church consultation through Churches Vitalized, an organization he designed to help congregations identify their sources of hurting and their paths to healing according to biblical principles of leadership and organization. These principles Don MacNair also taught to a generation of young men at Covenant Theological Seminary as a wise and thoughtful father in the faith. Donald J. MacNair's entry into glory is accompanied this year by the news of the pressures of age upon several of the men and spouses of that first generation of

493

<a id="ga29-p496"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=496 printed_page=494 -->

Covenant Seminary professors. Specifically I covet your prayers for Dr. R. Laird Harris, Dr. Wilbur B.Wallis, and Dr. W. Harold Mare – my own dear and honored professors. These are the men who, though no longer teaching at Covenant, we continue to honor with emeritus status for their noteworthy sacrifices made in the cause of defending the truth of Scripture and the historic Christian faith. When reputations, pensions and salaries had to be jeopardized to establish a school faithful to the truth of Scripture, they did not hesitate. Echoing the response of Isaiah they said simply, "Here am I, send me." Now God is calling these who have run the race with such integrity and courage close to home, and they are passing the baton to us. I have never felt that baton so weighty in my hand as in this past year, and I have never felt more thankful to these men – my fathers in the faith – for running the race so well. May God give us grace to do the same as we trust his Word, seek his face, and proclaim his Son for this generation and the next.

Respectfully Submitted,

Bryan Chapell, President Covenant Theological Seminary

## APPENDIX G

### REPORT OF THE BOARD OF TRUSTEES OF THE

### INSURANCE, ANNUITY AND RELIEF FUNDS

### TO THE TWENTY-NINTH GENERAL ASSEMBLY

### OF THE PRESBYTERIAN CHURCH IN AMERICA

Statement of Purpose The purpose of the Board of Trustees of Insurance, Annuity and Relief Funds of the Presbyterian Church in America is to glorify God through serving His servants who minister in the Church by offering financial products to provide for the health and welfare, retirement and relief needs of the denomination's ministers, missionaries, lay church workers and their families, and to serve the churches, committees and agencies of the PCA and related organizations by sponsoring and endorsing a denominational property and liability insurance program.

Summary

Year 2000 came and went with little, if any, of the dreaded predictions of Y2K computer problems that had consumed so much energy and time for several prior years. Your Board and Staff are happy to report another successful year for the PCA benefit plans and ministerial relief. We began two new programs the first of the year--longterm care insurance and a property and liability insurance plan.

The PCA retirement plan continued its growth pattern in both number of participants and assets. Our Ministerial Relief ministry continued to touch the lives of a growing number of retired and disabled pastors, missionaries and lay employees and their surviving widows and dependent children.

Total assets under management increased, but at a slower pace than in recent years, primarily because of the faltering stock market, which finally cooled and declined after the first quarter. Most benchmark indexes, including the Dow Jones Industrials, the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq, reflected negative returns for the year. At year end, assets stood at $176.7 million, compared with $172.1 million for 1999, an increase of 2.7%

Following are some of the initiatives pursued during 2000.

Implemented a new long-term care insurance program for PCA ministers, missionaries, lay employees, retirees and their families through CNA Insurance Company.

495

<a id="ga29-p498"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=498 printed_page=496 -->

Implemented a property and liability insurance program for PCA churches and other entities through Aon Religious Institutions Alliance. For 2001 we changed carriers to GuideOne Insurance Company. Reduced premiums for the Long-Term Disability and Term Life Insurance Plans for 2001. Added Chicago Capital Management as our fixed income manager for retirement, insurance and relief fund portfolios. Changed custodial banks from Wachovia to First Union. Began the process of changing insurance administrators, which was completed on April 1, 2001.

Please refer to Appendix One – PROGRAM SUMMARY – for comparative statistical information on the PCA benefit plans for the past three years.

Retirement Plans

New enrollments in the PCA Tax Sheltered Annuity Plan were slightly over 300. Total enrollment, including retirees on benefit, surviving spouses and those with frozen accounts, at year end stood at 4,328. Retirement plan assets were $171.2 million, compared to $167.5 million for 1999, a 2.2% increase. Net returns for the retirement funds are shown in the chart below.

1999 2000 PCA Equity Fund 15.2% 2.2% PCA Balanced Fund 1.1% -2.1% PCA Income Fund 3.2% 8.2% Aggressive Growth Fund 44.4% -10.3% Growth Fund 4.0% -20.3% Growth and Income Fund 14.7% 13.6% Stock Index Fund 20.7% -9.2% Foreign Fund 39.0% -3.7% Bond Fund 3.1% 8.9% Money Market 4.6% 6.0%

It is significant that, in a year in which the Dow Jones (-4.7%), S&P 500 (-9.1%) and Nasdaq (-39.3%) were all negative, two of our equity funds (PCA Equity and Growth and Income) produced positive gains. Overall, five of the ten funds were up for the year. Bonds generally out-performed equities, as reflected in the returns of the PCA Income Fund and the Bond Fund versus all the equity funds, except the Growth and Income Fund. The Money Market Fund produced its best ever gain.

Insurance Plans

Health Plans

The two health plans basically held their own for the year—beginning the year with total enrollments of 805 and ending the year with 800. The Pacific Life plan had favorable claims experience, resulting in an overall premium increase of only 4.8% for 2001, compared to a 14% increase for 2000. The Blue Choice HMO/Point of Service Plans for the Atlanta area had increases of 17-20%, effective August 1. Benefit changes also increased copays for prescription drugs and emergency room visits. We provide annual open enrollment for both plans, in December and July, respectively.

Long-Term Disability Plan

Standard Insurance of Oregon became our LTD carrier January 1, 2000, under a contract which, in most respects, duplicated the benefits under our prior contract with UNUM. Enrollment in the plan continued to increase. Based on good experience we were able to reduce premiums for 2001 from.75% to.65% of compensation for those covered under Social Security and from 1.00% to.90% for those not under Social Security.

Life Insurance Plans

Continued good claims experience and other favorable factors enabled the Trustees to approve a premium reduction for 2001 for the PCA Term Life Insurance Plan from $23 to $20 per month. This term plan maintains a single premium for all participants, but reduces the amount of coverage in five year age brackets. By contrast, the Optional Life Insurance Plan provides for participant flexibility as to amount of coverage—from $20,000 to $250,000—with age based premiums in five year brackets. It also provides for spouse and dependent children coverages, at the option of the participant.

Ministerial Relief

During 2000, 7 ministers, 1 minister's wife, 1 missionary's wife, 2 ministers' widows, 4 lay employees, and 1 lay employee's widow died. Mrs. Ann Llewelyn continues to minister to a growing number of ministry widows by telephone counseling, letters and personal visits. In addition we supply regular monthly financial assistance to needy retirees, disabled, widows and dependents. The Relief Fund also provides periodic payments on a case-by-case basis to help pay medical and dental bills for eligible recipients. We also pay health insurance premiums for limited time periods for PCA ministers between calls and for some disabled ministers and lay workers.

The annual Christmas Offering provides primary funding for Relief activities. Through March 20, 2001, the offering for Christmas 2000 was over $392,993.55. Many thanks to the churches and individuals who gave.

### Legislative Changes

### Social Security

The United States Congress passed legislation allowing ministers who had previously opted out of Social Security to opt back into the system during 2000 or 2001. Information about the time frames and procedures was provided in the Fall 2000 Benefit Bulletin, our semi-annual newsletter, and in the 2001 Ministers Tax Guide, distributed free to all PCA ministers. This information can also be found on our Web site at www.pcanet.org.

Congress also passed legislation during 2000 dropping the earnings limits for retirees receiving Social Security for those age 65-69 who continue to work. This is good news for PCA ministers and lay employees who would like to draw Social Security benefits while continuing to work beyond age 65. As normal retirement age for full benefits creeps upward for those born after 1937, so will the effects of this change. The earnings limits still apply to those who begin receiving benefits between ages 62-64. Those age 70 and above have never had an earnings limit.

### Housing Allowance

(The following three paragraphs are excerpted from a memo dated October 25, 2000, from attorney David A. Starr of Williams and Jensen, a Washington, DC law firm representing the Church Alliance.)

A U.S. Tax Court case in 2000, Warren v. Commissioner, has called into question the
scope of clergy housing allowance. In this case the Tax Court determined that the
amount of income that can be excluded as housing allowance is not limited to the fair
market rental value of a home. This decision is currently being appealed by the IRS to a
federal appeals court. A final judicial determination may be many months away. In the
mean time, the IRS is not obligated to alter its longstanding interpretation of the
housing allowance, and, as indicated by its appeal, continues to take the position that
housing allowance is limited to fair market rental value.

Churches and clergy should act with extreme caution in relying on the Tax Court
decision until the courts have made a final determination. In addition, the housing
allowance is a creature of statute, and Congress can always modify the special tax
treatment accorded the housing allowance. The legislative risk increases if Congress
believes that the courts have expanded the scope of the housing allowance to create
unintended results.

### * * *

In the event that the Tax Court decision is reversed on appeal, tax payers who either
amend their prior tax returns or prospectively exclude more than the fair market rental
value may be subject to deficiency determinations by the IRS. The IRS could assess tax

<a id="ga29-p501"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=501 printed_page=499 -->

penalties and interest. Increased housing allowance deductions can also impact the amount of other allowable tax deductions that are based on taxable income levels, such as deductible IRA contributions. (Or contributions to the PCA Tax-Sheltered Annuity Plan.) Staff

### THIRTEENTH AMENDMENT

### TO THE

### PRESBYTERIAN CHURCH IN AMERICA

### MONEY PURCHASE PENSION PLAN

## APPENDIX H

Interchurch Relations Committee Report to The Twenty-Ninth General Assembly, 2001

- **I.** Membership

TE Derek W. H. Thomas RE Robert Ashlock, Secretary TE R. Irfon Hughes, Chairman RE R. Meade Guy, TE Bruce Howes RE David R. Lambert TE M. Christopher Ehlers, Alternate RE Jack Merry, Alternate TE L. Roy Taylor, Stated Clerk (RAO III, 3-2, j., ex officio) TE Ken Thompson (MTW Consultant, Advisory Member)

II. Meetings

September 19, 2000 - Atlanta December 11, 2000 – Conference call subsequent to NAPARC fall meeting March 12, 2001 – Conference call subsequent to NAE meeting

III. Information Items

- **A.** The Twenty-eighth Assembly referred three matters to the IRC for action and report.

1. The National Association of Evangelicals' revising its rules so as to allow denominations that are members of the National Council of Churches, and are willing to endorse the Doctrinal statement of the NAE, to hold membership in both bodies simultaneously (Minutes of the Twenty-eighth General Assembly, p.63).

2. Communication with the Evangelical Presbyterian Church regarding their receiving a minister under the discipline of the PCA (Minutes of the Twenty-eighth General Assembly, p.63-64).

3. Clarification of the PCA's relationship with the World Fellowship of Reformed Churches (Minutes of the Twenty-eighth General Assembly, p.64).

- **B.** The committee met via conference call at its September 19, 2000 meeting with Dr. Kevin Mannoia, President of the NAE, Dr. Edward Foggs, Chairperson of the Board of NAE, and Mrs. Dianne Knippers, Chairperson of the Membership Committee. The committee discussed the issue of the National Association of Evangelical's revising Bylaw B-7 as follows:

510

<a id="ga29-p513"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=513 printed_page=511 -->

B-7 Dual Membership. Although denominations shall not hold <del>dual membership in the National Association of Evangelicals and</del> any other organization at a comparable ecclesiastical level, such as the National Council of Churches of Christ in America, the World Council of Churches, and the American Council of Christian Churches, local churches and organizations whose denominations who belong to other such bodies but who desire membership in the National Association of Evangelicals may be received provided they fulfill membership requirements. Denominations may hold dual membership in the National Association of Evangelicals and other organizations at a comparable ecclesiastical level. Denominations holding membership in other such organizations may be received into the NAE provided they fulfill the membership requirements.

The committee discussed the matter with the NAE representatives for about an hour. It was explained to the committee that the Reformed Church in America had initiated the request for the rule change so that the entire RCA, not just the Western Synod of the RCA could become a member of the NAE. The committee advised the NAE representatives of the concern the PCA has over the rule change and requested that it be changed. After the meeting the PCA Stated Clerk wrote the President of the NAE and formally requested that the rule change regarding "B-7 Dual Membership" be rescinded. The national convention of the NAE met March 5-7, 2001 in Dallas, Texas. TE Irfon Hughes, TE Bruce Howes and TE L. Roy Taylor attended, representing the General PCA IRC (See Attachment A). At the meeting of the Board of Directors the PCA Stated Clerk made the motion that the rule change regarding "dual membership" be rescinded and spoke to the issue. The motion was referred to the Bylaws Committee for study and report to the 2002 Convention. The PCA delegation believed that the PCA motion was well received by the general membership at the Board meeting. The Board also passed an resolution reaffirming the NAE's doctrinal commitment and resolved "not to seek out or respond to any overture of any body that would seek to subsume the NAE into the contemporary ecumenical movement, while continuing to partner with groups, as appropriate, to advance singular issues." Subsequent to the convention Dr. Mannoia issued a statement that the restudy [of Rule B-7] will occur to honor one of our own [the PCA] but that he does not expect it will result in the deletion of the bylaw from the NAE's books and that the chances are not great that it would be altered ("NAE Washington Insight" Church Edition, April, 2001). It is the intention of the IRC to seek to persuade the NAE Board of Directors, at the 2002 convention, to rescind Rule change B-7 and then to report the outcome to the 2002 General Assembly.

511

<a id="ga29-p514"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=514 printed_page=512 -->

- **C.** The Committee Chairman and the Stated Clerk met via conference call December 19, 2000 with the retiring Stated Clerk Dr. Ed Davis, the newly elected Stated Clerk Dr. Michael Glodo, and the Chairman of the Fraternal Relations Committee of the Evangelical Presbyterian Church, Mr. Paul Heidebrecht, to discuss with them the PCA's concern over their receiving into the EPC a PCA minister who was under discipline. (The Clerk had previously written the EPC Clerk advising him of the PCA Assembly's actions.) A procedure was agreed upon whereby the minister in question and representatives of the EPC Presbytery of the Mid-America would appear before Illiana Presbytery at their January 13, 2001 meeting to seek to effect reconciliation. When it was learned that there would be a proposal to proceed to depose and excommunicate TE David Baer at the January 13 meeting, the EPC delegation decided it would not be fruitful to attend. Illiana Presbytery did, in fact, depose and excommunicate Mr. Baer. The Presbytery subsequently adopted a motion that a committee be appointed to confer with the EPC Presbytery of the Mid-America to discuss reconciliation.

- **D.** The World Fellowship of Reformed Churches was formed in 1992 by the PCA, the National Presbyterian Church of Mexico, and the Presbyterian Church of Brazil under the World Evangelical Fellowship through our membership in the NAE, under the authorization of the Nineteenth General Assembly. (See Minutes of the Nineteenth General Assembly, 1991, II, Appendix B, p. 67; Minutes of the Twenty-second General Assembly, 1994 pp. 198, 521-522; Minutes of the Twenty-third General Assembly, 1995, pp. 166, 382-384). The WFRC only meets every three or four years, which is why there has not been a report in recent Assemblies. The WRFC Bylaws stipulate that officers are elected to serve a full term, which is why some PCA ministers who are no longer on the IRC have been serving as officers (TE Eric Perrin, TE Paul Gilchrist). The WFRC initiated contacts with the International Reformed Fellowship, founded in 1994, which is primarily composed of Churches in Asia. Representatives of the two groups met in Orlando, FL October 24-27, 2000 to discuss a possible merger of the two fellowships. A "joining and receiving" took place whereby the IRC was assimilated into the WRFC and the name of the organization was changed to "The International Reformed Fellowship." (See Attachment B). The doctrinal basis of the World Reformed Fellowship is the inspiration and inerrancy of Holy Scripture, the ancient universal creeds (Apostles, Nicene, Chalcedon) and adherence to one or more of the historic expressions of the Reformed Faith. The PCA representatives were TE Bruce Howes and TE L. Roy Taylor. The PCA representatives proposed a bicameral arrangement whereby denominations would vote on major policy decisions and institutions, individual members, and para-church ministry members would vote in a separate group, with agreement of both bodies being required and a weighed voting system to give larger denominations, such as the PCA, a

512

<a id="ga29-p515"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=515 printed_page=513 -->

greater voice. Bylaws were adopted along with the name change (see Attachment C). Of interest to the Assembly is that the World Reformed Fellowship as presently constituted is different in several respects from the World Fellowship of Reformed Churches: (1) The WRF is truly international and worldwide, whereas its precursor, the WFRC, was, to a great degree, inter-American (North, Central and South America), though there were some member Churches in India and East Africa, (2) The membership of the WFRC was limited to denominations, whereas WRF membership is open to denominations, institutions, particular congregations, mission agencies, and individuals, (3) The voting procedure is different as noted above, and (4) The membership of WFRC was limited to denominations holding to Reformed-covenantal Theology and Presbyterian polity. The WRF membership is open to conservative-evangelical denominations, institutions, particular congregations, mission agencies, and individuals, from the entirety of the Reformed Tradition as long as they held to the doctrinal basis of the Fellowship as specified in the Bylaws. For example, Reformed Episcopalians, Reformed Baptists, and Reformed Congregationalists would be eligible for membership. This recognizes the resurgence of the Reformed Faith in its various expressions around the world. Significant also is that, for perhaps the first time in history, a fellowship of the conservative, evangelical, Reformed Community has been formed that encompasses the various sub-divisions of the Reformed Tradition.

- **E.** The PCA is a member of the North American Presbyterian and Reformed Council (NAPARC). IRC chairman, TE R. Irfon Hughes, TE Bruce Howes, and the PCA Stated Clerk attended the NAPARC meeting, November 14-15, 2000 in Los Angeles, California. The PCA Stated clerk was re-elected chairman. The two main items of discussion were the similarities and differences among the member denominations with a view toward possible Church union(s) and the status of the Christian Reformed Church, now a suspended member.

1. Each denomination presented its distinctives. The present member Churches of NAPARC are: Associate Reformed Presbyterian Church, Korean American Presbyterian Church, Orthodox Presbyterian Church, Presbyterian Church in America, Reformed Church in the United States, Reformed Presbyterian Church in North America, and Christian Reformed Church in North America (suspended). TE Hughes was appointed to a committee to collate the reports and report to the 2001 meeting. The IRC will report in 2002 on the progress of those continued discussions regarding possible Church union(s).

2. The Christian Reformed Church of North America reconsidered and reaffirmed its stand on the ordination of women at its General Synod 2000, i.e. they reaffirmed that the portion of their Church Order (Article 3-a, the word "male") limiting the offices of minister, elder, and

513

<a id="ga29-p516"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=516 printed_page=514 -->

evangelist to men be declared "inoperative" so that the offices of elder, minister, and evangelist are open to women as well as men. A local option provision was approved for local churches and classes that differ with the General Synod's decision. The CRC delegation argued that The Belgic Confession, in both its French and Latin versions, in Article 30, uses a generic term, translated into English as "men," or "persons" when speaking of "The Government and Offices in the Church." The CRC delegation argued, that the matter of women's ordination is extraconfessional as far as the CRC is concerned and that the basis of NAPARC is the confessions of the member denominations. Others argued that; (1) The Belgic Confession specifically makes mention of "the rule prescribed by St. Paul in his epistle to Timothy," (2) The Basis of NAPARC is first of all the Bible and secondarily the Reformed Confessions,2 (3) the continental Reformed Churches in the Reformation era did not ordain women to ecclesiastical leadership, (4) for the General Synod to declare a portion of its Church Order "inoperative" without going through the process of actually amending the constitution circumvents that constitution and deprives the respective classes from voting as classes for an actual constitutional change.3 The PCA delegation made a motion that the CRC be expelled from NAPARC on the grounds of their action on women's ordination. A substitute motion passed that the matter to delayed until next year at which time more detailed specifications be presented. It is the intention of the IRC to ask again, at the 2001 NAPARC meeting, that the CRC be expelled from NAPARC on the ground of their action on women's ordination. We regard this as a matter of constitutional integrity.

- **F.** Communications from the United Reformed Churches have been received indicating their desire for pursuing further relations with the PCA. The matter will be discussed at the fall meeting (2001) of the IRC.

The sentence in question in the Belgic Confession Article 30 is, "By these means everything will be carried on in the Church with good order and decency, when faithful men [emphasis added] are chosen, according to the rule prescribed by St. Paul in his epistle to Timothy." I Timothy 3:1 and Titus 1:5 are cited as proof texts. 2 The Constitution of NAPARC states in Article II, the "BASIS OF THE COUNCIL. Confessing Jesus Christ as only Savior and Sovereign Lord over all life, we affirm the basis of the fellowship of Presbyterian and Reformed Churches to be full commitment to the Bible in its entirety as the Word of God written, without error in all its parts and to its teachings as set forth in the Heidelberg Catechism, the Belgic Confession, the Canons of Dort, the Westminster Confession of Faith, and the Westminster Larger and Shorter Catechisms. That the adopted basis of fellowship be regarded as warrant for the establishment of a formal relationship in the nature of a council, that is, a fellowship that enables the constituent churches to advise, counsel, and cooperate in various matters with one another and hold out before each other the desirability and need for organic union of Churches that are of like faith and practice." 3 A survey conducted by the General Synod of the CRC indicated that only 15% of the churches have female elders and 2% have female ministers; 37% of the classes have declared the word "male" inoperative in Article 3-a of the CRC Church Order. 514

### ATTACHMENT A

National Association of Evangelicals (Reprinted from PCANews.com)

The National Association of Evangelicals (NAE) held its annual convention in Dallas on March 5-7, 2001. The Presbyterian Church in America, which is a member of the NAE, was represented by TE Irfon Hughes, Chairman of the PCA Interchurch Relations Committee (IRC), TE Bruce Howes, a member of the IRC, and TE Roy Taylor, Stated Clerk of the PCA.

One of the issues debated at the meeting was qualifications for NAE membership. At its meeting last year, the NAE changed its membership rules to allow denominations who were members of the National Council of Churches (NCC) to be members of NAE as well. This change was made at the request of the Reformed Church in America, a member of the NCC.

The 28th General Assembly of the PCA (2000) expressed its concern over this rule change and instructed the IRC to raise this matter with the NAE leadership. This past fall the IRC met with representatives of NAE to discuss the PCA's concerns.

Another Christian organization, the National Religious Broadcasters, had already voted, 80-0 on Feb. 9, to formally end its relationship with the NAE because of this rule change. The conservative Christian broadcasters group had been affiliated with the NAE since 1944.

At the meeting of the NAE Board of Directors on March 5, Stated Clerk Taylor formally requested that the NAE rescind the membership rule change and return to its original policy. That original policy stated that denominations may be members of either the NAE or the NCC, but not both simultaneously.

Dr. Taylor offered five reasons for the motion to rescind:

1. Allowing dual membership in the NAE and the NCC is contrary to the original purpose for the founding of the NAE. The NAE was founded as an evangelical alternative to the theologically diverse Federal Council of Churches/NCC on the theological left and the fundamentalist American Council of Churches on the theological right.

2. Allowing dual membership is insensitive to the suffering some NAE-related evangelicals endured in their former connections with NCC-related denominations. For example, many of these ministers were denied opportunities

516

<a id="ga29-p519"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=519 printed_page=517 -->

for pastoral ministry and churches lost their buildings because of their evangelical commitments.

3. Allowing dual membership raises a question of maintaining doctrinal integrity. A number of NCC-related denominations use orthodox creeds in worship (e.g., the Apostles' Creed and the Nicene Creed) and have historic confessions of faith that are evangelical, yet ministers and church officers are not consistently required to adhere faithfully to and minister in accordance with these creeds and confessions. If doctrinal laxity is allowed regarding the historic creeds and confessions of the Church, could the NAE reasonably expect commitment to its doctrinal statement?

4. Allowing dual membership could prove to be a Phyrric victory. The NAE may gain some members of NCC denominations, but lose some denominations and organizations concerned about the membership rule change. The National Religious Broadcasters' recent action to withdraw its membership from NAE was cited as an example.

5. Allowing dual membership sends the wrong signal to our post-modern culture in which truth is regarded as relative. The NAE needs to take care that it not unwittingly communicate to NCC-related denominations that the bedrock truths of evangelicalism are negotiable.

After extended discussion, the motion was referred to the Bylaws Committee to study and report to next year's convention. Later in the day, the Board of Directors approved a Sense-of-the-Association resolution. This resolution recognized that the changes in membership requirements "have caused some concern and misunderstanding." It also indicated that the Bylaws would not allow the rescinding of last year's action at the present meeting.

The resolution also stated that, "We affirm that the NAE holds as firmly as ever to our sixty-year-old Statement of Faith that has defined our evangelical movement from its founding." It also affirmed "our desire to define evangelicalism by inclusion and affirmation rather than by exclusion."

The resolution concluded, "We affirm that our purpose in all matters related to the identity of the NAE is to advance the cause of Christ and to position the NAE to speak effectively as a voice for all Christians who will embrace our historic Christian faith expressed in our Statement of Faith."

### ATTACHMENT B

World Fellowship Of Reformed Churches Has "Joining and Receiving" with the International Reformed Fellowship to Become The World Reformed Fellowship (Reprinted from PCANews.com)

The World Fellowship of Reformed Churches (WFRC) and the International Reformed Fellowship (IRF) joined together October 24-26 at a meeting in Orlando, Florida, to create a worldwide fellowship among evangelical Presbyterian and Reformed Christians. The new name of the expanded organization is the World Reformed Fellowship (WRF).

The meeting took place on the campus of Reformed Theological Seminary and the Canterbury Retreat Center and included leaders from five continents and a number of countries which included: the USA, France, Scotland, Ghana, Nigeria, Argentina, Romania, Brazil, South Africa, Puerto Rico, Ecuador, the Philippines, Taiwan, Mexico, Peru, Honduras, Korea, Kenya, Uganda, Hungary, and Myanmar (Burma) attended the meeting.

PCA Stated Clerk Roy Taylor and Rev. Bruce Howes represented the PCA's Interchurch Relations Committee.

The World Reformed Fellowship's purpose is to encourage understanding and cooperation among evangelical Presbyterian and Reformed denominations and institutions, and links those having ministry resources with those possessing vision but few resources.

Also, the group promotes Reformed thinking and a Reformed world and life view, and fosters evangelism, missions and church planting, theological education and international communication.

WRF grew out of two fellowships established in the early 1990s. The World Fellowship of Reformed Churches (WFRC) was formed in 1992 by the Presbyterian Church in America, the National Presbyterian Church of Mexico, and the Presbyterian Church of Brazil and connected evangelical denominations from most of the countries of Latin America, plus churches from India, East Africa, and the United States.

The International Reformed Fellowship (IRF) was organized in 1994 to join evangelical Reformed leaders from across Asia. The IRF, which has held its meetings in Asia, included leaders from Korea, Indonesia, Taiwan, and Japan.

518

<a id="ga29-p521"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=521 printed_page=519 -->

Both organizations possessed similar visions to provide fellowship and opportunities for interaction that would encompass the entire world. In 1999, leaders of the WFRC and IRF discussed the possibility of the two fellowships coming together.

At the October meeting, the WFRC received the IRF into the WFRC by a "Joining and Receiving" to form a truly worldwide, conservative, evangelical Reformed fellowship and the name was changed to the World Reformed Fellowship (WRF).

The doctrinal standards for the newly-merged WRF were specified as the Scots Confession of 1560, the Gallican Confession, the Heidelberg Catechism, the Belgic Confession, the Canons of Dort, the Thirty-nine Articles of Religion, the Westminster Confession of Faith, the Westminster Catechisms, the Savoy Declaration, the Second Helvetic Confession, and the London Confession of 1689, as well as the Apostles Creed, the Nicene Creed, and the Chalcedonian Definition.

Membership eligibility was expanded to include not only denominations but also local churches, educational institutions, ministry agencies and individuals that would affirm the commitment to:

The full inspiration and inerrancy of Scripture The ancient universal creeds (Apostle's, Nicene, Chalcedon) Adherence to one or more of the historic expressions of the Reformed faith

On this basis virtually all Evangelical and Reformed branches of the Church could participate, that is, Presbyterian, Continental Reformed, Congregational, Reformed Baptist and Reformed Episcopal.

The WRF is a fellowship, not a council. A council issues position documents, certifies member church actions, and aims at eventual organic union of member churches.

A fellowship provides a context in which churches, ministries, and institutions may develop friendships with each other leading to more extensive and effective ministry, influencing each other toward greater consistency in biblical faith and witness.

The purposes of WRF are to:

Promote global evangelization on the basis of Reformed Theology Promote Reformed thinking and world-and-life view Inform and encourage churches and people who embrace the Reformed Faith Provide a network for communication and sharing of ministry Provide a forum for dialogue on current issues Be able to offer direction to the Evangelical and Reformed Communities Promote diaconal mercy ministries

519

<a id="ga29-p522"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=522 printed_page=520 -->

Reformed fellowships will be formed in Europe, Asia, Latin America, North America, and Africa as well as in specific countries.

A number of PCA people were involved in the meeting and several were elected to leadership positions.

Dr. K. Eric Perrin - Chairman Dr. Paul Gilchrist - Executive Secretary Dr. Luder Whitlock - Executive Committee member Dr. L. Roy Taylor - Governing Board member Dr. Woody Lajara - Treasurer

WRF has a 26-member Governing Board representing 18 nations.

One of WRF's goals of providing an information network will be enhanced by the development of a website. Face-to-face communication at the meeting produced one immediate discovery.

In an educational group meeting a Korean delegate remarked that several dozen ministers with PhD or ThD degrees were available in Korea but there were no seminary teaching positions open there now. A Mexican delegate responded, "Send us five professors. We need them right away."

It is hoped that WRF will be a vehicle for bringing opportunities, resources and people together throughout the worldwide Reformed family.

### ATTACHMENT C

### BYLAWS

### WORLD REFORMED FELLOWSHIP

Approved October 26, 2000 Corrected April 2001

### PREAMBLE

With gratitude to God, the International Reformed Fellowship joined the World Fellowship of Reformed Churches in October 2000, which then changed the name to the World Reformed Fellowship. Both fellowships were formed in the early Nineteen Nineties to seek to promote the Reformed faith as a witness to the world of the Sovereignty of God in the redemption of his people through the Lord Jesus Christ. This people of God, with diversified cultural and ethnic backgrounds, are one in Christ. God has enabled us to express the unity of the Church in the bonds of peace through

520

<a id="ga29-p523"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=523 printed_page=521 -->

cooperative agreements, having the same biblical, evangelical and missionary vision. Therefore, believing that these are but expressions of a well thought out Reformed perspective, we would invite other Reformed Churches, agencies, institutions and individuals to join with us under the following principles.

World Reformed Fellowship makes the distinction of being a fellowship, not a council. World Reformed Fellowship recognizes that barriers of distance, culture and language often make it difficult for a Church to develop and maintain binding ties with a Church or Churches of another country, which is essential to the conciliar model. A fellowship provides the context in which Churches, ministries and institutions may become acquainted with each other, and where their leaders may develop friendships and trusting relationships leading to closer, mutually beneficial cooperation. Members of a fellowship are not obligated formally to be responsible for one another's positions or actions, but in an atmosphere of free association, may lovingly influence each other toward greater consistency in Biblical faith and witness.

### ARTICLE 1. NAME

The name of this organization shall be World Reformed Fellowship, hereafter WRF.

### ARTICLE 2. AFFILIATION

WRF shall function in association with the World Evangelical Fellowship.

### ARTICLE 3. PURPOSE

The purpose of WRF shall be to promote understanding and cooperation in the following ways:

1. To promote Reformed thinking and a Reformed world and life view,

2. To inform and encourage Churches and people who embrace the Reformed Faith,

3. To provide a network for communication and the sharing of ministry resources,

4. To provide a forum for dialogue on current issues,

5. To be able to offer direction to the evangelical Reformed Community.

6. To promote evangelization in the Reformed Tradition.

7. To maintain, strengthen and defend the sound doctrines and biblicaltheological tenets that distinguish us as Reformed Christians.

WRF will promote its ministry with creativity, flexibility and efficiency. Our mission
goal should drive our structure and administration, as we adapt to the opportunity and
needs of the hour. We should proactively seek out individuals who can help WRF
attain its objectives.

521

<a id="ga29-p524"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=524 printed_page=522 -->

### ARTICLE 4. DOCTRINAL BASIS

1. We affirm the Scriptures of the Old and New Testaments as the authoritative, Godbreathed, and inerrant Word of God.

2. We stand in the mainstream of the historic Christian Faith in affirming the following catholic creeds of the Early Church: The Apostle's Creed, the Nicene Creed, and the Chalcedonian Definition.

3. More specifically, every voting member affirms one of the following historic expressions of the Reformed Faith: The Gallican Confession, The Scots Confession, The Belgic Confession, The Heidelberg Catechism, The Thirty-Nine Articles, The Second Helvetic Confession, The Canons of Dort, The Westminster Confession of Faith, The London Confession of 1689 and The Savoy Declaration.

### ARTICLE 5. MEMBERSHIP AND VOTING

1. The members of WRF shall include the following:

- **a.** Church denominations. Denominations may be represented in General Assembly by no more than the eligible votes which is as follows: Denominations with fewer than 10,000 members shall have one vote. Denominations of 10,001 to 50,000 members shall have two votes. Denominations of 50,001 to 250,000 members shall have three votes. Denominations of 250,001 to 1 million members shall have four votes. Those above 1 million members shall have five votes. However, all denominations may have two representatives, but limited to the votes as noted.

- **b.** Particular churches of non-member denominations may be represented at the General Assembly with one vote. Particular churches of member denominations may join WRF as non-voting members.

- **C.** Educational institutions and mission agencies which have no denominational affiliation may be represented and have one vote. Denominational institutions may join as non-voting members.

- **d.** Individuals who may not otherwise be a representative of any of the above organizations may join as members.

- **e.** Voting will be in two classes: (1) Denominations and (2) Single congregations, agencies and institutions, and individual members. Approval of both classes will be necessary for a matter to be adopted.

- **f.** Observers and non-voting members may participate but not have the privilege of voting.

522

<a id="ga29-p525"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=525 printed_page=523 -->

2. Prospective members shall make application to the Executive Committee. Applicants must meet the doctrinal criteria. The Executive Committee, after consulting with members in the local region, may vote to enroll the applicant as members.

3. Members shall be expected to contribute financially on an annual basis as determined by the Advisory Committee.

4. Members who no longer adhere to the purposes and doctrinal positions of WRF may be suspended from membership by the Executive Committee, but may be removed from membership only by action of the General Assembly.

### ARTICLE 6. GOVERNING BOARD

1. There shall be a Governing Board of twenty-six members of which eleven shall comprise the Executive Committee.

2. The officers of WRF shall be the Chairman, the first Vice Chairman, the second Vice Chairman, the first Secretary, the second Secretary and the Treasurer. In addition, these officers together with five members-at-large shall serve as the Executive Committee. The members-at-large shall be representatives from regional areas not otherwise represented by the officers.

3. The quorum for the Executive Committee shall be the majority of its members who participate in a duly called meeting. Stated meetings and special meetings with a thirty-day notice shall be considered duly called meetings.

4. The Executive Committee shall meet at least once every year.

5. In addition, the Executive Committee shall be responsible for the following functions: Programs, Planning, Budget and Finance, and Personnel. It shall also be responsible for processing applications for membership of prospective members. The Executive Committee shall establish subcommittees as needed to carry out the business of the WRF. The Executive Committee, on behalf of the General Assembly, may convene a major congress for Reformed thinking and theology. It shall be responsible for hiring staff to accomplish the administrative work of the organization.

6. The Executive Committee shall serve as a Nominating Committee for the WRF.

### ARTICLE 7. MEETINGS

1. A General Assembly of the WRF shall ordinarily meet at least once every four years. The General Assembly of WRF shall be called by the Executive

523

<a id="ga29-p526"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=526 printed_page=524 -->

Committee with a six-month written notice. A special called meeting of the General Assembly may be called with a three-month written notice. Since the World Evangelical Fellowship meets approximately every six years, the Executive Committee should plan to schedule the meetings of the WRF to coincide with that of WEF when possible.

2. The Governing Board shall meet at the time of the General Assembly of the WRF.

3. The matters to be voted on by the General Assembly will include the following:

- **a.** Policy issues,

- **b.** Budget and financial matters,

- **C.** Election of Officers and committee members,

- **d.** Membership applications,

- **e.** Bylaws,

- **f.** Meeting dates.

### ARTICLE 8. COMMITTEES

In addition to the Governing Board, the WRF may erect the following or similar committees to serve until replaced by the next General Assembly:

1. Contemporary Issues Committee: This committee shall seek to address critical and emerging issues facing Christianity both globally and regionally.

2. Missions Committee: This committee shall seek to address strategic, cultural and theological issues facing the Church in seeking to obey the Great Commission.

3. Education Committee: This committee shall seek to address problems and issues relating to all levels of education: local churches, elementary and secondary education, college and university education, as well as theological seminary education.

4. Communications Committee: This committee shall serve as public relations committee and publications for WRF.

5. Diaconal Ministries Committee: This committee shall address issues of mercy ministries such as orphanages, hospitals, medical clinics, etc.

6. Nominating Committee: The Executive Committee shall serve as the nominating committee of the WRF.

- **a.** The General Assembly shall elect Officers and members of the Advisory Committee from a slate provided by the Nominating Committee.

524

<a id="ga29-p527"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=527 printed_page=525 -->

Nominations may be made from the floor to run against any nomination made by the committee.

- **b.** The term for election shall be for four years or until replaced by the next General Assembly of WRF.

- **C.** Denominations may certify their representatives to the General Assembly of WRF. These representatives, if elected to serve as an officer or member-at-large shall serve to the end of the term of office.

- **d.** If an officer or committee member resigns or dies, or otherwise is not eligible for service, the Executive Committee may present a name in nomination on a ballot to the Advisory Committee by mail or e-mail for election to complete the term of service vacated.

### ARTICLE 9. BOARD OF TRUSTEES

The Executive Committee shall serve as the Board of Trustees of WRF.

### ARTICLE 10. REGIONAL FELLOWSHIPS

The WRF shall assist and oversee in the formation of national and regional fellowships to carry out the stated purposes of the WRF as seems good to the members of that respective area. The bylaws of the regional fellowships shall not be in conflict with the bylaws of WRF.

### ARTICLE 11. DISSOLUTION

In case of dissolution, the assets of WRF shall be distributed to some existing evangelical and Reformed fellowship which is a qualified 501(c)(3) organization [under the United States Tax Code].

### ARTICLE 12. AMENDMENT OR SUSPENSION OF BYLAWS

These Bylaws of the WRF may be amended or suspended only by a two-thirds vote of those members present and voting at a duly called meeting. Amendments may only be made when there has been at least a one-month prior notice to the membership.

Advancing the Gospel through Renewing the Church

The Spirit of the Sovereign Lord is on me, because the Lord has anointed me to preach good news to the poor. He has sent me to bind up the brokenhearted, to proclaim freedom for the captives and release from darkness for the prisoners, to proclaim the year of the Lord's favor and the day of vengeance of our God, to comfort all who mourn, and provide for those who grieve in Zion – to bestow on them a crown of beauty instead of ashes, the oil of gladness instead of mourning, and a garment of praise instead of a spirit of despair. They will be called oaks of righteousness, a planting of the Lord for the display of his splendor. Isaiah 61:1-3

North America today is experiencing a rapidly growing state of urgency or even emergency when it comes to our spiritual condition. This needs no documentation to those committed to biblical distinctives in the way we are in the PCA. Some recent illustrations:

Portland, Oregon, is a city in North America that has never been reached with the Gospel. One of the biggest "churches" in Portland, Oregon, is a congregation of several thousand of the New Age "faith." By God's grace, Charles Garland began a church plant in the city of Portland early in 2001, joining other churches in the suburban and greater Portland area pastored by Nathan Lewis, Jeff Doerr, Stephen Lewis, Jim Bordwine and Ted Shin. The population of the state of Oregon is estimated to be well under 5% evangelical. Clear across the continent, Portland, Maine, represents a similar population. While the light of the Gospel was once strong in most of New England, and while in New England as a whole the Gospel now shines much more dimly, the state of Maine has never been a Gospel stronghold. Estimates here also are that less than 5% of the population is evangelical.

Similarly, Exeter Presbyterian purchased a building that will serve 200 near the town square for $165,000. Such is the state of the evangelical church in New England – church buildings that once teemed with people now sit vacant.

ile many North Americans profess the Christian faith and attend worship each Lord's, the loss of influence of the Christian faith and moral values is apparent on every

Advancing the Gospel through Renewing the Church

1973, we believed that the Lord founded us to be faithful to the Scriptures, the rmed faith, and the Great Commission of Jesus Christ. Our assessment is that while advancement in the Gospel may be strong in comparison with others in our land,

527

even that strong advancement – at its current level – will accomplish little more than maintaining the PCA in its current strength.

If we are to wait upon the Lord for a greater work – for a renewal of His work through us – what are the essential elements of this renewal?

A renewed realization that the church is built by our Lord: "I will build my church," (Matthew 16:18), by the power of His Spirit – "But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes on you; and you will be my witnesses...to the ends of the earth."(Acts 1:8). We call upon the church to a renewal of expectation that the church will be built by God's power – that we will trust God for a bold advancement that exceeds the humanly predictable. Particularly as we venture into church planting in our cities with all of their great challenges, or in our smaller non-growing communities, with their sense that "everyone has already decided," we will see success in the advancement of the Gospel only by the power of God's Spirit.

A renewed commitment to prayer: We talk much of prayer in the PCA, but at least in our worship services and stated meetings, we devote little time to prayer. In Acts 6:4, the apostles recognized the necessity of commitment to prayer (mentioned first in the text) and to the ministry of the Word. We call upon the church to a renewed commitment to directed prayer beginning with our pastors, ruling elders and other key leaders that the Lord will build His church and that the PCA will grow substantially in reaching people with the Gospel.

A renewed commitment to unity in the church: We have our debates on issues of biblical direction, confessional standards and procedures, many of which are good and necessary. But when the votes are taken, we call upon the church to be subject to one another in the Lord, moving ahead together in a united effort to advance the Gospel throughout North America – for the sake of presenting a united testimony to the watching world and for the effective use of the abundant resources with which the Lord has blessed us. Whatever may divide us internally, we are called to a united effort in the Great Commission.

A renewed commitment to reaching the many cultures, ethnic/racial groups and socioeconomic groups in North America: The Gospel is for the nations. North America, as it always has been, is increasingly a land in which the nations seek refuge and a new beginning. Our calling is to reach these people with the Gospel – in all the variety of their needs, with all the challenges with which that calling presents us.

A renewed commitment to mercy ministries – preaching the Gospel in Word and showing the mercies of Christ in deed: While we live in a land of great affluence, we also live in a land with great socio-economic, emotional, educational and medical needs. The abundance of resources with which the Lord has blessed us represents a great opportunity to show the mercy of our Lord to those in need – and even to bring real solutions to the needs experienced by many.

528

<a id="ga29-p531"></a>
<!-- PAGE ga=29 pdf_page=531 printed_page=529 -->

A renewed commitment to the kind of stewardship of the Lord's resources that will give greater priority to the advancement of the Gospel: The PCA is a denomination greatly blessed by the Lord with an abundance of time, talent and treasure. For the church to advance, a greater stewardship of these resources is essential. Current Partnership Share giving to Mission to North America and the other committees and agencies of the PCA is sufficient for maintenance only. If the Gospel is to be advanced, members and churches of the PCA must devote greater resources to provide the necessary leadership and training for those who will lead in planting new churches and in the revitalization of our existing congregations. For an increase in giving of around $150,000 per year, GA/MNA could put in place the staff resources that could potentially double the number of church planters placed annually. Project support for church planters, for Church Vitality, for Chaplain Ministries and for Urban and Mercy Ministries (Thanksgiving Offering) must see major increases if the church is to advance.

A greater commitment to functional teamwork: With great joy, at GA/MNA we have witnessed a great increase in commitment to church planting and revitalization at the "grassroots" level over the past several years, among our churches and presbyteries. Without any question, PCA commitment to church planting and revitalization is at an all-time high. But the field is white for harvest and the laborers are few (Matthew 9:37). We are gratified that the team effort is growing, and we call upon the church to take steps for even greater commitment.

How shall we respond to these challenges?

Specifically, we propose the following:

1. That the General Assembly pause now for a 15 minute season of prayer for the advancement of the Gospel in North America – praying for the "renewed commitments" included above.

2. That the General Assembly call upon our presbyteries to set aside a significant portion of their meetings to pray for the advancement of Gospel through the revitalization of our existing churches and through the planting of new churches - throughout North America and throughout the world.

3. That the General Assembly encourage each congregation and presbytery of the General Assembly to seek with a greater zeal the Lord's calling for them in the advancement of the Gospel. I Corinthians 12:7 and Ephesians 4:7 promise that the Spirit of God has given each a gift for the common good and the building of the church. Just as there is a calling to every local church in reaching the local community and the world with the Gospel, so there is a calling for every congregation in church planting – reaching our "Judea and Samaria," as well as our "Jerusalem" and the "uttermost parts."

529

<a id="ga29-p532"></a>

This is a bold calling. It is bold because the needs are great. GA/MNA is grateful for the zeal for the Gospel that has marked the PCA from her inception. We are committed to the Scriptures, the reformed faith and the Great Commission. But let us call upon the Lord for a greater commitment to the Gospel and the renewal of the church. If these grow markedly, then North America will be reached for Christ – and North America will continue as a major sending church for missions throughout the nations.

The Lord will build His Church – and His promise to advance His Kingdom indeed will be renewed and fulfilled in each generation. The question before us is, will the PCA continue to be a part of that blessing? May we as a church be able to say with the Apostle Paul, I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith. Now there is in store for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous Judge, will award to me on that day--and not only to me, but also to all who have longed for His appearing. 2 Timothy 4:7-8

The church in the United States is not growing enough to keep pace with the population. Today a smaller percentage of the population go to church than in 1995 2, and almost 10% fewer than in 1991.3
